sources.news_title: Trump's war in Iran doomed Republicans in the midterms
Republican reckoning starts after midterm losses
sources.text:
Republican leaders are wrestling with what went wrong and how to move forward after the party’s devastating losses on Election Night. Some are even beginning to point fingers at President Donald Trump
“This was a huge message that the people of this country have sent to Republicans,” Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., said. “That we need to reset here and focus on what the American people have been asking for.”
Across the country, GOP leaders and elected officials are starting to admit that Trump’s agenda and leadership played a direct role in their party losing control of the House and Senate as well as several governorships.
After Vice President JD Vance posted Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war” against Iran, his fellow Ohio Republican, outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine, agreed.
“Because of the war, we certainly have higher gasoline prices,” DeWine said. “Because of higher gasoline prices, this is certainly one of the things that people were complaining about and were very upset about when they went to the polls.”
Some top Republicans are openly talking about what a post-Trump GOP should look like.
“I think the reality is there's nobody in our party, you know, that has that outsized persona and brand,” Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “And so how do you then go forward? I think it's got to be ideas-based.”
Republican Congresswoman Nicole Malliotakis of New York says the results show public pushback to the president’s most sweeping policies, like DOGE cuts and aggressive immigration enforcement tactics.
“Where it was too fast, too fast, too far for the American people, and what they want is really, I believe, a centrist government and hopefully we'll see that kind of reset coming,” Rep. Malliotakis said.
The word “reset” is being used by many frustrated Republicans.
“The American people are a forgiving people if you recognize where you made the mistakes and you explain what you're going to do differently, but if you double down on dumb, you're going to get the same result,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.
In a social media post, former Republican Sen. Mitt Romney blamed Trump without using his name, writing: “Bad policy, bad character make bad politics.”
President Trump said Wednesday he stands by his decision to go to war against Iran, and he has so far blamed GOP candidates for Tuesday’s losses instead of himself.

sources.news_title: Democrats Sweep 2026 Midterms as Republicans Blame Iran War
sources.text:
Democrats delivered a sweeping political upset in the 2026 midterm elections, capturing control of both chambers of Congress and flipping governorships and state legislative chambers in Republican strongholds. The results have triggered a reckoning within the GOP, where frustration over the Iran war, rising living costs, and American foreign policy is emerging as a central explanation for the party’s losses.
Texas delivered one of the election’s biggest surprises, with Democrat Gina Hinojosa winning the governorship in a state long dominated by Republicans. Her victory has already prompted political maneuvering among Texas lawmakers seeking to restrict the incoming governor’s emergency powers before she takes office.
Vice President JD Vance reportedly acknowledged the depth of voter dissatisfaction, pointing to polling that identified several reasons former Republican supporters abandoned the party. Among them were demands to end the Iran war, address inflation and household expenses, restore America-first priorities, and reconsider Washington’s relationship with Israel.
The backlash has also revived interest in Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, whose opposition to foreign military entanglements has resonated with voters questioning American involvement overseas. A “Massie Was Right About Everything” cap gained traction online, reflecting growing frustration with the party’s direction.
Meanwhile, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro is advancing an agenda centered on raising the minimum wage and strengthening reproductive rights protections, signaling how Democrats intend to capitalize on their electoral momentum.
The implications extend well beyond congressional leadership. With Democrats preparing to exercise greater oversight of the Trump administration, Republicans face mounting questions about whether their foreign policy commitments and economic messaging have alienated critical segments of their own electorate.
The 2026 midterms have fundamentally altered Washington’s political landscape, setting the stage for a contentious final two years of Trump’s presidency.

sources.news_title: ‘Skip the TED talk’: Iran trolls Vance over midterm defeat analysis
sources.text:
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf gestures while speaking during a meeting with Iranian and Iraqi business representatives in Baghdad on Aug. 20, 2026. | Hamed Malekpour/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
A senior Iranian official mocked JD Vance on Thursday for a lengthy social media post in which the U.S. vice president conceded that the American-Israeli war on Iran caused the Republican Party’s midterm election meltdown this week.
“Losing gambler energy, can’t walk away from the table. Boss is prepping the next war phase while America teeters on an Israel-First cliff. Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, shot back at Vance.
In his screed on X, published less than 24 hours after the Republicans suffered an election wipeout, Vance pointed to four things that needed to happen for voters to return to the party in future ballots.
Advertisement
“1) End the war. 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation. 3) Put America First. 4) Change our relationship to Israel,” Vance argued, in a missive that he personally drafted and which marked his first post-election attempt to distance himself from a war that U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended.
The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28 this year, decapitating much of its top leadership. But the Tehran regime retaliated by attacking U.S. targets in the Middle East and closing off the Strait of Hormuz — a vital maritime chokepoint for the supply of oil and gas — by threatening ships attempting to traverse the waterway.
The standoff drove up the price of fuels and fertilizer, which raised the cost-of-living in the U.S. and contributed to a brutal electoral environment for the Republicans, who suffered a generational defeat on Tuesday night.
While Vance stated that “the reason we lost is the war,” Trump has been insistent that the conflict is necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

sources.news_title: Trump blames GOP midterm defeat on the Iran war
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump conceded the Iran war was the defining issue that drove a Republican pummeling in midterm elections, though analysts were skeptical that any long-term truce was on the horizon. Oil prices fell for a fourth successive day, with the international benchmark dropping to nearly $93 a barrel on traders’ bets that Democrats’ sweeping victories reduced the risk of escalation between Washington and Tehran.
Yet Trump nevertheless insisted that “if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” and one leading expert said the oil selloff “has been somewhat baffling,” arguing that “the risk of escalation structurally grows post midterms, and the outcome (a Dem victory) has been the base case for months.”

sources.news_title: Column: Point: Americans rejected MAGA’s broken promises
sources.text:
By Ben Olinsky
InsideSources.com
Since August, President Trump told voters in places like Texas, Georgia, Ohio and South Carolina to vote as if he were on the ballot. They did.
Last night, their message was unequivocal: It’s time for change. States that haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 90 years voted to do so. Texas finally went blue. Voters turned out in huge numbers because their families are struggling to make ends meet, repudiate corruption and check a president who has gone too far. They cast their votes to hold Donald Trump and Republicans accountable for having total control of Washington but making their lives worse off.
Exit polls confirm voters were driven by the high costs of gas, food and utilities — blaming Trump’s tariffs, cuts to healthcare, and his baseless war with Iran. Trump’s broken promises to lower prices echoed against his focus on oil company profits and vanity projects.
Corruption also dominated voters’ concerns across party lines, as Americans see politicians getting richer while in office through insider trading and self-dealing.
It’s been impossible not to see taxpayer money go to Trump-linked firms, pardons for sale, and government funds held hostage for political reasons. Americans increasingly understand that corruption directly affects their pocketbooks.
Many voters were concerned about the immigration crackdown that has torn so many families apart and resulted in American citizens being shot dead by federal agents. The coalition that helped hand Trump a victory in 2024 came apart, with Latinos, Black men, and young voters shifting back toward Democrats. These voters helped fuel wins by Democrats in House races across the South, including in Texas and Florida, where Republicans redrew districts at Trump’s direction. Those efforts to subvert voters’ will through unprecedented gerrymandering largely backfired.
Americans also rejected billionaires’ attempts to buy elections via extreme spending. Elon Musk alone spent nearly half a billion dollars to drown out voters’ voices. Most of the $168 million he gave to the Senate Leadership Fund was used to boost Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. Musk didn’t succeed this time, but no billionaire or corporation should decide who represents us.
Ruby red Montana, with a long history of combating money in politics, led the way and voted overwhelmingly to pass a ballot initiative that removes corporations’ state-granted power to spend money in politics. Montana joins Hawaii, where a similar law passed nearly unanimously earlier this year — and together, this momentum paves the way for citizens in other states to do the same.
We also learned that Americans do, in fact, care about character and civility. Democratic candidates like Adam Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas won their bids to join the Senate by imbuing their campaigns with moral messages rooted in their faiths. Others like Abdul El-Sayed stood fast under vile attacks on their religion.
Americans rejected hate, sending a message that it’s time to rebuild the bonds between us. America has aspired to a radical idea that it doesn’t matter where you’ve come from or how you pray, only that you buy into a democratic government in which people hold the power, not a king.
This year’s elections stood as a testament to the thousands of brave state and local election workers who did their jobs with little fanfare. They upheld the law, even in the face of vile threats of prosecution from the Trump administration, ensuring our elections remain some of the best-run in the world. Every vote will be counted, winners will be certified and seated, and we will look back on a free and fair election.
For congressional Republicans, Tuesday night’s results should be evidence that Donald Trump is a losing proposition. His time shaping our political landscape is coming to an end. It was his policies, broken promises, crassness and incompetence that left Republicans routed. The party now has a choice to stand up to the president and work with Democrats to deliver on the policies Americans are demanding, or else drown with a sinking ship.
Democrats would be wise to remember that Trump was on the ballot this year; next time they will be judged. They must act aggressively to put ordinary families first, lower costs, hold the administration accountable, and root out corruption. Votes are rented, not owned, and elected leaders must show they’re truly willing to put Americans first.
Ben Olinsky is the senior vice president for structural reform and governance policy at the Center for American Progress Action Fund. He wrote this for InsideSources.com

sources.news_title: Midterm Losses Complicate Trump’s Options On Iran War
sources.text:
“President Trump’s loss of the House and Senate intersects with one of the most consequential decisions of his presidency: whether to resume intense combat operations against Iran, in a war that Mr. Trump’s vice president said Wednesday was the primary reason for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat,” the New York Times reports.
“The results across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections drove home how deeply unpopular the war was among Americans — and how much backlash Mr. Trump could face if he renewed major strikes against the country, which the United States and Israel jointly attacked in February.”
“The political blow deepened the challenge Mr. Trump faces in ending a war of his choosing.”

sources.news_title: Iran War: Trump Freezes as Israel and AIPAC Assess Damage, Vance Admits Iran War as Key to Epic Defeat; White House Clip Touting Trump Defiance Includes "Wolf of Wall Street" Fraudster
sources.text:
Trump is now under tremendous internal pressure over what to do in response to his epic humiliation by US voters, including critically many who had been in his MAGA base. It is unfortunately necessary to ponder the mental state of the fabulously erratic and impulsive president. Even with his habit of denying past statements and actions, he has a few consistent behaviors. One is his desperate need to dominate. Another is his off-the-charts dysfunctional responses to humiliation. A fresh one:
Thank you for your attention to this matter. https://t.co/Q1ZGYM7idV
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 4, 2026
And ZOMG, the White House compilation includes a Leonardo DiCaprio from the movie The Wolf of Wall Street, about the real life pump-and-dump-fraudster Jordan Belfor talking himself out of a settlement of criminal charges:
We aren’t going anywhere. We play for the United States of America. 🦅
Lock in, patriots. We’ve only just begun. https://t.co/3M5GMWf2iQ
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 5, 2026
See the pertinent segment from the movie:
The real Belfort eventually did knuckle under but still did time. From Wikipedia:
Jordan Ross Belfort is an American former stockbroker and businessman who pleaded guilty to fraud and related crimes in connection with stock-market manipulation and running a boiler room as part of a penny-stock scam in 1999.[3] Belfort spent 22 months in prison as part of an agreement under which, becoming an informant for the FBI and wearing a covert listening device (“wire”), he gave testimony against numerous partners and subordinates in his fraud scheme.
Have we been duly warned that despite the bravura, Trump will opt for an exit, even if at some personal cost, or is this just messaging of the day?
Trump’s loudly proclaimed plan to give Iran anther big thumping after the midterms was in no small measure acting out on those two core ego drivers. But not just Trump but even members of this team who should have known better seemed utterly surprised by the midterm wipeout, as opposed to having seen it as a possible outcome. Unless the Democrats completely blow it (which is not impossible), they are set to run the table for at least the next three election cycles, and perhaps longer.
The latter two will no doubt play a significant role in how Trump rationalizes his defeat and copes with his coming considerable loss of freedom of operation. As Judge Napolitano pointed out in a fresh talk with Glenn Diesen, when a party has less than 200 seats in the House, it cannnot get anything done. It is not just that it has too few votes to advance legislation. It is also that it has too few seats on committees to have much influence their debates.
On top of that, there is an open question as to how severe Republican infighting will become and how hard they will try to distance themselves from Trump. Trump’s interventions in the election made matters worse. All of his hand-picked candidates lost. And as John Kiriakou described long-form, Trump backed jerrymandering based on the misguided premise that the midterms would be a Republican romp. That resulted in larger losses in the House.
However, where Trump will retain the most freedom of action is in his warmaking. We don’t have clear signs of how Trump will respond to the considerable change in his standing, particularly the near-certainty of intense investigations into pretty much everyone in his his cabinet, as well as members of his inner circle like Steve Witkoff. Hegseth is set to be impeached. I wish the incompetent and arrogant Scott Bessent was also in the impeachment line of fire, but he does not seem to be a high priority, even with him escalating with Iran in the face of voter rejection and even a Trump reassessment:
As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us. We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air.
— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) November 4, 2026
Trump is begrudgingly admitting that the Iran war was central to the Republican rout, even though he is now blaming voters, contending it was still necessary to go after monstrous Iran, but voters were unduly attached to cheap gas and affordable food. In a public effort to herd Trump into a less self-destructive course of action, Vance admits that many MAGA voters turned on Trump over his betrayal:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was “composition”—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.
So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? “No,” he told me. “We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us.”
Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.
There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true.
But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.
Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:
1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel
Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)
In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.
The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.
If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.
But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.
I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.
— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 4, 2026
From the body of the tweet:
Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points…He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:
1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel
It is possible that Trump will throw Hegseth and other Iran hawks under the bus and attempt a retreat:
BREAKING: Donald Trump and his top White House aides are reportedly preparing to directly blame Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for the Republican midterm defeat, along with military commanders who pushed for war with Iran, per CNN and CBS News.
“Trump, always one to crowdsource an opinion, has asked allies about their thoughts on Hegseth’s performance of late,” sources told CNN.
CBS News also reports that Trump believes the election results would have been entirely different without the Iran war. Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and CENTCOM commander Gen. Brad Cooper are also reportedly facing scrutiny as Trump looks for someone to blame for the Republican midterm defeat.
— The Hormuz Report (@HormuzReport) November 4, 2026
Robert Barnes also says that the magnitude of the wipeout is leading Trump to reassess what to do next in Iran, as shown by the fact that the big beautiful bombing campaign is on hold for the moment:
However, Israel has agency. Admittedly, the Trump loss is a shock and leading to some serious worries. The landing page of the Times of Israel:
And Jerusalem Post:
But Trump may try to square that circle by throwing Netanyahu under the bus while quietly backing Israel. A fresh banner headline at Times of Israel shows that Netanyahu support is eroding:
On Judge Napolitano, Max Blumenthal discussed at length whether Trump can divorce or at least distance himself from Israel. He is doubtful:
From a lightly-edited machine transcript:
Donald Trump at the last minute before voters went to the polls attempted something that I think is highly significant. He actually said, I think this was on Fox, that he was going to end $4 billion in aid to Israel. Obviously, he’s referring to, you know, transforming the aid into military integration with Israel, but he thought that this would appeal would work with voters because even Donald Trump recognized that Israel had become a strategic liability, a poison pill. and he was attempting the same con job that he pulled when he went to Dearbornne, Michigan along with I think Tom Barrack and some of his uh you know Arab-American team to cut into Kamala Harris and Joe Biden’s base in a swing state where they had scarcely campaigned and promised an end to the Gaza genocide. That con worked momentarily because voters were so desperate to end the genocide in this heavily Arab-American district.
But it’s not working this time. It totally failed. Everyone has seen through it. So there’s there’s nothing that he can do to stop the bleeding.
The only rational course for him to take right now would be to completely isolate possibly in Belleview. I don’t know if that mental institution is still functional. Laura Loomer, who he praised as a great Republican strategist, Mark Levvin, Mark Dubowitz, who’s been advising Centcom chief Bradley Cooper and helped basically design the blueprints for this war through his Israel first think tank FDD and Mark Sisson at the Washington Post. Just isolate all of the figures that were Netanyahu’s proxies that helped get Trump into this war.
And I don’t know if he has the strength to do that. Also, Ben Shapiro, will Trump even will he do that? Will he clear the way for JD Vance? I don’t think he has it in him, and I don’t know if he can. He may be so compromised by how deeply integrated he and the White House and MAGA have become with Netanyahu’s Likud infrastructure that he can’t do the rational thing at this point.
But one thing is for sure, judge. It’s going to be much harder for Trump to do what we thought he was going to do, what Mark Levvin and Netanyahu were lobbying for several days ago, which is to launch a massive third allout assault on Iran.
On top of that, Blumenthal points out that Chuck Schumer and Hakim Jeffries are both AIPAC stooges, so the Democrat leadership is still loyal to the ethnosupremacist genocidal state. We’ll see if this is just posturing or if Schumer means it:
Chuck Schumer, who until today was the leader of the Democratic minority in the Senate, and is now the leader of the Democratic majority:
– Will you end the war with Iran? Will you use defense spending as leverage?
– Yes, we will end this war. Some Republicans are already on our side in this. The Founding Fathers of America also foresaw a way to punish presidents who start wars without consulting the American people, using the dollar as a tool.
— Sprinter Report (@SprinterReport) November 5, 2026
The Bloomberg landing page also shows that investors hanker for an Iran war wind-down:
But Iran has not taken its foot off the gas (or here, the oil). At the top of Aljazeera’s Iran War live page:
- Iran’s IRGC says two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after attempting to pass through an “unauthorised route”, while its electronic warfare units claim to have captured two US drones intact.
- Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has dismissed the idea that the outcome of the US midterm electionschanges anything, saying US hostility towards Iran will persist.
However, Robert Pape contends that Trump will escalate. Keep in mind that Pape’s scenarios have consistently failed to acknowledge US weapons depletion, strained logistics due to Middle East base destruction, and exhaustion of the troops. Nevertheless, from Trump’s Humiliation of a Historic Scale — What Comes Next in Iran (emphasis his):
IMPLICATION 1: THE LEGACY TRAP
Trump cares about his legacy as much as anything in politics. Tuesday told him the Iran war is how history will judge him. Presidents recover from midterm losses. They do not recover from losing a war. If Iran comes out of this war stronger than it went in, with Hormuz in its grip and its nuclear capacity intact, the defeat of Nov. 3 becomes a permanent verdict: the president who lost a war to Iran, and lost his party with it.His own advisers are already blaming the war, and MAGA’s “no more wars” wing is turning on the loyalists who backed it.
Fear for his legacy could push Trump toward a deal he can sell as a win. In an Escalation Trap, though, the fastest way to avoid looking like the loser is to escalate.
IMPLICATION 2: THE JANUARY CLOCK
Until Jan. 3, Trump controls the political timetable. After Jan. 3, Democrats do.Hakeem Jeffries has already promised to “bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country.” Trump answers with his veto: “Otherwise I’d just veto everything.” Vetoes can block bills. Hearings, subpoenas, war powers votes and the war’s budget stay with Congress.
That makes the next 60 days the last window in which Trump can make dramatic moves abroad on his own schedule.
THE BIG WINNER: IRAN
Trump is not the only one reading the results. Tehran is reading them too, and it sees a winner: itself. “Trump lost in war and politics, and we will inflict further defeats on him,” said Iran’s judiciary chief. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, posted: “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” Iranian officials say their core demands will not change.
Those demands add up to a path to regional hegemony. In my assessment, Iran will insist on keeping the near-term capacity to build a bomb, refusing widespread inspections, holding leverage over Hormuz, and in the end getting US forces out of the region. After Tuesday, Iran wants that more than ever, because it can see Trump weakened and his clock running.
That is why Trump cannot easily say yes to a deal with Iran. Anything short of the 2015 deal reads as losing the war, and a deal on Iran’s terms springs the legacy trap. Iran can also wait, because the January clock runs on Trump, not on Tehran. “Yes” on Iran’s terms looks like permanent historic defeat. So does no deal.
Pape ignores Robert Barnes’ warning, and keep in mind Barnes (with MAGA pollster Richard Baris) were alone in accurately predicting the scale of the Republican rout: that the only way for Trump to escape removal from office if the Democrats get 55 seats in the Senate (they are now at 54 with two still being counted) is to retreat bigly from Iran and Ukraine. Being impeached and removed is an even worse stain than losing a war. And Pape seems to presuppose that the US has a record of victories after World War II (and there Allied victory rested disproportionately on Russian sacrifice). The US success tally is thin: yes, the 1990-1991 Gulf War but the later Iraq was a battlefield win and a strategic failure.
Briefly on Ukraine: Many Democrat party grandees and some members of the PMC still hate Russia with the passion of a thousand burning suns, even though voters have loudly said they want more butter and fewer guns. As David in Friday Harbor reminded readers in comments on a post on the Ukraine war backstory (emphasis his):
First and foremost in the performative Putin-hate of the Democrats is their comprehensive and all-encompassing corruption. Not merely the obvious pay-offs to the Biden Crime Family during the then-Vice President’s “viceroyalty” in Kiev, but the Clintonite “Harvard Boys” who set out to loot the former USSR until Yeltsin pulled a fast one on them and appointed a cop, Putin, to rein-in the oligarchs who were bleeding Russia dry. The “Harvard Boys” could never forgive Putin for slowing down their gravy train. Donald Trump (still ostensibly a Democrat at the time) pulled himself out of bankruptcy laundering this money while the IRS and FBI looked the other way; a dispute over his practices caused the falling-out with Jeffrey Epstein.
Congress can constrain a bellicose president but they cannot initiate or escalate conflict. Admittedly, as several commentators have pointed out on Judge Napolitano shows, keying off the fact that John Kiriakou described how the CIA can and does fund itself from outside sources (from drug-running to handouts from interested parties), that the CIA has been undermining Trump’s occasional efforts to wind down the Ukraine conflict, so the CIA will carry on. But the European backing, already budget and weapons constrained, is producing a Trump-level voter revolt, albeit across a broader front. From former UK diplomat Ian Proud in The Iran war killed Trump’s Presidency: the Ukraine war will kill European mainstream governments:
Foreign policy must serve a country’s core interests, or it fails. Those interests are always the same.
- Is your border secure?
- Are your people safe?
- Is your country growing more prosperous?
Everything else is incidental. Values, feeling bad about Ukraine, in the final analysis, voters are uninterested.
Iran is thousands of miles from the United States. It does not threaten American territory. The idea that it poses an existential threat to ordinary Americans has never been credible. The war made Americans poorer. That is why it failed.
The same lesson applies in Europe. For nearly five years the mainstream parties have treated the war in Ukraine as a moral crusade that ordinary people must simply pay for. Most Europeans know little about Ukraine or Russia and care even less.
For a while governments managed consent with the daily carpet bombing of propaganda. That is now wearing thin.
Europeans do not feel safer because of the war. They feel poorer. Energy costs are high, industrial jobs are disappearing in Germany, debt is rising in Britain, and public services are strained in France.
When German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock said she did not care what her voters thought and would put Ukrainians first, she epitomised where Europe has gone badly wrong; it lost sight of its core strategic interests.
Values and being kind to Ukraine aren’t core strategic interests.
The globalists got away for it for a few years but voters have now noticed.
Support across Western Europe is shifting toward parties that prioritise domestic priorities and interests. Germany has seen cost-of-living protests. France has protests over schools and services while money continues to flow to Ukraine. Britain has just sent another £10 billion to Ukraine while debt interest approaches £109 billion a year. Poland’s government is already nervous about the next elections and Tusk’s government tried to orchestrate a constitutional coup….
The Ukraine war is a war of choice.
The longer it continues without clear benefit to ordinary citizens, the harder it becomes to justify….

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Gives Unexpected Answer After Vance Blames White House
sources.text:
President Donald Trump surprisingly backed Vice President JD Vance‘s blunt criticism of the administration’s own priorities after Republicans suffered sweeping midterm losses. Vance blamed the White House’s focus on the Iran war and other issues for driving 2024 Trump voters toward Democrats, and Trump’s response stunned observers.
Why the president agreed with criticism of his administration’s priorities
Speaking at a press conference at his ballroom construction site, Donald Trump was asked whether he agreed with JD Vance’s post. The president said he did, stating: “I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine; I thought it was good. We knew that; I knew that when I went in.”
Trump further added, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up… At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again because long-term. It’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” The president said he had spoken with Vance but did not elaborate.
Vance’s post declared that the GOP had lost even in reliably Republican areas due to a failure to deliver on campaign promises. He said 2024 Trump supporters largely abandoned the administration over the Iran war, cost of living, a lack of “America First” policies, and the U.S.’s relationship to Israel — policies on which the vice president holds starkly different views than Trump. Don Jr. amplified Vance’s post, replying: “Every word of this is ???.”
However, Trump’s early reaction to the midterm results differed sharply. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote about an hour after polls closed. Hours later, he blamed his hand-picked candidates: “They didn’t like the candidates in most cases. Just one of those things.”
Overall, the comments also sparked an on-air debate on Fox News, where Washington Post columnist Marc Thiessen called Vance’s remarks “disloyal to the president of the United States,” saying, “All I heard was, ‘We lost because of the Iran war.’ Why is his vice president saying something different?”
As such, the midterm aftermath has placed the Vance–Trump dynamic under scrutiny as Republicans weigh their path forward.

sources.news_title: 'The Primary Reason is Iran War': JD Vance on Republican Midterm Losses
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance stated that the Iran war was the primary reason Republicans lost control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats secured both the House and Senate, marking a significant setback for President Donald Trump’s administration. Vance’s remarks came as he sought to distance himself from the conflict, which began in February, and as discussions intensified regarding the party’s future direction and leadership.
According to The Hindu, Vance publicly declared, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” referencing Trump’s own acknowledgment of the conflict’s electoral impact. Vance emphasized the need for an honest assessment within the party, stating, “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
As reported by Hindustan Times, Vance’s comments followed weeks of internal debate within the White House regarding the war’s unpopularity. He had previously expressed skepticism about the conflict in private, despite publicly supporting the administration’s position. The article noted, “Vance blaming Trump’s war for the catastrophic results of the midterm election is a rare moment of distance between himself and the president, to whom he owes his political career.”
As highlighted by BBC, Vance’s statement was unprecedented for a sitting vice president, marking a sharp public break with the president on a major foreign policy issue. Vance outlined a four-point strategy for Republicans to regain voter support: ending the war, focusing on cost of living and inflation, prioritizing “America First” policies, and changing the US relationship with Israel. The report observed, “It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it’s hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.”
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance stated in his post.
Trump responded to Vance’s remarks by partially agreeing with the assessment as coverage revealed. Trump said, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” but maintained that military action against Iran was necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. He added, “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again.”
Exit poll data supported Vance’s claims, with 34% of voters citing the Iran war as a crucial factor in their decision and 62% believing the US made the wrong decision by using military force against Iran according to polling data. Other significant concerns included the cost of living and government corruption, but the war remained a central issue for many voters.
Vance’s critique also included the observation that many 2024 Trump voters switched to Democrats in 2026, a trend he attributed to dissatisfaction with the war and related policies as analysis showed. Trump, while defending the necessity of the Iran campaign, acknowledged that the party “just couldn’t transfer that love” from his rallies to other Republican candidates.
“We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” Trump said, reflecting on the party’s inability to convert his personal popularity into broader electoral success.
Vance’s post-election remarks have intensified debate within the Republican Party about its foreign policy direction and electoral strategy as reporting indicated. Some party members, including Representatives Thomas Massie and Marjorie Taylor Greene, echoed Vance’s concerns, arguing that the party failed to deliver on its promises and underestimated voter opposition to the war.
Trump reiterated that he would not have changed his decision regarding Iran, emphasizing national security imperatives over electoral considerations as details emerged. He maintained that preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons justified the administration’s actions, despite the political cost.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump stated, underscoring his commitment to the policy despite electoral setbacks.
Note: This article is produced using AI-assisted tools and is based on publicly available information. It has been reviewed by The Quint's editorial team before publishing.

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the Iran war has been worth it despite acknowledging its role in losses in US midterm elections in which his Republican party lost control of Congress.
"The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," he told reporters.
Trump said he was okay with Vice President JD Vance's social media post earlier on Wednesday in which Vance referred to deep electoral losses and said "the reason we lost is the war."
"I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," Trump said.
Iran has yet to respond publicly to Trump's latest remarks.
Meanwhile, the US Treasury on Wednesday issued fresh sanctions against companies and individuals based in India and Türkiye for their ties to Iran, warning that it would continue to go after anyone who supported Iran.
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut off Iran's ability to sell oil to fund the war with the United States.
On the military front, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that it had shot down a US MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island, according to the Fars News Agency.
"With the destruction of this drone, the number of US MQ-1 drones destroyed has reached 15," the IRGC said, describing the tally as evidence of the "continued interception and confrontation by the country's air defense against American drones in our airspace."
Besides, Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Wednesday warned that neither partisan changes in the United States nor concessions to Washington would end US hostility toward the Iranian nation.

He said the only way to achieve a state of "absolute deterrence" is to continue to make Iran stronger, noting that "on this path, (national) solidarity and unity, and social cohesion serve as the fundamental pillars of success."
The supreme leader said that should the "acts of aggression" be repeated, Iran's fight will expand to encompass a much broader scope.

(End of the American Dream)—The war with Iran is not over. There isn’t going to be peace in the Middle East. In fact, the most apocalyptic chapters of the Great Middle East War are still ahead of us. President Trump continues to stand behind the war with Iran.

President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he remains “totally convinced” that launching the Iran war was the right decision.
Trump doubled down on the importance of the Iran war in multiple interviews with Fox News and Politico on Tuesday night.

Then on Wednesday, he told reporters that if he could go back to before the war, he would do it all over again…
“Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” he told reporters at an event related to the ballroom’s construction. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again. Because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Mr. Trump was responding to a question about Vice President JD Vance blaming the losses on the war in a post on X earlier in the day.
“But I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” Trump continued. “We’ve totally broken their military. The navy’s gone. Their air force is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone.”
But looking forward, it does appear that Trump’s thinking may have changed a bit.
When asked about what is coming next, he admitted that there are no “immediate” plans to bomb Iran again…
President Donald Trump discussed the possibility of renewed military action against Iran, saying he remains open to a binding agreement preventing Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons but warning he could “finish the job” if negotiations fail.
Trump said there are no “immediate” plans to carry out fresh strikes against Tehran.
This could be interpreted as good news by those that are hoping for a quick end to the war in the Middle East.
However, military transports continue to carry heavy equipment to the region, and a third U.S. aircraft carrier is still on the way…
Some time about the middle of this month the USS Theodore Roosevelt will be in position.
Will that be the moment when the U.S. and Israel start conducting airstrikes?
The number one target that the U.S. and Israel would like to take out is the nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
The problem is that it is hundreds of feet underground…
Some estimates put the heart of Pickaxe Mountain as far as 100 meters (nearly 330 feet) underground—meaning even the most destructive non-nuclear U.S. bombs, such as the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, or “bunker busters,” would be hard-pressed to destroy it.
I agree with that assessment.
I do not believe that conventional weapons would be able to get the job done.
But using nuclear weapons would be absolutely insane.
Unfortunately, that is precisely what some are suggesting that we should do.
A B61-13 tactical gravity bomb would likely get the job done, but it also has “around 24 times the yield of the bomb dropped on Hiroshima”…
Instead, it is more likely to use a tactical nuclear weapon, although any form of nuclear strike remains very unlikely. The U.S. has an estimated 200 B61 gravity bombs, half of which are deployed in bases across Europe. They can be launched from fighter jets like the F-35A.
The U.S. is rolling out the upgraded B61-13, which is designed to blast apart well-defended targets. Only strategic bombers can carry the B61-13, which has a yield of up to 360 kilotons—around 24 times the yield of the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
Hypothetically, the U.S. could drop several GBU-57s on Pickaxe Mountain, opening up the way for a follow-up tactical nuclear strike with a B61 gravity bomb.
If we use a tactical nuclear weapon on Pickaxe Mountain, the entire world will be absolutely horrified.
And it would also give Iran a perfect excuse to use everything in their arsenal against Israel.
If the Iranians destroyed the nuclear facility at Dimona or used unconventional weapons against Israel, the Israelis would likely respond by using nuclear weapons against Iran.
We are dangerously close to a point of no return.
If there is any sort of attack on Iran at all, the Iranians are threatening to use “new conventional weapons technology”…
“If America or the Zionists take any action, Iran will respond differently than before, using a new doctrine and new conventional weapons technology,” said Hamidreza Moghaddamfar, an adviser to the IRGC’s commander in chief.
Should Arab states such as the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain allow their territory to be used for attacks, he added, “Iran’s strikes will go further” than the US bases. He said the assassination of Iranian officials or commanders would draw “surprising responses”.
Iran, Mr Moghaddamfar said, had “set aside the principles of symmetry and proportionality a long time ago”, and would retaliate “beyond any geographical limits”.
In addition, the IRGC is warning that they now have missiles that can “target areas beyond the Middle East”…
Ziaeddin Aghajanpour, head of the ministry’s political-ideological organization, made the remarks at a government event in Karaj, near Tehran.
“Our scientists, experts and intellectuals in the defense ministry and armed forces have produced surprise weapons, and the missiles we have developed can target areas beyond the Middle East,” he said. “We also warned the Americans that if they do not stop their hostile actions, we will target all US interests in the region, and you saw that we did so.”
One wrong move could spark all-out war.
Chuck Schumer is promising that Congress is going to end the conflict with Iran…
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer vowed that Congress will end the war in Iran once the newly-elected Democrats take office in January.
Schumer made the statement during a press conference on Wednesday morning.
“Look, we are gonna end the war,” Schumer told reporters. “We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the founding fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people.”
But there is only so much that he can do, and he knows it.
An apocalyptic showdown is looming, and the clock is ticking.
On Wednesday, there were reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was about to hold an “urgent security meeting”…
Netanyahu wanted to attack Iran in October, but Trump was able to persuade him to wait until after the elections.
Now the elections are behind us, and Netanyahu appears to be quite eager to take action.
In anticipation of what could be coming, a number of municipalities in northern Israel are already opening up their bomb shelters…
Several municipalities in northern Israel have opened public bomb shelters as concerns grow over a possible resumption of hostilities with Iran, while the United States is reportedly reinforcing air defence capabilities in the region.
Kiryat Shmona and Safed have opened public shelters, while authorities in Karmiel have made shelters across the city accessible to residents, according to Israeli media reports.
Karmiel Mayor Moshe Kuninski said the decision was taken as a precautionary measure amid the evolving security situation. He urged residents to continue their normal routines while adhering to instructions issued by Israel’s Home Front Command.
I don’t think that a major campaign of airstrikes in Iran is imminent.
But just a little while ago Israel was conducting airstrikes in southern Lebanon.
From this point forward, any moments of peace will just be temporary.
The Great Middle East War has already been raging for more than 3 years, and there is no end in sight.
Israel and Iran are ultimately headed for a final showdown, and the level of violence that we will witness will shock the entire globe.

sources.news_title: After midterm loss, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP debacle – WTOP News
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
And in an Oval Office exchange with reporters Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren’t weighing on his calculations.
“If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in,” Trump said.
The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.
Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated
While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out.
The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.
The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.
The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.
“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”
Trump has at least a few options, analysts say
Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.
Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.
Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran’s nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.
Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.
But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.
Iran, of course, also has a say, analysts note.
“Once you start a fistfight, you can stop throwing punches. That doesn’t mean the other combatant will stop throwing punches,” said Bradley Bowman, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “We can try to end the war, but what do we do if the Islamic Republic of Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz?”
Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next
Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.
Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he’d have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.
A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP’s candidates for the big loss.
“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”
Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump’s decision once he made it.
Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue
Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets on Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.
“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he’d approach Iran exactly as he has.
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different,” the president said.
___
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Collin Binkley in Washington, Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, and Kathleen Foody in Chicago contributed reporting.

Iran wary of new U.S. attacks despite Trump noting war's role in election losses

And it used that closure to make gas more expensive, hoping to anger President Trump's core supporters and help Republicans lose the midterms. Here's NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi.
HADEEL AL-SHALCHI, BYLINE: On Wednesday, President Trump was asked if the war with Iran cost his party the elections. He said...
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term.
AL-SHALCHI: Since the outbreak of the war with Iran in late February, U.S. retail gasoline prices have surged by nearly 44%.
TRITA PARSI: I think reality is that it's not the Democrats that won this election. It's Iran.
AL-SHALCHI: That's Trita Parsi. He's an Iran expert with the Washington-based think tank the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. He says it wasn't really a Democratic vision that drove voters to the polls on Tuesday.
PARSI: But rather absolute fury with the cost-of-living situation, which is directly driven by Trump's decision to go to war, which in and of itself was a result of an Iranian strategy to create an energy crisis for the precise reason of defeating Trump and the Republican Party. That has now been completed.
AL-SHALCHI: In a statement on Wednesday, the Iranian speaker of parliament, Mohammad Ghalibaf, also a top negotiator in peace talks, said that Americans said no to the war with their vote and that Iranians endorse this message, but that if the U.S. returns to war, it will face an Iranian, quote, "nightmare." But Parsi says Iran understands that the proponents of war see the next two months before the next Congress is sworn in as the last chance for an escalation.
PARSI: The combination of that and Trump's own anger over this humiliation may very well drive him in the direction of doing something very reckless.
AL-SHALCHI: Parsi says the Iranians were capable of doing something that was never achieved in previous U.S. wars.

sources.news_title: Trump Says He Alone Will Decide When Iran Conflict Ends, Defends Decision Despite Midterm Losses
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the ongoing conflict with Iran will end when he decides it should, defending his handling of the war during his first press conference with the White House press corps since Democrats won sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Asked when he expects the war to end, Trump spoke to reporters at the site of the White House ballroom construction project, where workers had installed the last piece of structural steel earlier in the day.
“Whenever I want it to, but it’s gotta be done right, and we’re never going to let them have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
The president also agreed with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that the war contributed to Republicans’ midterm losses. “Well, I think it’s largely true, because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term, and… probably it’s true,” Trump said when asked about Vance’s remarks.
He added that he would make the same decision again regardless of the political cost. “But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again, because long term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
When a reporter asked whether losing control of the Senate was “worth it” given the war, Trump responded, “I do,” and added, “You have no choice.”
“I mean, I thought the oil would go up a lot more, and I did it on that basis. You have no choice. You have to do it. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or everything that you see here someday might not exist,” Trump said.
Voter concerns about both gas prices and the Iran war appear to have shaped Tuesday’s results. A CNN exit poll found that 87 percent of voters surveyed said they were concerned about the cost of gas, with 59 percent describing themselves as “very concerned” and 28 percent as “somewhat concerned.”
The same poll found that 34 percent of voters said the war in Iran was a “crucial” factor in their vote, while another 40 percent called it “a major factor,” suggesting the conflict weighed heavily on the electorate’s decisions even as Trump signaled no change in course.

sources.news_title: McClintock cites Iran war, tariffs in GOP losses
sources.text:
U.S. Rep. Tom McClintock won another term representing California's 5th Congressional District in Tuesday’s election, though he cited the war in Iran and tariffs as factors in Republican losses across the country and called on Congress to reclaim powers it has given up to the president.
McClintock, R-Elk Grove, received 102,646 votes, or 56.2%, compared to 79,957 votes, or 43.8%, for Democratic challenger Michael Masuda, according to unofficial results released Wednesday morning with all 399 precincts reporting districtwide.
In Tuolumne County, McClintock also led Masuda with 10,325 votes, or 56.07%, to Masuda's 8,090 votes, or 43.93%, according to the county's latest election-night results released after 4 p.m. Wednesday.
Masuda conceded the race Wednesday and thanked his supporters, while McClintock released a statement addressing his reelection and the national results that saw Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress.
"I want to begin by thanking the people of the Sierra Nevada and Central Valley for their support in a very difficult election cycle," McClintock stated. "Their continuing confidence is the greatest honor I could hope for, and I will do everything I can to be worthy of it."
McClintock, who has served in Congress since 2009 and will begin his 10th consecutive two-year term in January, also acknowledged economic concerns that he believes contributed to the Republican Party's sweeping losses.
"In the meantime, the American people spoke loudly and clearly that they are hurting and angry about the economic impact of the war in Iran and the tariffs on their quality of life," he stated.
McClintock called the election a "strong wake-up call" for Republicans to “return to our constitutional and free-market moorings.” He also stated Congress has given up too much authority to the president over declaring war and imposing tariffs.
"Congress has surrendered too much of these responsibilities to the executive branch and it is time for Republicans and Democrats alike to restore the constitutional balance," he stated.
McClintock compared Tuesday's results to Republican losses during President Ronald Reagan's first term, though he stated that he remains confident that tax cuts and reduced regulations under Trump will improve the economy and help the GOP recover politically.
The statement concluded with McClintock criticizing what he described as the “growing influence of avowed socialists within the Democratic Party.”
Masuda, an electrical engineer and former State Department foreign affairs officer who lives in Riverbank and grew up in Amador County, acknowledged his defeat in a statement released Wednesday morning.
"This is not the result we worked for, and I know how much it means to everyone who gave their time and energy to this campaign," Masuda stated. "I'm disappointed, but I'm deeply grateful to the people who believed in me and in what we could accomplish together."
Masuda campaigned on lowering costs, improving access to health care and addressing the needs of rural communities in the district, which stretches from the Sierra Nevada into the Central Valley and includes all of Tuolumne and Calaveras counties.
Masuda thanked his campaign team, supporters and family, and said he hopes their work will continue beyond the election.
"Together, we've laid a foundation that future campaigns can build on: relationships, trust and a network of people determined to make their communities heard," Masuda stated. "That work will continue beyond this election."

sources.news_title: Vance blames Iran war for Republicans’ midterms defeat. Trump says he would ‘do it again’ - Regional Media News
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the Trump administration’s ongoing war with Iran was to blame for Republicans’ massive losses in Tuesday’s midterm election, during which Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress.
But President Donald Trump, asked about Vance’s comments, remained committed to the ongoing military action despite “largely” agreeing with Vance about the impact of the war on the election.
The vice president wrote in a lengthy social media post that “the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.”
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said of the Trump administration’s ongoing conflict with Iran. “The president himself said so last night.”
Vance said he spoke with pollsters who told him that many people who voted for Trump in 2024 switched to the Democrats in this election because they were “angry.”
The ABC News Voter Poll found about 4 in 10 House voters nationally said they were angry about the way things were going in the country today and a similar share were dissatisfied.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance wrote.
The vice president in the past has publicly been supportive of the war and slammed the president’s critics over the issue.
Trump often suggested on the campaign trail that the war, and inflated gas prices, were “a small price to pay” to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon.
Asked about Vance’s comments during an event at the White House on Wednesday, Trump called them “largely true,” however he defended his decision to attack Iran, which he has done in the past.
“If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer,” Trump told reporters. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump said he knew Vance’s view of the war from the beginning.
“I know how he feels about it. I think it was — I think it was fine. Yeah, I thought it was good,” Trump said of Vance’s social media post. “I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Asked if he felt the war was worth it, Trump said he did.
“I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice,” he said, later adding, “I can tell you that, as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing differently.”
ABC News’ Voter Poll of House voters found that voters nationally were more focused on other factors, including the cost of living, than the Iran war.
Nationally, 34% of U.S. House voters said that the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote, while 49% said the same about the cost of living and 55% said government corruption was crucial to their vote.
Although the Iran war has led to rising gas prices, voters have said that their concerns over the cost of living weren’t just limited to their receipts at the pump.
The Voter Poll found 59% of House voters nationally saying they were “very concerned” about the cost of healthcare.
About 6 in 10 U.S. House voters said that the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare and 55% said the Trump administration’s policies have made their healthcare costs worse. Just 10% said the Trump administration has improved their healthcare costs, according to the Voter Poll.
Trump’s tariffs have also been costing the typical American household almost $1,000 a year.
Vance said in his X post that an unidentified pollster told him that their “economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch.”
Vance argued that Republicans were not failed by turnout among Trump 2024 voters, saying they “showed up,” but that those Americans, according to a pollster, were “pissed and planning to vote for the other guys.”
He also claimed of Republican turnout that “in no state was it catastrophic.”
“The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” the vice president said.
-ABC News’ Elizabeth Schulze contributed to this report.

Trump And Vance Are Right. The Iran War And High Oil Prices Cost GOP The Midterms.
sources.text:
“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up… but at the same time if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long-term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
That was President Donald Trump’s reaction to Congressional Republicans’ crushing losses in the 2026 midterm elections that could see Democrats reach 56 seats in the Senate and 260 seats in the House, according to a Polymarket projection.
He was agreeing with Vice President J.D. Vance who wrote in an X post: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
Quite simply, before the U.S. and Israel launched their renewed attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil prices were very low, hitting $56 a barrel on Jan. 7, and after the war escalated hit $114 a barrel by April 7. As of this writing, it is still trading at $88 a barrel.
Similarly, gasoline prices were before the war was $2.70 a gallon and now it’s about $4.15 a gallon. It’s worth noting that before the post-Covid inflation it was $2.21 a gallon in Jan. 2021, skyrocketing in 2021 and 2022 especially following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Before we the war escalated in February, the American people were on track to finally break even on post-Covid inflation (which began with the checks in 2020 let’s be honest) by the end of 2026, according to an Americans for Limited Government Foundation analysis of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics inflation and average weekly earnings data.
Now it’s out to 2028 and counting.
Going to Iran absolutely, unquestionably prolonged the inflation.
It was the Iran war. Even the President and Vice President say so. Iran definitely had it coming. But high oil prices are nearly undefeated at the polls: 1976, 1980, 1992, 2008 and 2024 so there were obvious economic and political consequences.
Complicating matters, Trump was already upside down on approval by March.
Wars are not so great either. There hasn’t been a popular war ever. 1942, 1950, 1966, 1990 and 2006 were all political midterm losses for the White House incumbent party.
Coming into the year, the President absolutely knew what the score was, warning the House Republican Member Retreat on January 6 that Congressional losses were imminent: “[T]hey say that when you win the presidency, you lose the midterm.” He was right.
The reason is because coming into the year, the fact is President Trump was already upside down on approval, with Gallup reporting it at just 36 percent at the beginning of the year.
That usually means greater losses in Congressional midterms, according to an Americans for Limited Government analysis of midterm elections dating back to 1906.
Lower approval also shows greater losses in the dataset. In 1946, Harry Truman was registering just 33 percent approval as Democrats lost 54 House seats. In 1966, Lyndon Johnson had 44 percent approval and lost 47 House seats. In 1974, Gerald Ford only had 47 percent approval and Republicans lost 48 House seats amid the fallout from Watergate. In 1994, Bill Clinton had 46 percent approval and Democrats lost 54 House Seats. In 2006, George W. Bush had 38 percent approval and Republicans lost 30 House seats. In 2010, Barack Obama had a 45 percent approval rating, and Democrats lost 63 House Seats, and in 2014, he had a 40 percent approval rating and lost another 13 seats. And in 2018, Donald Trump had a 40 percent approval rating and Republicans lost 42 House seats.
The approval or lack thereof was absolutely a red flag headed into 2026 and the midterms — let alone escalating the half-a-century war with Iran, leading to its predictable rise in oil and gas prices that ultimately exacted a political toll.
Republicans weren’t demoralized they were complacent. Another contributing factor were Republican “influencers” spending the last two months of the campaign telling everyone the polls forecasting imminent catastrophe were wrong. Well, they were wrong. They understated Democrats who trounced Republicans in the worst House and Senate losses in a generation.
Political parties ignore the economy and inflation at their own peril. Every election is a referendum on the incumbents. Every. One. Of. Them.
Robert Romano is the Executive Director of Americans for Limited Government Foundation.
