WASHINGTON (AP) — As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.
For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.
In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.
And in an Oval Office exchange with reporters Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren’t weighing on his calculations.
“If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in,” Trump said.
The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.
Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.
Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated
While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out.
The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.
The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.
The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.
“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”
Trump has at least a few options, analysts say
Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.
Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.
Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran’s nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.
Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.
But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.
Iran, of course, also has a say, analysts note.
“Once you start a fistfight, you can stop throwing punches. That doesn’t mean the other combatant will stop throwing punches,” said Bradley Bowman, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “We can try to end the war, but what do we do if the Islamic Republic of Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz?”
Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next
Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.
Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he’d have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.
A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP’s candidates for the big loss.
“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”
Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump’s decision once he made it.
Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue
Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets on Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.
“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he’d approach Iran exactly as he has.
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different,” the president said.
___
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Collin Binkley in Washington, Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, and Kathleen Foody in Chicago contributed reporting.

sources.text:
By Rachel Roberts 
Contributing Writer 
President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the Iran war played a role in his Republican Party’s resounding defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
“I think a part of it was Iran,” Trump told Fox News.
“Iran was a piece of it,” he said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal.
Trump stood by his decision for the United States to join Israel in attacking Iran, despite the heavy election losses that are likely to make the remaining two years of his second term a very difficult time for the president to pass new legislation.
“I did the right thing,” he told The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday. “I would have done it again.”
Vance: ‘Everyone Knows’
Vice President J.D. Vance gave his blunt verdict on the election result on X on Wednesday.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
The vice president said he remained “hopeful about our country.”
Vance urged Republicans who are angry because they had warned that this would happen, “Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.”
The war, now in its ninth month, has been deeply unpopular with Americans since it began, with Trump’s rhetoric alternating between threats to ramp up U.S. military strikes and statements that he was ready to end the conflict.
Democratic candidates out on the campaign trail across the country blamed the war for driving up the cost of gas and other essential goods.
‘International Blackmailers’
Iranian officials reacted on Wednesday to the election results.
“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, wrote on X. “If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.”
Democrats made significant gains in traditionally solidly Republican states, capturing the governorships of Texas, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio. Among the most striking Democratic gains were in Texas, where Republicans have held the governor’s office since 1994, and Georgia, which had not elected a Democratic governor since 2002.
Following the verdict of the American people, many in the Middle East and politicians around the world are now waiting to see how the results could affect the Iran war.
Iranian leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father and predecessor was killed in the opening strikes of the war in February, cast doubt on any major change in the U.S. approach to the Islamic Republic.
“If there are still those who harbor even a slight hope for a change in behavior or partisan and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who imagine that by giving concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken,” he said in a statement posted to his social media channels.
The wider region has been on edge for weeks over the prospect of the United States resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
Trump has alternated between threatening major military action and saying he wants to secure a peace deal.
Talks aimed at preventing renewed fighting are continuing, while other U.S. allies in the region have urged Washington not to resume the war, which began more than eight months ago, causing huge disruptions to the global economy.
Despite repeated diplomatic efforts and ceasefire agreements, military confrontation has continued in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a social media post that Americans had sent a clear message and warned Washington against ignoring it. The spokesman said that if the United States continues the war, “the consequences of this grave miscalculation will extend far beyond what you have already witnessed.”
Thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a demonstration organized by the regime to commemorate the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy.
Hostage Crisis Anniversary
Effigies of Trump and Netanyahu were displayed alongside caricatures of the two leaders. Demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy on Nov. 4, 1979, taking American diplomats and other citizens hostage, with 52 Americans held for 444 days before they were released.
The hostage crisis cemented the rupture between the two countries, which have had no formal diplomatic relations since 1980.
The United States and Israel began their war against Iran on Feb. 28, killing the country’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and triggering a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and shipping through the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Addressing the crowd on Wednesday, Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani said the United States and Israel had collectively suffered a resounding defeat, which he said was also reflected in last week’s Israeli elections.
“The decisive defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime in recent developments and elections is the result of the Iranian nation’s steadfastness and strength,” Zakani said.
The U.S. elections took place one day after what appeared to be a limited strike on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited before the war. Iran has sought to choke off shipping to put pressure on Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports.

sources.news_title: Trump Admits Iran War Cost Republicans Votes, Insists: ‘I’d Do It Again’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the conflict with Iran cost Republicans votes in the midterm elections but insisted he would launch the military operation again, arguing that preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons outweighed the political consequences.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House a day after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Trump was asked about Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that the Iran conflict was a major factor in the Republican defeat. The president largely agreed but attributed the political fallout primarily to higher gasoline prices.
“Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” Trump said, before insisting he would make the same decision again. “Long term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Asked whether the operation had been worth the political cost, Trump said it had, acknowledging that he had anticipated an even greater increase in oil prices when he authorized the campaign.
“You have no choice,” he insisted. “You have to do it.”
Trump insisted that confronting Iran was necessary regardless of the immediate political and economic costs, warning of potentially catastrophic consequences if Tehran acquired nuclear weapons.
Trump also distinguished between opposition to the military operation itself and frustration over rising energy costs, arguing that gasoline prices had driven much of the electoral backlash.
“We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Hormuz right now,” Trump said, contrasting current shipments with the disruption at the beginning of the conflict. He emphasized that the electoral damage stemmed from “the price, not the war, the price.”
His remarks came in response to a lengthy post on X earlier Wednesday in which Vance argued that Republicans had lost not because their supporters failed to turn out, but because many voters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 had instead supported Democrats.
The vice president cited polling of disaffected Trump voters who identified four leading concerns: ending the conflict with Iran, addressing the cost of living, putting America first, and changing Washington’s relationship with Israel.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote.
Vance also challenged those who believed the operation justified the political losses to acknowledge that trade-off openly.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
Although Trump placed greater emphasis on gasoline prices than Vance did, he voiced approval of the vice president’s assessment and reiterated that preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons remained his overriding priority.
“I knew the war was going to impact it, but whether it impacted or not, Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
Asked specifically about Vance’s lengthy post, the president said he understood the vice president’s position and approved of his remarks.
“I thought it was good,” Trump said.
Trump had acknowledged the conflict’s electoral impact the previous night during an interview with Fox News as Republican losses mounted. He argued that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons would ultimately prove far more consequential than the election results.
“I think a part of it was Iran,” Trump said. “But at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran. I think historically it’s going to be much more important than this evening, because you can’t let the number one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon.”
In a separate Tuesday-night interview with the Wall Street Journal, Trump was equally emphatic in defending his decision, declaring: “I did the right thing. I would have done it again.”
Iranian officials, meanwhile, seized on the Republican defeat to claim a political victory over Washington. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, sought to portray the election results as the latest in a series of supposed Iranian victories over the United States.
“The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz—and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington,” Rezaei declared, claiming Americans had been left to bear the financial costs of the conflict.
The administration, meanwhile, pressed ahead with its campaign to isolate Tehran economically. The Treasury Department announced new sanctions Wednesday under Operation Economic Outcast targeting a maritime network accused of facilitating Iranian petroleum shipments through fraudulent vessel registrations and certifications.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reinforced that message, warning that Washington would continue sanctioning those supporting the Iranian government, “whether by land, sea, or air.”
Trump also addressed when the military operation might end, making clear that any conclusion would depend on achieving his objective of preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
Asked when the conflict would end, Trump replied, “Whenever I wanted to, but it’s got to be done right,” before insisting: “We’re never going to let them have a nuclear weapon.”

(AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) Trump defends Iran war, admits it cost Republicans the election Tweet Join Group Join WhatsApp Group Email https://worldisraelnews.com/trump-defends-iran-war-as-vance-blames-republican-defeat-on-conflict-and-us-israel-ties/ Email Print Trump denies promising to end Iran war after elections, says conflict will end on his terms. By Vered Weiss, World Israel News President Donald Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the war with Iran contributed to the Republicans’ sweeping midterm election losses, agreeing with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment of the results while maintaining that the military campaign was necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. “I knew the war was gonna impact [the election results]. Whether it impacted it or not, Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters during a tour of the White House ballroom construction site. “I would’ve done nothing different,” he added. His comments followed a post on X in which Vance identified the Iran war and Washington’s relationship with Israel among the principal reasons voters abandoned Republicans, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. Vance cited a pollster who had questioned former Trump supporters about what might persuade them to return to the Republican Party. Respondents identified ending the Iran conflict, addressing inflation and living costs, putting “America first” and changing US relations with Israel. https://worldisraelnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/WhatsApp-Video-2026-11-04-at-8.26.57-PM.mp4 “Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results,” Vance wrote. Read 'Wait till you see what we do' - Trump threatens new attacks on Iran “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” Asked about Vance’s remarks, Trump expressed approval. “I know how he feels about it… I think it was fine. I thought it was good,” he said. Despite acknowledging the political consequences, Trump defended the decision to launch the joint US-Israeli offensive against Iran in February. He also rejected questions concerning his earlier declarations that the conflict would end immediately following the midterm elections, falsely denying that he had made such statements. “I said nuclear weapons would be destroyed. And that’s what happened with Midnight Hammer,” Trump said, referring to the June 2025 strikes that he previously claimed had obliterated Iran’s nuclear program. “The war will end whenever I want it to. But it’s got to be done right,” he added. Vance, meanwhile, challenged Republicans to confront the electoral consequences directly. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Donald TrumpJD VanceMidterm Elections

sources.news_title: Trump and Vance lead GOP blame game as fingers point at Iran war
sources.text:
US midterms briefing: Trump and Vance lead GOP midterms blame game over Iran war
Hello! Well, yesterday was huge!
The Democrats have emerged victorious from the midterm elections, claiming massive gains in both the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.
Click here to read a quick catch-up on how the results panned out, click here to see how popular Trump is today, and click here for a breakdown on what the midterms are all about.
Here's what you need to know today
- GOP blame game: In the aftermath of their huge losses, Republicans have turned to examining what went wrong. "I don't blame anybody," Trump told Politico. Earlier, he acknowledged that the Iran war played a role, but stood by his decision to attack Iran — something Vice-President JD Vance has echoed. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so." Trump also said if he had been on the ballot "we would have won". "But they just, you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible, and we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates," he said. But with Trump's approval rating sitting below 40 per cent since April, many Republicans feel differently. "Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not them," veteran Republican strategist Doug Heye told Reuters.
- A potential dummymander: Going into the election, Trump encouraged Republican states to redraw their electoral maps in a bid to give the party an advantage in House races, leading to a proverbial arms race between the two parties. For the most part, that gambit failed to net Republicans any extra seats. But there's also a chance it may have cost the party a once-safe seat where a comfortable majority was shaved down to bolster other areas. At the time of writing, the race for Tennessee's fourth congressional district is separated by just 280 votes, with the Democrats in the lead. Still, experts have said the new maps had some impact, stifling Democrats' abilities to flip even more seats across the country.
- Looking ahead: The new Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, but the work starts now. Parties in both chambers are expected to choose their leadership teams when Congress returns next week. Hakeem Jeffries, who is currently the House Democratic leader, is expected to remain the party leader for the chamber for the next two years. That would make him the first Black speaker in the 237-year history of the House. The current speaker, Mike Johnson, has announced he will not serve as House minority leader next year, opening the way for a Republican leadership bid. In the Senate, Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and Senate Majority Leader John Thune are expected to remain leaders of their respective parties.
Answering some of your questions
We had plenty of questions come through on yesterday's live blog. Here are some of the most frequently asked, and how our ABC staff answered.
How does this affect Australia?
The US is one of Australia's closest allies, so any political changes there could have an effect in the medium to long term.
Can Donald Trump be impeached now?
For those not familiar, impeachment means to formally charge a public official with misconduct. Democrats do now have the numbers in the House to pass articles of impeachment — only a simple majority of 51 per cent is required.
But that doesn't mean they will. Even if they put forward a solid case alleging Trump has engaged in misconduct, they need a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate to convict. Democrats won't be leaving this election with that big a margin, so Republicans would need to cross the floor to do so. You might remember this was where the two impeachment motions in Trump's first term ended up getting stuck.
And as my colleague, Casey Briggs, wrote on Tuesday: "[Democrats] would need to have a reason to [impeach] as well. You would think that Democrats would want to have an issue that would be seen as worthy of impeachment by the American public. The risk is that Democrats are seen as overplaying their hand. Of course, people will disagree on exactly what the threshold is for 'high crimes and misdemeanours'."
Can a Democrat-controlled Congress put an end to US involvement in the Iran war?
Trump did not seek permission from Congress when he launched strikes on Iran in the first place. I think from his point of view, he certainly wouldn't expect that the Democrats would affect what he's going to do here. He has hinted in the lead-up to today that the strikes on Iran might resume once these midterms are over. But he's kind of backed away from that and come back to it again. So, with Trump, we never know exactly what he is going to do.
Got a question of your own? Submit it to our live blog running today. We can't promise to answer them all, but we'll do our best to get to as many as possible throughout the day.
Democrats stormed to victory in the midterms, winning control of both the US House of Representatives and the US Senate as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke of Trump.
The party scored sweeping victories in several Republican strongholds for the first time in generations, including in Texas and Kansas.
In the Senate, Democrats have flipped at least seven seats. Mississippi could become an unexpected addition to the party's spoils as the count continues in an extraordinarily tight race that has at times been separated by less than 50 votes.
Going into the election, almost all forecasters had tipped the House would turn blue, making the Democrats' emphatic victory somewhat less of a surprise. Still, the party has won at least 237 races — 19 more than the minimum needed to form the majority.
Once seated next year, Democrats are expected to use their new power to investigate Trump's administration and family.
Despite concerns from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the results of the election, as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome and congratulated the party in an interview with Fox News.
Here's how the results are looking this morning.
You can get the latest on every House and Senate race here.
Click here to go back to the top.
How popular is Donald Trump today?
US President Donald Trump might not be up for election at the midterms, but his popularity has had a strong influence over the outcome.
The president's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections and that trend gets steeper when the president is unpopular.
Historic polling data collated by analytics firm Gallup shows presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their party lose an average of 37 House seats.
Presidents with approval ratings above 50 per cent have netted smaller loses, with an average of 14 seats.

Thanks for joining me! This is the last edition of the daily midterms briefing, but ABC News will continue covering the latest updates across its network.
ABC/Reuters

sources.news_title: Trump acknowledges Iran war contributed to Republican losses but defends military campaign
sources.text:
President Donald Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran was one of the reasons for Republicans’ heavy losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections but defended his decision to launch the military campaign in February.
The election delivered a major setback to Trump, with Democrats gaining control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The results have raised questions about the political cost of the war, which disrupted energy supplies and fueled inflation, driving up household expenses.
Asked whether the war had contributed to the Republican defeat, Trump told Fox News, “I think a part of it was Iran.” However, he stood by his decision, saying it was the right thing to do and that he “would have done it again.”
READ: Trump warns Iran as Hormuz talks raise hopes (August 26, 2026)
“I think historically, it’s going to be much more important than this evening because you can’t let the number one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump also said he would cooperate with Democrats during the second half of his second term, a departure from his earlier position, when he threatened to veto legislation introduced by Democrats.
During election rallies, Trump had repeatedly urged voters to elect Republican candidates, framing the election as though he “himself is on the ballot.” However, in his post-election reaction, he rejected the idea that the results represented a personal setback.
“Well, I say this: congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job. They’ve been looking for this one for 11 years, and they finally got it. But I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump said.
Trump’s allies and Republican strategists have pointed to the economic consequences of the ongoing war as a major factor behind the party’s poor performance. Some also blamed Trump for dragging Republican candidates down with his unpopular policies.
“We got destroyed because of Iran,” a top Republican strategist said. “Iran is what caused gas prices and diesel prices to skyrocket — not tariffs. If Republicans want to rebuild, the first step is ending the war in Iran and embracing an actual America First foreign policy,” the Trump supporter added.
“It’s on him. It’s not on anybody else. It’s a total, complete rejection of President Trump,” another top Republican lobbyist in Texas said.
READ: Oil shipments near Strait of Hormuz turn costlier as sailors risk attacks for $25,000 (October 5, 2026)
During the campaign, Republican candidates struggled to defend the administration’s policies on issues including the war, immigration and inflation. Democrats, meanwhile, linked ongoing geopolitical tensions to rising household and transportation costs. Some Republican supporters argued that the Trump administration should end the war and refocus on its “America First” agenda, prioritizing domestic issues.
In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
Republicans also lost traditionally safe Senate seats, including in Texas, ending a decades-long stronghold. Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton. Several other Trump-endorsed candidates also lost their races.

Trump, Vance Say Iran War Hurt Republicans After Electoral Defeat
Error: Contact form not found.
by Reuters and Algemeiner Staff
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the Iran war has been worth it despite acknowledging its role in losses in US midterm elections in which his Republican party lost control of Congress.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he told reporters.
The Iran war was responsible for a spike in gasoline prices that were seen as a strong factor in why Democrats made big gains in the elections.
Trump said the war has been worth it to stop Tehran from “having a nuclear weapon.”
He said he was okay with Vice President JD Vance’s social media post earlier on Wednesday in which Vance distanced himself from Trump’s war and blamed it for deep electoral losses.
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” Trump said.
Trump also said that if he had been on the ballot, he believed “we would have won.”
“But they just, you couldn’t transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible and we weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said.
Earlier on Wednesday, Vance questioned the worth of the Iran war and largely blamed it for the stinging electoral rebuke by voters that delivered control of Congress to Democrats.
Vance’s extraordinary remarks in a post on X could further complicate Trump‘s deliberations as he weighs whether to restart major combat operations against Iran, a step US officials have told Reuters is still under consideration.
They also raise questions about the political fortunes of senior Pentagon officials, most notably Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth is already deeply unpopular in Congress, where some lawmakers are expected to seek his impeachment.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said on X.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
Vance also said an earlier recommendation to end the war was “sound advice.”
Democrats secured control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations.
Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living, and anger at Trump‘s stewardship of the country.
Vance sought to play down any difference of opinion with Trump, saying the president had also acknowledged that the Iran war cost Republicans the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump‘s comments were far more measured, saying the Iran war was only one of multiple reasons.
“I did the right thing,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal. “I would have done it again.”
Trump told both the Journal and Fox News that the war was “part” or a “piece” of why Republicans lost on Tuesday.
The war, now in its ninth month, has been unpopular among Americans since it began. On the campaign trail, Democratic candidates across the country blamed the conflict for driving up the cost of gas and other goods.
Some political commentators have noted that Trump’s approval ratings began to sink last year following his imposition of a sweeping package of import tariffs that hit countries around the world. The tariffs, which helped lead to price hikes, preceded the Iran war by several months.

Trump: Iran cost us midterm elections but I would do it again
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to Republican losses in the midterm elections, agreeing with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment of the defeat, but insisted that he would make the same decision again.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Trump insisited the conflict had been necessary to prevent Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons, despite the political and economic costs.
“The Iran issue was something we had to do and we continue to do,” he said, arguing that the military operation had been worth the price.
Trump also acknowledged that rising petrol prices caused by the war had hurt Republicans at the polls, with fuel costs emerging as one of the factors behind Democratic gains.
He said he had no objection to a social media post by Vance earlier on Wednesday in which the vice-president attributed the party’s heavy electoral losses to the conflict.
Asked in regard to such an assessment, Trump said he agreed that the conflict had played a role in the result but maintained that the decision to go to war had been necessary.
“As far as this war is concerned, I wouldn’t do anything differently,” he said.
The president also claimed that Republicans would have performed better had he personally been on the ballot, saying he believed he would have won.
Trump argued that the support he received at campaign rallies had not translated into votes for Republican candidates.
“There was so much love at the campaign rallies, it was incredible, but we didn’t manage to transfer this love to the candidates,” he said.
The conflict with Iran and its impact on fuel prices had become major issues for voters, placing pressure on the administration as it defended its military campaign with Israel.
Despite acknowledging the electoral consequences, Trump maintained that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon justified the decision to launch the war.

sources.news_title: Trump agrees Iran war cost votes, but insists: 'I'd have to do it again'
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the war with Iran was a major factor in the Republican Party's losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, agreeing with Vice President JD Vance's assessment but insisting that he would make the same decision again.
Asked by a reporter about Vance's assertion that Republicans lost because of the war, Trump responded, "Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term."
However, the President defended his decision to launch the military campaign, saying, "If I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again, because long term it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
Asked whether he believed the war had been worth the political cost, Trump answered, "I do, yeah," before emphasizing that he believed there had been no alternative.
"I thought the oil would go up a lot more, and I did it on that basis. You have no choice. You have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or everything that you see here someday might not exist," Trump said.
The President also addressed the impact of the conflict on oil supplies, claiming that the situation in the Strait of Hormuz had improved significantly.
"We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Hormuz right now. At the beginning there was none," he said, suggesting that rising prices, rather than the war itself, were the primary factor behind the Republican defeat.
Trump also indicated that he was prepared to work with Democrats following their electoral gains.
"I'll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive," he said, adding that Democrats had already contacted him about holding discussions.
Trump's remarks came after Vance published a lengthy post on X examining the reasons for the Republican Party's defeat in the midterm elections.
In the post, the Vice President identified four principal concerns among voters who had supported Trump in 2024 but switched to the Democrats in 2026: ending the war, addressing inflation and the cost of living, putting America first, and changing the United States' relationship with Israel.
Vance argued that the election results reflected dissatisfaction among former Republican voters rather than a failure of the party's supporters to participate in the election.
"The main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," he wrote.
He also disclosed that internal polling had identified dissatisfaction with US-Israel relations as a significant concern among voters who had abandoned the Republican Party, although he did not specify what changes those voters wanted.
Vance placed particular emphasis on the war, writing, "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."
Asked specifically about Vance's post, Trump expressed approval of the Vice President's remarks.
"I thought it was good. I knew that when I went in. We stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they'll never have a nuclear weapon," Trump stated.
The President was also asked about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth amid a CBS News report that Trump had been consulting advisers about possibly replacing him following the Republican Party's electoral defeat.
According to the report, Trump had raised questions about Hegseth's future in conversations with advisers, although no decision had been reached.
Asked about Hegseth on Wednesday, Trump responded, "I think he's doing a very good job."

sources.news_title: Trump says Republicans harmed by Iran war, inability to ‘transfer the love’ for him
sources.text:
Hours after his Republican Party suffered historic losses in the midterm election, President Donald Trump on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) focused his first public event on lengthy remarks about the White House ballroom.
In the early afternoon, after a morning of silence from the administration, Mr. Trump abruptly called reporters to a ceremony where crews hoisted what he said was the new structure’s final steel beam.
The President met with construction workers and provided his second update of the week on a series of beautification projects he is undertaking in the nation’s capital.
“They’re being carved out of beautiful limestone,” Mr. Trump said of the ballroom’s pillars. “And they’ll be Corinthian, Corinthian design, which is considered the creme de la creme.”
Democrats took control of the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday (November 3, 2026), winning seats in deeply conservative states that typically favour Republicans by double digits. The strength of the political reversal prompted the White House to acknowledge the unpopularity of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Some Republican strategists have called for the administration to wrap up the war and shift its focus to bringing prices down for American consumers instead of building opulent structures throughout Washington.
On Monday (November 2, 2026), Mr. Trump dedicated most of his final television speech before Tuesday’s (November 3, 2026) election to his administration’s renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Other projects include a granite White House helicopter landing pad, a public golf course renovation and a 250-foot arch he plans to build beside the Potomac River.
Mr. Trump’s first appearance after the election gave little indication that he wanted to change course.
During Wednesday’s (November 4, 2026) nearly 20-minute event, Mr. Trump acknowledged that he had taken flak for spending so much time and energy on prestige projects, but he said the ballroom was needed for the glory of the country.
“I like it,” he said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026). “For me, it’s relaxing.”
Mr. Trump, a billionaire former New York real estate developer, discusses his renovation projects in Washington regularly with reporters. At one point during Wednesday’s (November 4, 2026) event, Mr. Trump paused to watch the beam’s installation during a back-and-forth with reporters about the possibility of his impeachment by a Congress led by Democrats.
“Now, envision chandeliers all over,” Mr. Trump said. “Envision marble floors. Oh, it’s going to be good.”

sources.news_title: Largely true: Trump says Iran war led to loss after Vance comments; reiterates Iran cant have nuclear weapon - The Tribune
sources.text:
"Largely true": Trump says Iran war led to loss after Vance comments; reiterates Iran can't have nuclear weapon
Washington, DC [US], November 5 (ANI): US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) agreed with Vice President JD Vance's assessment that the war with Iran contributed to the Republican Party's defeat in the 2026 US midterm elections, acknowledging that the conflict drove up gasoline prices in the short term but insisting that military action against Tehran was necessary to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons.
Responding to media questions about Vance attributing the party's electoral setback to the Iran war, Trump said the assessment was "largely true", while maintaining that he would make the same decision if given another opportunity.
"Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term, and probably that's uh probably it's true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
The US President also suggested that his personal popularity had not translated into electoral support for Republican candidates, claiming that the party failed to transfer the enthusiasm witnessed at his rallies to other candidates.
"If I were on the ballot, we would have won. You saw the people—they were packed, thousands and thousands of people were there... But you couldn't just transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies; it was incredible. We weren't able to transfer that love to the candidates," Trump said.
Reiterating his defence of the military campaign, the US President said Washington had no alternative but to act against Iran, despite the political and economic consequences of the conflict.
"You have no choice. I mean, I thought the oil would go up a lot more, and I did it on that basis. You have no choice. You have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
Trump also argued that the increase in fuel prices, rather than the war itself, was the primary factor behind voter dissatisfaction, pointing to the resumption of oil flows through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
"We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Hormuz right now. At the beginning, there was none. And probably that's the primary reason, the price, not the war, the price," he said.
The President further indicated that he was willing to work with Democrats following their strong performance in the midterm elections, but warned that he would use his veto power if he disagreed with their legislative agenda.
Asked about the possibility of Democrats pursuing impeachment proceedings against him, Trump dismissed the prospect, saying such an initiative would damage the Democratic Party.
"I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that. Because impeachment for no reason. What? For having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history," he said.
Trump made the remarks while signing the final steel beam for the White House Ballroom, adding his name alongside the signatures of workers involved in the construction project.
Earlier, Vice President JD Vance had directly attributed the Republican Party's sweeping midterm defeat to the war with Iran, arguing that voter dissatisfaction over the conflict had prompted a significant number of supporters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 to vote for Democratic candidates in 2026.
In a lengthy post on X, Vance rejected arguments that inadequate Republican voter turnout was primarily responsible for the defeat, saying internal polling indicated that many former supporters had switched sides.
"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone... The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote.
Citing internal polling, Vance identified four major concerns among voters who had abandoned the Republican Party: ending the war, addressing the cost of living and inflation, prioritising an 'America First' agenda, and changing the country's relationship with Israel.
He also defended calls for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, saying that criticism of the administration's approach reflected the concerns of Republican voters.
Vance urged party members to acknowledge the reasons behind the electoral setback rather than shift blame to other factors, calling on supporters to channel their frustration into electing Republicans who shared their America First outlook.
This comes amid a broader Democratic resurgence in the 2026 midterm elections, with US networks projecting that the party will reclaim control of both chambers of Congress, significantly shifting the balance of power in Washington.
A Democratic majority in the House would allow the party to intensify congressional scrutiny of President Donald Trump's administration through investigations and hearings. Control of the Senate would also give Democrats greater influence over legislation and presidential nominations. (ANI)
(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

sources.news_title: Trump responds as JD Vance launches extraordinary attack on president's Iran war
sources.text:
Donald Trump has responded to JD Vance's claim that the Republicans lost the midterm elections because of the Iran war.
The Vice President posted a long message on social media suggesting that the obvious reason for the Republicans' comprehensive loss to the Democrats was because of the ongoing war with Iran, which has increased the price of goods not only for Americans but across the world.
Although Vance claimed that Trump did agree that the Iran war played a significant part in why so many voted for the Democrats, including in Texas which has been Red since 1988, the 80-year-old seems to have no regrets about the conflict in the Middle East.
Advert
"The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," Trump told reporters today (4 November) following the historic loss.
'The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone'
Vance had written: "The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true.
"But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."
Despite the significant spike in oil and gasoline prices, Trump added that the war has been worth it to stop Tehran from 'having a nuclear weapon'.
Trump also emphasised that there's no love lost between him and Vance, despite his social media post earlier today, as he made it clear that he wouldn't have done anything different when it comes to the conflict.
'I would have done nothing different'
"I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," Trump said.
Trump also said that if he had been on the ballot, he believed 'we would have won'.
"But they just, you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible and we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates," he said.
Although the White House did put out an eerie response to the election result that stressed that Trump will remain the president for the next two years, there could potentially be a way for the Democrats to oust him from his position.
The Blue side now control the Senate and the House, which puts them in a very strong position ahead of the planned elections in 2028, where Trump will almost certainly have to step aside given it's impossible for him to serve a third term, unless he can find himself a loophole.
JD Vance's statement on the midterm elections in full
"One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.
"So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are p****d and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."
"Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.
"Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:
1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel
"Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)
"In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.
"I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are p****d off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just p****d at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."
Topics: Donald Trump, JD Vance

sources.text:
Defiant Trump vows he'd 'do it again' as Iran backlash grows and MAGA empire implodes
The US President insisted he was still the boss after American voters gave his Republicans a double kicking, handing Democrats control of both houses of Congress
Defiant Donald Trump has vowed to cling on as US President despite taking an almighty walloping at the ballot box. The US President insisted he was still the boss after American voters gave his Republicans a double kicking, handing Democrats control of both houses of Congress.
And the White House rammed home the message with a picture of a thunder-faced Trump declaring: “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.”
He appeared to concede that the Iran war caused the election bloodbath. Trump said: “I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit. At the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again.”
But Grumpy Trumpy’s MAGA empire was imploding as his own supporters stuck the boot in and Democrats prepared to unleash the lawyers. Even his own deputy appeared to be edging away from the wreckage.
Vice-President JD Vance blamed the election disaster on Trump’s Iran conflict, declaring: “The reason we lost is the war.” His comments sparked speculation that he is already limbering up for his own shot at the White House in 2028.
The election bloodbath, dubbed a “blue tsunami”, saw Republican strongholds turn Democrat as voters punished Trump’s party over soaring prices and the war.
Trump refused to shoulder the blame, insisting: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
But his MAGA faithful are raging, with right-wing podcaster Matt Walsh branding the results “a political catastrophe of historic proportions”.
Conspiracy theorist Alex Jones even believes Trump is secretly working for the Democrats. He fumed: “He’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them. I’m 100 percent at war with Trump.”
And Trump could face looming legal wrangles. Democrats are preparing to investigate his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal and the Trump family’s business deals.
Robert Garcia, who is set to lead investigations, issued a chilling two-word warning in which he simply said: “Lawyer up.”
Billionaire Trump cheerleader Elon Musk could also face scrutiny over his controversial DOGE cuts and whether his Tesla and SpaceX empire benefited from his White House links.
Democratic senator Edward Markey joked: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”
Trump could even face a third impeachment attempt, although booting him out of office would require a huge Senate majority. The 80-year-old can still issue orders and block laws, but Democrats can now scupper much of his agenda.
Fears have been raised by some observers that a cornered, vengeful Trump could lash out by unleashing atomic hell on Iran. But Dr Tim Galsworthy, a lecturer in history at Lincoln Bishop University, reckons political insiders would move to neutralise the threat before he can strike.

sources.news_title: In First Speech After Midterm Loss, Trump's 'Magnificent' Ballroom Monologue
'Largely true': Trump acknowledges Iran war impacted midterm polls, but says it was something he had to do
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged that the Iran war was the key factor in his party's sweeping midterm election losses, after Vice President JD Vance urged Republicans to be "honest" about the unpopular conflict's impact.
Asked if he agreed with Vance's remark that the Iran was "the reason we lost," Trump, speaking to reporters at his White House ballroom construction site, said: "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term."
"But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he added.
Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump's likely successor at the White House, blamed the president's war in Iran for Republicans' midterm wipeout.
The president had no public events on his schedule originally, but called reporters together at the last minute. He also briefly took questions, insisting, “If I were on the ballot I would have won.”
He spoke at length about his new White House ballroom, delivering his first public remarks since the midterm election rout of his Republican Party from the construction site.
"It's going to be not only one of the biggest, but it'll be the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world," Trump told reporters -- without initially talking about the midterms in which Democrats swept Congress.
Meanwhile, Trump ruled out firing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth despite suffering bruising midterm election losses that the US president has blamed on the war against Iran.
"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump said when asked if he was considering replacing Hegseth, a staunch proponent of military action against the Islamic republic.
Trump further said that if the Democrats were to launch an effort to impeach him when they take control of Congress next year, it would "destroy" their party.
Asked about prospective impeachment a day after his Republican Party suffered a sweeping midterm election loss, Trump said: "I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that," insisting there was "no reason" for him to be impeached.
Trump usually blames anyone and everyone but himself
Trump has a long history of passing the buck, on issues large and small, but especially when there are ballot-box failures.
After Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, he blamed defeated members of his own party.
Utah Rep. Mia Love, who had tried to distance herself from him, “gave me no love, but then she lost. Too bad," the president said.
He mocked other losing lawmakers for not embracing him — Florida's Carlos Curbelo, Colorado's Mike Coffman, Virginia's Barbara Comstock, and Illinois' Peter Roskam — with the same words he would use eight years later: “My name wasn’t on the ballot."
Now he's trying to deflect blame once more, despite having urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”
An Associated Press analysis of the 39 Trump speeches and rallies Trump staged since Sept. 1 showed the president used a version of the phrase in 30 of them. In some addresses he returned to the subject more than once, though, meaning there were at least 40 instances where he appealed to voters to engage in that bit of make-believe.
(With inputs from AFP, AP)

sources.news_title: Trump defends Iran war after GOP loses control of Congress - American Press
sources.text:
Trump defends Iran war after GOP loses control of Congress
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
The midterm election blowout delivered a new era in Washington, with Democrats in Congress eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their majorities evaporate after a revolt against President Donald Trump and his party in power.
Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, in a decisive rejection of unified GOP control for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by unusually wide margins in both the House and the Senate.
The staggering results are setting up a starkly divided government, with an emboldened Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch when Democrats take over in the new year. They are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.
“We hear you,” said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Jeffries called the election a “stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism” and “a great victory for the American people.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer acknowledged the political reality that voters may have been more willing to reject Trump’s party than to embrace the Democrats.
“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday are still skeptical, and that’s OK,” the New York senator said Wednesday at the Capitol.
He said the history-making scale of his party’s wins — picking up long-shot Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas — creates “the opportunity to prove ourselves worthy of their trust.”
All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new openings and challenges for governing. The tally was bewildering for the scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses, which indiscriminately wiped out GOP firebrands, moderates and veteran conservatives nationwide. The swelling majorities, with some races still too early to call, underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda.
“I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
Later, he acknowledged the Iran war impacted the midterm elections, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the 8-month-old conflict.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters.
He said he was not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite voter dissatisfaction with the war, saying Hegseth was “doing a great job.”
Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump’s likely successor at the White House, pointedly blamed the president’s war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House Republican leader, according to two people familiar with his decision, setting up a potentially brutal leadership battle following the party’s trouncing by the Democrats. The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.

sources.news_title: Trump Acknowledges Role of Iran War in Election Losses
sources.text:
President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the Iran war played a role in his Republican Party’s resounding defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
“I think a part of it was Iran,” Trump told Fox News.
“Iran was a piece of it,” he said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal.
Trump stood by his decision for the United States to join Israel in attacking Iran, despite the heavy election losses that are likely to make the remaining two years of his second term a very difficult time for the president to pass new legislation.
“I did the right thing,” he told The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4. “I would have done it again.”
Vance: ‘Everyone Knows’
Vice President J.D. Vance gave his blunt verdict on the election result on X on Wednesday.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post.
“If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.
“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
The vice president said he remained “hopeful about our country.”
Vance urged Republicans who are angry because they had warned that this would happen, “Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.”
The war, now in its ninth month, has been deeply unpopular with Americans since it began, with Trump’s rhetoric alternating between threats to ramp up U.S. military strikes and statements that he was ready to end the conflict.
Democratic candidates out on the campaign trail across the country blamed the war for driving up the cost of gas and other essential goods.
‘International Blackmailers’
Iranian officials reacted on Wednesday to the election results.
“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, wrote on X.
“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.”
Democrats made significant gains in traditionally solidly Republican states, capturing the governorships of Texas, Georgia, Iowa, and Ohio. Among the most striking Democratic gains were in Texas, where Republicans have held the governor’s office since 1994, and Georgia, which had not elected a Democratic governor since 2002.
Following the verdict of the American people, many in the Middle East and politicians around the world are now waiting to see how the results could affect the Iran war.
Iranian leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father and predecessor was killed in the opening strikes of the war in February, cast doubt on any major change in the U.S. approach to the Islamic Republic.
“If there are still those who harbor even a slight hope for a change in behavior or partisan and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who imagine that by giving concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken,” he said in a statement posted to his social media channels.
The wider region has been on edge for weeks over the prospect of the United States resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
Trump has alternated between threatening major military action and saying he wants to secure a peace deal.
Talks aimed at preventing renewed fighting are continuing, while other U.S. allies in the region have urged Washington not to resume the war, which began more than eight months ago, causing huge disruptions to the global economy.
Despite repeated diplomatic efforts and ceasefire agreements, military confrontation has continued in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a social media post that Americans had sent a clear message and warned Washington against ignoring it. The spokesman said that if the United States continues the war, “the consequences of this grave miscalculation will extend far beyond what you have already witnessed.”
Thousands marched through Tehran on Nov. 4 at a demonstration organized by the regime to commemorate the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy.
Hostage Crisis Anniversary
Effigies of Trump and Netanyahu were displayed alongside caricatures of the two leaders. Demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy on Nov. 4, 1979, taking American diplomats and other citizens hostage, with 52 Americans held for 444 days before they were released.
The hostage crisis cemented the rupture between the two countries, which have had no formal diplomatic relations since 1980.
The United States and Israel began their war against Iran on Feb. 28, killing the country’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and triggering a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and shipping through the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway.
“The decisive defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime in recent developments and elections is the result of the Iranian nation’s steadfastness and strength,” Zakani said.
The U.S. elections took place one day after what appeared to be a limited strike on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited before the war. Iran has sought to choke off shipping to put pressure on Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports.
