sources.news_title: Iran Watching For Trump's Next Move After Stunning Midterm Elections Blow
sources.text:
The landslide victory by Democrats in US midterm elections is expected to bring change to Congress and foreign policy in Washington. But inside Iran, many officials said they expect the country will remain in the crosshairs of President Donald Trump, even if the vote has left him weaker.
As the results poured in late on November 3, showing Democrats had taken control of both the House of Representatives and Senate from their Republican rivals, Trump admitted the war he launched on Iran on the last day of February had taken a toll on his party.
But Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a statement on November 4 -- the anniversary of when radical students cemented Iran's toppling of the US-backed Shah by storming the US Embassy and holding 52 Americans hostage there for 444 days -- that anyone expecting any fundamental change in US policy simply because one party had replaced another is "gravely mistaken."
He warned against "even the slightest inclination toward submission" to the United States, adding that "the US sees the end of its hegemony as distant; we see it as near."
While Iranian and American negotiators have actively engaged in indirect talks in recent days -- primarily mediated by Qatar and Pakistan -- to end the military conflict, Trump has declined to rule out resuming strikes on Iran as the United States still has to "take care of" one or two more targets, including a suspected nuclear site.
Jalal Rashidikoochi, a reformist former Iranian lawmaker, said he saw little difference between Democrats and Republicans, though he still described the election as a "historic and humiliating" rejection by American voters of those who had pushed for war against Iran. He also urged newly elected members of the House and Senate to heed that message.
To be sure, many officials took the opportunity to gloat over the results, with some crediting Iranians' "popular resistance," the "bravery of Iranian fighters," and Iran's "historical revenge" against those responsible for the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on February 28, the first day of US and Israeli air strikes in the conflict.
But such statements do not necessarily reveal how Iran's leadership will act.
And the election may change less than Iranian officials suggest, as Trump still has some powerful foreign policy levers and will remain in office until January 2029.
Harder Line Or A Waiting Game?
Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, told RFE/RL that senior Iranian officials see the results as a victory for the Islamic republic and a vindication of its uncompromising approach.
"In that context, I expect the results to lead to a further hardening, rather than a softening, of Iran's position," he said.
That, he said, applies especially to Tehran's core demands: that Washington take the first step by lifting sanctions and the blockade, and that any agreement should not involve major nuclear concessions.
Azizi warned that such a stance could raise, rather than lower, the risk of a new clash, particularly if Trump decides he has nothing more to lose and gambles that a victory abroad could offset his setback at home.
Another possibility, according to Damon Golriz, a lecturer at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, is that Tehran might opt to wait out Trump's term.
Golriz told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that Iran may conclude it is better off avoiding major concessions to Trump and holding out for a future US administration with which it believes a more durable agreement could be possible.
He pointed to the negotiations under President Barack Obama that produced the 2015 nuclear deal, as well as what he described as serious diplomatic engagement under former President Joe Biden, as evidence that a different political environment in Washington could offer Tehran better prospects.
Golriz also expects the period ahead to remain volatile, with Trump potentially seeking to project strength after the electoral setback and continuing to rely on military and economic pressure to force Iranian concessions.
But Golriz argued that military strikes cannot resolve the disputes over Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz. A lasting solution, he said, would require negotiations that are "secret, direct, sustained, long-term and serious," potentially even more extensive than the talks that produced the 2015 nuclear deal.
Azizi said Tehran's leadership seems aware of the danger, pointing to Khamenei's warning as a clear sign of it. But the outcome, he said, rests largely in Washington.
"The stakes remain high," he said. "Much depends on how Trump assesses his own position and that of the Republican Party, and how he responds to domestic pressures pushing him in either direction."

sources.news_title: Trump admits Iran war hurt Republicans in midterms but says ‘Iran thing’ had to be done
sources.text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Responding to Vice President JD Vance’s charge that the war cost Republicans the 2026 midterms, Trump said the claim was “largely true” because the war “drove the gasoline up a little bit for a short term”. But he made clear he would do it again.
Also read: US midterm election results: What Trump & Republicans' loss means for
“You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. You have no choice,” he told reporters in Washington on Wednesday. He said he had expected oil prices to rise much more and went ahead on that basis. Without action, he warned, “everything that you see here, someday might not exist”.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he said.
On the new Democratic majority in Congress, Trump struck a mixed note. He said he would “get along” with the Democrats “unless they want to be destructive”, and pointed to the power of the veto if he did not like what they were doing. He said they had already called and wanted to talk about things.
JD Vance had gone further in a post on X earlier on Wednesday. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote. He challenged those who back the war to argue that losing the Senate for six years was worth it. Vance said many voters who backed Trump and him in 2024 had switched to Democrats. He listed ending the war, the cost of living, putting America first and changing ties with Israel as their demands.
Trump had called the war only “part of it” on Tuesday night, not the whole reason. At the start of the war, he had said Vance was “maybe less enthusiastic about going”.
Democrats won back the House, with at least 228 of the 435 seats declared and leads in several dozen more. That puts them on course for a margin well above the 218 needed for control. In the Senate they flipped seven Republican-held seats, in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. That takes them to at least 54 of the 100 seats, up from 47, with a couple of races still uncalled. The Senate was 53-47 in Republicans’ favour before the vote.
It is the first time in two decades that a Republican president has lost both chambers of Congress. The last was George W Bush in 2006. The cycle was also the most expensive midterm on record. Early exit polls put Trump’s approval rating at 38 per cent.
Several of the upsets came in states Trump won comfortably in 2024. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico beat state Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton ousted Republican Senator Roger Marshall, the first Democrat to win a Kansas Senate seat since 1932.
In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated veteran Republican Senator Susan Collins, and in North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper beat Michael Whatley, Trump’s chosen candidate. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Trump-backed Darline Graham in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio seat for the party. Democrats also held Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won re-election, and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas won.
Governors’ races and historic firsts
Democrats now hold 28 of the 50 governorships to the Republicans’ 20, with two races yet to be called. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa unseated three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott. She becomes the first Democratic governor of the state in more than 30 years and its first Latina governor. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the state’s first woman governor.
The night also produced a string of firsts. In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, beating billionaire Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200 million of his own money. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor of a US state. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed beat Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
Pappas is the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, while Minnesota Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan is the first Native American woman elected to it. Illinois’s Juliana Stratton means three Black women will sit in the Senate together. Xavier Becerra becomes California’s first Latino elected governor, and Republican Byron Donalds became Florida’s first Black governor.
Costas Panagopoulos, a political scientist at Northeastern University, called the result “a full-blown repudiation” of Trump and the Republican agenda. In South Carolina, counties Trump won swung about 21 points to the left on average.
Trump said he was “a little bit surprised” by the scale of the defeat. He accepted the results, unlike after his 2020 loss, and said he would work with the Democrats. He said he would veto legislation he opposed, and he ruled out any Cabinet changes. He also claimed Republicans would have won in a landslide had he been on the ballot.

Donald Trump has admitted that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses in the midterms but insisted he would launch the military campaign again to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to the Republican Party's crushing defeat in the midterm elections, particularly by driving up petrol prices and adding to the financial pressure on American households. However, he has refused to reconsider the military campaign, insisting that preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons was worth the cost.
"I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up... At the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. He made the remarks while speaking to reporters at the White House ballroom construction site, where he was discussing renovation work at the White House and other projects in Washington.
"...but the Iran thing, we had to do it, and we continue to do it. We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz right now. At the beginning, there was none. And that's probably the primary reason," he added.
His remarks nevertheless offered a significant admission of the consequences of the Iran war, which has emerged as a major issue within Trump's own party following the November 3 midterm elections. Democrats swept control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, dealing Republicans a major setback and handing the opposition party considerable power to challenge Trump's administration during the remaining two years of his presidency.
IRAN WAR, PETROL PRICES BECOME GOP' LIABILITY
The conflict with Iran has become an increasingly difficult issue for the Trump administration as its economic consequences have reached American households. Military confrontation in the Middle East has disrupted energy supplies and heightened concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil transit routes. A significant portion of internationally traded crude oil passes through the narrow waterway, making any disruption a concern for energy-importing countries.
The resulting pressure on oil markets has translated into higher fuel costs, putting additional pressure on motorists and businesses in the United States.
For American voters already concerned about inflation and the cost of living, higher petrol prices have become another source of frustration. The issue is particularly sensitive because Trump had repeatedly promised to prioritise domestic economic concerns under his 'America First' agenda.
JD VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR POLL LOSS
Trump's acknowledgement came shortly after Vice-President JD Vance identified the Iran war and Washington's relationship with Israel as major reasons behind the Republican Party's electoral losses. In a lengthy statement on X, Vance argued that the party's defeat was not simply a result of poor voter turnout. Instead, he said, many Americans who had supported the Trump-Vance ticket in the 2024 presidential election had switched sides and voted for Democrats in the midterms.
Pointing to internal polling, Vance identified four major reasons behind the voter backlash: the war, rising living costs, concerns over the administration's commitment to its 'America First' agenda and dissatisfaction with Washington's relationship with Israel.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote.
He said Republican analysts had initially been encouraged by voter turnout figures, believing that the party's supporters were showing up in sufficient numbers. However, one of the data analysts he consulted warned that turnout figures did not necessarily mean those voters would support Republican candidates.
Vance recalled the analyst telling him: "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."
According to Vance, the warning proved accurate. He also cited a pollster's findings that voters who had abandoned Republicans wanted the administration to end the war, address inflation, return to its 'America First' priorities and reconsider its relationship with Israel.
WHY TRUMP SAYS IRAN CANNOT BE ALLOWED TO HAVE NUCLEAR WEAPONS
At the centre of Trump's justification for the military campaign is Iran's nuclear programme and Washington's longstanding concern that Tehran could eventually develop nuclear weapons.
Iran has maintained that its nuclear activities are peaceful and intended for civilian purposes. However, its uranium enrichment programme has been a major source of international concern for years.
Uranium enrichment involves increasing the concentration of uranium-235, an isotope that can sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Low-enriched uranium can be used as fuel for civilian nuclear power plants, while highly enriched uranium can be used in nuclear weapons.
The distinction between the two is crucial. Uranium enriched to around 90 per cent purity is generally considered weapons-grade material. Iran had previously accumulated uranium enriched to 60 cent, a level far beyond what is normally required for civilian nuclear power generation.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Iran had accumulated an estimated 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 per cent purity. However, possessing highly enriched uranium does not automatically mean a country has a functioning nuclear weapon. Developing a nuclear warhead also requires additional technical work, including weaponisation and the ability to deliver it.
The question of what remains of Iran's nuclear programme has become particularly complicated following repeated US and Israeli attacks on its nuclear infrastructure in 2025 and 2026.
IAEA WARNS IT CANNOT VERIFY IRAN'S NUCLEAR STOCKPILE
The latest developments have complicated Trump's argument that military action has eliminated the threat posed by Iran's nuclear programme.
In an update to the United Nations Security Council on October 27, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said the agency had found no evidence that Iran had attempted to repair or reconstruct nuclear facilities damaged in the US-Israeli military strikes of 2025 and 2026.
"Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026," Grossi said.
However, there is another significant concern. The nuclear watchdog has been unable to independently verify the whereabouts and condition of Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium since the June 2025 strikes.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Hypes White House Ballroom After GOP Midterm Wipeout
sources.text:
President Donald Trump touted construction of his massive White House ballroom on Wednesday, hours after Republicans suffered a sweeping midterm election defeat that cost the party control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump discussed the ballroom progress and raised the final construction beam on the ballroom during his first public appearance following Tuesday’s elections. Meanwhile, Democrats celebrated victories across the country and prepared to take control on Capitol Hill.
Trump had no public events initially scheduled Wednesday but summoned reporters for a last-minute appearance at the White House. After 20 minutes of remarks and before taking questions from reporters, he watched as the final beam was put into place for the ballroom project after he signed it.
Read More on Politics
“I just want to thank everybody for being here. This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere,” Trump said at the building site.
Trump addressed the Republican losses while taking questions on Wednesday, insisting: “If I were on the ballot, I would have won.” He suggested that the enthusiasm he saw at his midterm rallies did not carry over to other Republicans, saying that “we weren’t able to transfer love to the candidates.”
Trump’s Renovations Draw Scrutiny Amid Midterms
Trump's continued focus on the ballroom comes after midterm voters expressed broad dissatisfaction with his priorities. About two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities, according to the AP Voter Poll, with an overwhelming majority of those voters backing Democratic House candidates.
The emphasis on Washington, D.C. renovations extended to the eve of the midterms, when Trump devoted his final speech before Election Day to the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Trump said Wednesday that he had no regrets about his Election Eve speech at the reflecting pool, defending his decision to focus on the renovation project during his final pitch to voters. Asked whether he regretted emphasizing the project at a time when polls showed voters were primarily concerned about pocketbook issues, Trump instead discussed details of the pool’s renovation, including its plumbing and paint color.
“I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews,” Trump said while touring construction of the White House ballroom.
Republican strategist Doug Heye argued that Trump’s focus on renovations sent the wrong message to voters concerned about affordability.
“Trump kept signaling to voters that his renovations were more important than voters being able to afford their own renovations. Or beef. That’s a problem,” Heye told Newsweek via email.
The White House rejected that criticism, saying the president’s renovation projects did not detract from his economic agenda.
“President Trump’s commitment to restoring our Nation’s treasured landmarks should be celebrated and does not distract from his work to lower costs, strengthen our economy, and improve the lives of American families,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Newsweek via email.
In a statement released Wednesday night titled “President Trump Will Again Defy the Odds, the Fake News, and the Radical Left,” the White House predicted Democrats would attempt to reverse Trump’s policies on immigration, taxes, energy and diversity initiatives and could pursue another impeachment effort.
“Every time the Radical Left, the Fake News, and the professional panic class have written President Trump’s obituary, they have been wrong. They will be wrong again,” the statement said, concluding: “President Trump will never stop fighting.”
Trump Signs Final Ballroom Beam
Trump added his signature Wednesday to what a contractor described as the final steel beam.
Standing before the large white beam, already covered with dozens of signatures in red and black ink, Trump signed his name in black marker between two gold seals and wrote “Love!” above it.
“Everybody in the room signed it,” Trump told reporters beforehand. “All of the workers, not just the steelworkers, the plumbers, electricians, the painters—everybody signed it. And I’m going to be the last to sign it.”
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum signed the beam after Trump.
After signing the ballroom’s final beam, the president paused to admire the project and again raised the prospect of using its roof for drones.
“You can land anything on top of that roof,” Trump said. “But it will be all drones.”
Trump has cited the potential for the U.S. military to use the ballroom roof as a drone port as part of his justification for the project. Experts have questioned the practicality of operating attack drones from the site. The U.S. Secret Service already operates a drone port from a nearby White House rooftop for security surveillance.
The project has become a source of political and legal controversy. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed construction to continue after an August 31 ruling while making clear that it had not decided whether the project was lawful. Chief Justice John Roberts, dissented and said the construction was “likely unlawful.”
The ballroom project has been estimated to cost $400 million, with the administration previously saying construction would continue into 2028.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

sources.text:
Trump cheers himself up after midterm wipeout by touting White House ballroom, helipad
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WASHINGTON — A beaming President Trump described plans to install Corinthian columns inside his under-construction White House ballroom Wednesday — turning to renovation projects to lift his spirits after Republicans suffered a devastating election blowout fewer than 24 hours earlier.
“You’ll be able to have dinners for as many people as you want,” Trump said as he expounded on his plans to renovate or build various DC landmarks.
Follow for live updates on the 2026 Midterm Elections
“We ordered the marble for the floor. The marble is really magnificent marble. It’s a cut, it’s a vein that people have been after for 50 years, and the owner of the quarry didn’t want to sell it, but he liked me.”
The new White House helipad, meanwhile, was “so good I never even got sued,” he added.
A planned Garden of American Heroes along the Potomac featuring grand statues “will be something beautiful,” Trump went on before touting plans to develop East Potomac Park near the Jefferson Memorial into a “beautiful” 18-hole championship golf course.
Trump spoke for 25 minutes about his construction projects before getting around to taking reporter questions about Republicans losing the House and Senate.
He agreed with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that his war with Iran, which caused higher energy prices and inflation, contributed to the staggering defeat.
“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” he said. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump also predicted that once the 120th Congress convenes Jan. 3, “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive.”
The president spoke shortly after presumptive Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) struck a different tone, vowing to bring the “wannabe king” Trump’s agenda to a screeching halt with “legislative razor wire.”
More coverage of the 2026 midterm elections:
Trump rejected blame for the massive Republican losses — even though exit polls found that 71% of voters said Congress must do more to check Trump and 62% blamed him personally for higher prices.
“There was such love at those rallies; it was incredible. We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said.
Trump then paused questions and asked journalists to watch the raising of the final steel beam to the roof of his new ballroom — after he signed his name with a black Sharpie and added “Love!” to the metal segment.
The beam, with a Christmas tree balanced in the middle of its span, was raised by a crane as the president provided play-by-play.
“They rarely have to do any chopping. Watch. Pretty amazing, huh? The entire building, every single hole was perfect, which is rare, but we had great people,” he boasted, adding, “If one bolt fell down you’re history.”
Returning to the Q-and-A, Trump denied speculation he will oust Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, a proponent of Operation Epic Fury, and said that while he understood Vance’s opposition to the Iran conflict, “I knew that when I went in.”
The president added, however, that Hegseth would ”be very popular” if he accepted an appointment to fill Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s Senate seat, which would head off a potential House impeachment vote later this year.
Returning to Vance, long seen as the MAGA movement’s heir apparent, Trump raised eyebrows by suggesting the Ohioan may not seek the presidency in two years after all.
“You can have a lot of people, maybe a lot of people running. Maybe nobody’s going to run. Maybe he won’t run,” he said.
The bizarre event mirrored Trump’s final election appeal to voters at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday, where the president spoke at length about re-lining the shallow body of water, and took 24 minutes to get around to mentioning the looming election.
Trump said he didn’t regret that appearance, which drew widespread scorn for reminding voters of an initially botched renovation effort over the summer.
“I heard it was a very good speech. Got great reviews,” Trump said. “That was only a speech on the reflecting pool. That had nothing to do with anything else.”

Donald Trump says Iran war 'worth it' as son and JD Vance blame conflict for US midterm wipeout
sources.text:
Donald Trump has declared the Iran war was "worth it," amid claims from JD Vance and the President's son the conflict was to blame for the Republican Party's wipeout in the US midterm elections.
In a bruising night for the President, the Democrats surged in several traditional Republican strongholds and broke long-standing records as the party reclaimed control of both chambers of the US legislative branch.
Mr Vance appeared to take aim at the President in an explosive post on social media, declaring: "The reason we lost is the war. The President himself said so last night.
He warned Republicans had lost the support of voters who backed Trump in 2024, writing: "The main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026."
The astonishing social media post was reposted by the President's son, Donald Trump Jr, who said: "Every word of this is," followed by a "100" emoji, appearing to agree with the Vice President.
However, a defiant President has hit back at his second-in-command and son, proclaiming the Iran conflict was "worth it."
When asked by the media at the White House if the war was worth it - his first on-camera comments since the damaging midterms - the President responded: "I do, yes. Well, you have no choice."
He later said Mr Vance's statement was "largely true," admitting: "It drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term."
However, Mr Trump said he would have done the war again, and added that it was the rising gas prices furtrating voters, not the actual conflict.
In his extraordinary social media post last night, Mr Vance revealed that internal polling had exposed widespread dissatisfaction among former Trump supporters, with the conflict emerging as a central concern.
According to Mr Vance, a respected Republican pollster asked disillusioned GOP voters what would persuade them to return to the party.
Their four leading demands were: "End the war", "Focus on cost of living/inflation", "Put America First" and "Change our relationship to Israel".
Mr Vance concluded: "Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats."
The Vice President also suggested the conflict had cost Republicans control of the Senate, challenging those who believed the military campaign had justified the electoral consequences.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
He wrote: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."
In a further warning to his party, Mr Vance insisted: "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
In the aftermath of the electoral bloodbath, Mike Johnson told staffers he will not run for minority leader in the new Congress next year, a source told CBS News.
The senior Republican is said to have informed his team of the decision on Wednesday morning.
Last month, the Speaker of the House of Representatives said he intended to stay on in his post even if his party lost its control in the lower chamber of the legislature.
However, Mr Johnson previous cast doubts over his future in an earlier interview, when he suggested he may step away from political life.
He told Fox News: "If heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don't know what my next chapter of life is. I'm just open to it.
"If God moves on our hearts and says we should go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I'll do that with equal fervor."
The crushing results across the country for Republicans mean Mr Trump's final two years in the White House could prove far more unstable, with his ability to pass legislation now hampered by the opposition party's control of Congress.
A Democrat-controlled legislature will also bring more aggressive oversight of the Trump administration with more investigations, subpoenas and congressional hearings on the horizon.
The President is also staring down the barrel of the same impeachment proceedings which plagued his first term in office, leading to him being impeached twice.
Despite an incredibly bleak night for the President, he said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” after insisting if he had been on the ballot, Republicans "would have won in a landslide".
The President has acknowledged skyrocketing petrol prices and the war in Iran as possible factors behind the disastrous results but insisted they were not a "hit" on his presidency.
Mr Trump told Fox News the Democrats had been "looking to do this", admitting they had "finally" pulled off a victory before congratulating the party on a "good job".

Vance says Iran war cost GOP the midterms; Trump says he would have done nothing different
sources.text:
Vance says Iran war cost GOP the midterms; Trump says he would have done nothing different
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Confronted with a tidal wave of Democratic midterm victories that cost Republicans control of Congress, Vice President JD Vance issued a stern missive Wednesday about how his party lost so much support, placing the lion's share of blame on the Iran war – a war he spent eight months justifying to the public.
The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said in a post that was shared and praised by President Donald Trump's eldest son.
The president said Vance's assessment was "largely true" because the war caused a surge in gas prices but stood by his decision to go to war.
"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Vance said a pollster he consulted surveyed voters who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 but planned to vote for Democrats in the midterms. When asked what the Trump administration could do to win them back, Vance said it came down to four things: end the Iran war, focus on inflation, put America first and change the United States' relationship with Israel. Given historical trends and Trump's low approval ratings, Republicans were expected to lose seats in Congress. Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, said he felt negatively heading into Tuesday, "but even I was shocked by this."
Democratic National Committee communications director Rosemary Boeglin questioned the authenticity of Vance's critique.
"Vance started this deadly, costly war with Trump. If Vance has felt this way all along, why didn’t he speak out forcefully? Why didn’t he resign? And most importantly, why didn’t he stand up for Americans? Because Vance will always do what’s most politically convenient for him in the moment — even if it means throwing Americans under the bus. Vance owns this administration’s failures," Boeglin said.
On Tuesday night, as it became clear that Democrats dominated this election cycle, Trump did a handful of interviews in which he brought up the economic impact of the war and speculated about potential future attacks. The next day, he was asked when the war would ultimately end.
“Whenever I want it to, but it’s got to be done right," Trump said. "And we’re never going to let them have a nuclear weapon, it’s got to be done right.”

U.S. News
- Democrats win Senate and House in historic landslide, upending Trump’s second term and GOP agenda: Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate following midterm elections on Tuesday. It is the third time in 50 years that control of both chambers has changed in a single election. Democratic candidates flipped seven seats in the Senate, giving them a 54-46 majority in the upper chamber. The Democrats are estimated to win 258 House seats, and 55 Senate seats. Democrats also won gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, and Iowa.
- Trump is relatively conciliatory in late-night comments: President Donald Trump congratulated the Democrats in a call to CBS News, saying that he was “looking forward to working with [them] for the good of the country.” But on Fox News, he said that he would veto anything passed by Democrats that was “insane,” and on Truth Social he posted an image of a hat with “VETO” on it. 
  - He also addressed the prospect of resuming the Iran war now that the midterms had concluded with CBS, saying the war would conclude “when I say it’s over, basically. It’ll end when I say it ends.”
- Here are the results from the night’s marquee races: 
  - Democratic victories in “toss-up” Senate races: Going into the election, seven Senate races were rated “toss-ups” by Cook Political Report: Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Alaska, and Kansas. Democrats won all of those races except for Alaska, which has not yet been called.
  - Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim senator, beating back Islamophobic attacks and pro-Israel opposition: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive physician, defeated Mike Rogers by nearly 10 points to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. President Trump and other Republicans used Islamophobic rhetoric to rally voters against him. “To AIPAC, who spent $42 million against us, thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice,” he said in his victory speech.
  - James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa turn Texas blue: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. Talarico, a 37-year-old Democratic state legislator and seminarian, is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate in Texas since 1993. Gina Hinojosa, another state legislator, defeated incumbent governor Greg Abbott, making her the first Democrat to win a Texas governor’s race since 1995.
  - Annie Andrews’ surprise victory in South Carolina: The night’s biggest upset was in South Carolina, where pediatrician Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, the sister of recently deceased Sen. Lindsey Graham and interim Senator appointed to fill his seat in July. Andrews is the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate since 1998, and is the first woman elected to the post in the state’s history.
  - Amy Acton, Sherrod Brown take Ohio: Democrats Amy Acton and Sherrod Brown won in Ohio, a state that has been solidly Republican since Trump won the state in 2016. Acton, a former state health official, defeated the Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, an entrepreneur and former head of the Department of Government Efficiency. Brown took back a seat he had lost in 2024 to Bernie Moreno. Brown previously served for 18 years in the Senate; he is regarded as one of the strongest pro-labor voices in the Democratic Party.
  - Adam Hamilton wins Kansas: Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, making him the first member of his party to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years. The race attracted huge interest: Political spending topped $110 million, and Trump hosted two rallies in support of the Republican candidate. Hamilton’s victory was largely secured by the state’s moderate voters: About seven in 10 moderates backed him over Marshall, according to an AP voter poll. (Read the Barn Raiser x Drop Site profile of Hamilton to understand why he won.)
  - Democratic socialists advance in House: After winning primaries in safe districts, candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America secured victories in the general election. Winners include Darializa Avila Chevalier, Brad Lander, and Claire Valdez in New York City, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, and Analilia Mejia in New Jersey. Matt Little, a progressive running to replace outgoing Rep. Annie Craig, won in Minnesota’s second congressional district.
  - Mississippi Senate race too close to call: The Mississippi Senate race remained deadlocked as of Wednesday morning. Democrat Scott Colom is in an unexpected dead heat with incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Colom is ahead by just 28 votes out of more than 1 million votes cast. If Colom wins, he would be the state’s first Democratic senator since 1982, and its first Black senator since Blanche K. Bruce, elected in 1875.
  - Climate activist William Lawrence declares victory in Michigan: William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, declared victory in his Michigan congressional race, citing an unofficial tally that had him up by several percentage points. As of Wednesday morning, he leads his Republican opponent, incumbent Tom Barrett, by three percentage points, 51% to 47.8%. Over 95% of votes have been received, according to AP election results.
  - Sanders-backed progressive beats Central Valley, Calif., Republican: Randy Villegas, a community college professor and son of immigrants, defeated incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao in California’s Central Valley. Villegas received an early endorsement from Sen. Bernie Sanders in his primary contest. Valadao, who served five terms in Congress, was one of 10 Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021.
  - Socialist wins Providence, Rhode Island, mayoral race; city votes to divest from Israel: State representative David Morales, a 28-year-old member of the Democratic Socialists of America, was elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, easily defeating his Republican opponent, Dave Talan. Separately, Providence voters approved a referendum on divesting from “countries and companies committing genocide.” The group that organized the referendum, Providence for Palestine, said that the language of the item was a reference to Israel. At least 75 percent of voters supported the measure.
  - Major Democratic gubernatorial victories: Democrats scored several high-profile gubernatorial victories. In Iowa, State Auditor Rob Sand defeated moderate Republican Zach Lahn; in Wisconsin, David Crowley defeated Trump-endorsed Rep. Tom Tiffany; and in Michigan, Jocelyn Benson defeated Republican Rep. John James. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won in Georgia, becoming the first Black female governor in U.S. history. Deb Haaland, Secretary of the Interior under Joe Biden, won in New Mexico, making her the first Native American to lead a U.S. state.
  - House flips in Pennsylvania: Democrats flipped two high-profile seats in Pennsylvania. Democrat Paige Cognetti, mayor of Scranton, won in Pennsylvania’s eighth congressional district, unseating first-term Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan. Democrat Bob Brooks, a firefighter, also defeated a first-term Republican incumbent, Rep. Ryan Mackenzie.
  - Other notable House races: Incumbent Republican Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart appeared poised to win in his unexpectedly close re-election race against Democrat Nicole Locklin. The Miami-area representative is the longest-serving member of Florida’s congressional delegation. Lauren Boebert lost in Colorado, after switching districts this cycle to one she believed was easier for a Republican to win. Sam Forstag, a labor leader backed by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is leading the Republican in Montana’s first congressional district, but the race has not been called. Richard Ojeda, a former state senator in West Virginia known for supporting the 2018 teachers’ strike, won in North Carolina.

We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” Trump said. 
  - Referring to ongoing negotiations with Tehran, he added, “We seem to be getting everything we want.” Trump said the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports was damaging Tehran’s economy, calling it “a brilliant situation.”
  - Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said that Tehran remained committed to diplomatic talks through its seven-day roadmap presented to Qatari mediators but was “ready for any scenario.” Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that any renewed U.S. attacks would result in “much broader dimensions” of war.
- Europe approaches winter with lowest gas reserves since 2013 amid Hormuz supply disruptions: Europe is approaching the winter season with its lowest natural gas storage levels in more than a decade, raising the risk of tight global gas supplies and higher prices through 2027, according to the International Energy Agency. The effective halt of liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has cut exports from Qatar and the UAE by more than 60 billion cubic meters between March and October, pushing Asian and European gas prices to their highest levels since the 2022–23 energy crisis.
- Iran claims four oil tankers destroyed by mines in Hormuz, U.S. MQ-9 drone shot down: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that four oil tankers attempting to cross a “prohibited” corridor south of the Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines and were destroyed, with the vessels still burning. Two other vessels were stopped, according to the IRGC. 
  - The group also claimed its air defense forces shot down a U.S. MQ-9 drone over the strait, bringing the number of MQ-9 drones it says it has downed to 56.
Palestine
- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, Israeli attacks killed three Palestinians—two in new attacks and one due to wounds sustained in an earlier attack—and injured 21 others across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. 
  - The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023, has risen to 74,618 killed and 175,920 injured. Since October 11, 2025, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,602 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 5,794, while 847 bodies have been recovered.
- Palestinian journalist loses 16 kilograms amid solitary confinement in Israeli prison: Palestinian journalist Bushra Al-Tawil, from Al-Bireh in the occupied West Bank, lost 16 kilograms since her arrest on February 5, amid severe food shortages, medical neglect, and prolonged solitary confinement, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs. 
  - Al-Tawil has been held in isolation since August 17 and is currently detained at Israel’s Ohalei Oz prison. Her isolation was extended for another month on November 2.
  - The commission said that she is suffering from dark skin lesions caused by scabies, as well as painful tendon inflammation in her hands and feet. Israeli prison authorities have ignored repeated requests for medical treatment.
- Israel declares 627 acres of Palestinian land near Ramallah “state property”: Israeli authorities issued an order on November 3 declaring 627 acres (2,536 dunams) of Palestinian land in Beitillu, Al-Mazra’a Al-Qibliya, and Deir Ammar, northwest of Ramallah in the West Bank, as “state property,” according to the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission. 
  - The land surrounds the Israeli settlement of Kerem Reim, and the commission warned that the declaration would facilitate the expansion of settlements. Palestinian landowners have 45 days from the order’s publication to file legal objections.
- Israeli forces displace 25 families in Tulkarm, arrest 45 Palestinians across the West Bank: Israeli forces carried out raids, demolitions, and arrests across the West Bank on Wednesday, WAFA reported. The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society reported at least 45 arrests, including five women and two journalists. 
  - Tulkarm: Israeli forces forcibly displaced 25 families from homes near Tulkarm refugee camp, converting some into military barracks. Israel’s assault on the Tulkarm, Nur Shams, and Jenin refugee camps has continued for 647 days, displacing more than 32,000 Palestinians in what Human Rights Watch found amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
  - Ramallah: Israeli forces fired tear gas toward a school in Al-Mughayyer, causing students to suffer from tear gas inhalation. Soldiers also detained a teacher and closed the school entrance.
  - Tubas/Northern Jordan Valley: Israeli bulldozers demolished residential and livestock structures belonging to three Palestinians in the Al-Deir area of the northern Jordan Valley.
  - Hebron: Under military protection, armed Israeli settlers destroyed olive trees in Surif, northwest of Hebron.
- Israel’s election committee approves results: Israel’s Central Elections Committee presidium voted Wednesday to certify last week’s election results, despite efforts by Netanyahu’s Likud party and other outgoing coalition parties to delay certification over unsubstantiated claims of election fraud. 
  - The committee found no irregularities indicating that the vote had been compromised, it said. The results will be submitted to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, after which he will consult party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
- Trump says U.S. will cut $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel: The U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel “at the end of the year,” President Trump said on Tuesday, but will sell arms to Tel Aviv. “We give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money,” Trump told Fox News as voting was underway. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” he said, a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, a forthright critic of Israel who was elected in Michigan to the U.S. Senate. 
  - Trump’s announcement comes as Congress considers phasing out aid to Israel, instead expanding U.S.-Israel cooperation in the countries’ military-industrial operations.
  - In 2016, President Barack Obama signed an unprecedented security agreement giving Israel $38 billion to its military over 10 years, which is set to expire in 2028. Trump seemed to suggest on Tuesday that he may cancel the agreement two years early, with Israel’s consent, though such a decision would probably require Congressional approval. Even if U.S. aid were suddenly cut, there are still many years of already purchased weaponry yet to be delivered, according to AP.
Yemen
- 20+ killed in Ansarallah missile strike on Saudi-backed government camp: More than 20 people were killed, and several others wounded, in an Ansarallah ballistic missile strike targeting a military training camp in the Maris area of Dhale governorate, Sky News Arabia reported. 
  - Meanwhile, Saudi-backed forces claimed that they captured the Al-Dahida heights and surrounding areas in eastern Al-Jawf governorate, backed by airstrikes targeting Ansarallah positions and supply lines.
  - The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia announced that a second Indian national injured in the October 10 Ansarallah attack on Riyadh airport had died, following an attack that killed at least 12 people and wounded hundreds.
- Hezbollah denies sending military experts to Yemen: Lebanon’s Hezbollah denied claims that its military experts are operating in Yemen and helping Ansarallah develop weapons, train fighters, and manage military operations. 
  - On Tuesday, the Yemeni Saudi-backed government claimed that 21 foreign military experts, including 14 from Iran’s IRGC and seven from Hezbollah, were working with Ansarallah. Their roles extended beyond financing, arming, and training fighters to directly overseeing military operations and political and media activities, according to the government.
  - In a statement on Wednesday, Hezbollah called the accusations “completely baseless.” The group said that Yemenis can defend their country without outside intervention, and called for dialogue to preserve Yemen’s unity and sovereignty.
Lebanon
- Again violating ceasefire, Israeli forces burn homes and shell towns in southern Lebanon: Israeli forces set fire to homes in the town of Hadatha in the Bint Jbeil district, while Israeli artillery shelled Baraachit in the same district, violating the ceasefire, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported on Wednesday. Israeli forces also shelled Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin in the Tyre (Sour) district earlier in the morning.

Trump's Iran War triggered a midterm massacre — And MAGA may be over
Frank Wright
See More
Donald Trump’s war with Iran has triggered a devastating political backlash against the Republican Party, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections. Frank Wright cites reported election results and polling: opposition to the Iran war, rising gasoline and food prices, and disillusionment among younger male voters contributed to the Republican defeat. A reported 45-point shift among young white male voters tells the story. Trump’s decision to pursue military intervention abroad alienated the very electorate that brought him back to the White House. Conservative commentator Curt Mills attributes the outcome to the Iran war.
The Republican defeat could lead to congressional investigations into the Trump administration, including scrutiny of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and renewed demands for the release of the Epstein files. Criticism attributed to former National Security Adviser John Bolton frames Trump’s intervention in Iran as a fundamental betrayal of the MAGA movement and America’s national interests. The administration could face significant personnel changes, escalating political instability, and further confrontation with Iran.
The election is a rejection of foreign interventionism and a turning point that could bring the MAGA movement to an end. The war was sold as strength. The voters called it betrayal. And the consequences are only beginning. The question is whether the Republican Party will learn from the defeat or continue down the path that led to it. The answer may determine the future of American politics.

sources.news_title: How Iran conflict shaped the US midterm elections
sources.text:
New Delhi: It’s a mid-term hammer, and the failure is epic, but US President Donald Trump prefers to downplay ‘it’. Congress has been flipped, and the legislative brakes are on for the remainder of Trump’s term.
Trump has acknowledged the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republican rout in the American midterm elections concluded on November 3. “Iran was a piece of it,” he told the Wall Street Journal, adding he did the right thing by launching the war and would do it again.
For weeks, Trump was indicating he would strike Iran after the midterms. But just hours before the polls closed, Trump, in an interview with the Financial Times, said the US has no immediate plans to strike Iran, nor is there any reason for it, though the US forces remain ready to act if necessary.
Democrats swept the Congress, with America’s war on Iran playing a decisive role in the Republican defeat. An exit poll by US-based Responsible Statecraft shows that about 74 per cent of voters said the Iran war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote, with 62 per cent believing that using military force against Iran was the “wrong decision”.
The 2026 midterms show the localisation of foreign policy. The midterms are typically conducted halfway through the incumbent’s presidency, and they are widely regarded as a referendum on the President’s governance.
‘It’s the war, stupid!’
Though Trump did not launch a full-fledged war before voters went to the polls, he carried out a series of smaller-scale military operations a day before the midterms, attacking Iran’s Qeshm island near the Strait of Hormuz. Officials described the action as “defensive” in nature to prevent Tehran from having the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The war on Iran, launched jointly with Israel on the last day of February this year, has cost American taxpayers at least $47.1 billion so far, according to the Pentagon’s latest estimates. It has also led to a domestic skyrocketing of energy and fuel prices, which along with the US support for Israel, became among the central issues in the polls, challenging Republicans even in their strongholds.
On the day of the election, Trump’s disapproval rating was at 60 per cent, with his approval standing at 37 per cent, as per The New York Times; many other polls put the disapproval even above 60 per cent. The last time an American President’s approval was at a comparable low this close to midterms was in 1946. This is even considering the party in power typically loses seats in both chambers of the Congress – the Senate and the House. A vast majority of pre-election polls showed the Democrats outpacing the Republicans, even in staunchly red states.
Trump’s approval ratings slumped as an upshot of the Iran war, with the dragging of the war at odds with his 2024 presidential campaign pledge to not start new wars. The US president’s biography on the White House website credits him with “putting a stop to endless wars”. In the war’s initial days, Trump repeatedly said he would finish the war in mere “weeks” – sometimes three, four, five or six.
Far from ending the Iran war, it has only dragged on. Meanwhile, President Trump has repeatedly issued ultimatums, at one point threatening to wipe Iran off the face of earth by stating, “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again” unless an agreement is reached. Such comments have undermined his attempt to portray himself as the “President of Peace”.
Also Read: US midterm election results ‘not a hit on me’, says Trump after Republicans lose key seats
More strikes?
Roughly a week before midterms, the Wall Street Journal on 28 October reported that the US had told several Gulf countries to be prepared for a “short, intense military campaign” after the midterms, subsequently reporting that the top US Commander in the Middle East, Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed the White House in person on military options for Iran.
Amid these reports, a US Senator from Connecticut, Chris Murphy, speaking at a Middle East Institute event, described Trump’s plan to attack Iran after midterms as “insane”. Murphy warned that it would lead to devastating escalation and would likely destroy US commitment to the rule of law. He added that some were privy to the plan, which in his view will lead to “prolongment and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our [US] security interests”.
Soon after, on 2 November, a former ally of Trump who broke away from the President in April this year, Tucker Carlson – also a conservative commentator – put out a post on X that sent alarm bells ringing across the world. He said the Trump administration, under pressure from Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu, may be “within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran”. The target, according to Carlson, would be Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence claims that Iran has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. The catch is that because the supposed site in Pickaxe Mountain is an underground storage facility, no conventional weapons could penetrate through, thus requiring “a nuclear strike”.
“An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final”, read his X post.
Carlson argued that Netanyahu, who has so far been unable to form a government after Israel’s recent elections, needs the war for political gain and is pressing US officials hard to resume it. Netanyahu reportedly wanted to resume attacks on Iran before Israelis went to the polls, but Trump wanted to wait until after the midterms. Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Opposition has a clear majority, and forming a coalition government could take weeks of wrangling, or even more. Until then, Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister, a role which would curtail his powers, and by extension, his capabilities to launch strikes against Iran. But experts say that Netanyahu would still retain significant legal powers to wage a war on Iran.
Abdul El-Sayed: The leading Democrat against the Iran war
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat candidate from Michigan who defeated Trump’s close ally, Mike Rogers, openly opposed the war on Iran and American support to Israel. El-Sayed, whose wife traces her origin to a town in Karnataka, has become the first Muslim Senator.
El-Sayed’s manifesto under the category of ‘Sensible Foreign Policy’ opposed what he calls the “illegal and unjustifiable war” in Iran. He has spoken of utilising taxpayer dollars at home instead of providing direct blank-check funding to foreign militaries–including Egypt, Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and others.
“Right now, our tax dollars and American-made weapons are being used to perpetrate a genocide in Gaza, illegal settlements in the West Bank and Jerusalem, and the attempted annexation of Southern Lebanon. That must end… I support an immediate arms embargo on Israel and reject the false differentiation between “offensive” and “defensive” weapons”, it further adds.
El-Sayed’s campaign, coupled with others who have taken a similar stance during electioneering, appears to have resonated with a substantial share of Americans, cutting into Trump’s support. The effect was visible on election day itself, when Trump announced that aid to Israel, amounting to $4 billion, would be cut off at the end of the year. This aid would be replaced with an agreement where Israel would have to pay to purchase weaponry from the United States.
Explaining the U-turn in his decision, Trump said, “They don’t need it”, and, “why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?”.
However, the current memorandum of understanding between the two countries provides Israel $3.8 billion annually through September 2028. Trump’s comments suggested this would be cancelled two years early with Netanyahu’s consent. Trump may also have recognised that winning congressional approval for aid packages would be difficult, particularly if Republicans lose their majority in the midterms, which has now happened.
Netanyahu’s chief opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, swiftly used Trump’s statement to make his case for why the former prime minister cannot be trusted and must be replaced. “The fact that the defence establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning through the media about a change in the strategic relationship shows just how much Netanyahu’s conduct poses a real danger,” said Eisenkot.
What now?
Now, with Democrats having captured both chambers of Congress – the Senate and the House – Trump may find it difficult to get approval for fresh strikes on Iran or further military support for Israel. However, presidents often have latitude to chart the course of their foreign policy. Many have thus pointed to how Trump’s loss at home could spur him toward even more aggressive actions globally, including renewing the military campaign against Iran.
Rather than launching a kinetic campaign, the Trump administration is currently pursuing a punitive economic policy, having imposed tighter sanctions and a naval blockade on Iran whilst shutting down much of its air links and cutting into its overland trade routes. The resulting pressure has squeezed Iran’s already suffering economy.
Experts across the board have said officials in the US and Israel still continue to believe, erroneously so, that another round of strikes against Iran, either decapitating senior officials or striking critical infrastructure, will lead Tehran to concede and bring down the regime. In reality, however, this will only harden the Iranian regime, since for the latter it is a question of survival, with fresh strikes perhaps strengthening Iran’s resolve to up its ante on the missile and nuclear programme.
Reports suggest that regional mediators led by Qatar have restarted negotiations between US and Iran to stave off a potential war after midterms. For its part, Iran has threatened massive retaliation not only on American targets, but also in neighbouring countries in the Persian Gulf, should the US and Israel renew their military campaign.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

Republicans were so busy targeting our community which is around 1% and does not do any crime or his depended on welfare. But what do we get ? Just unbridled targeting because we are an easy target.
I hope Indian Americans realize that you can change your name to Elizabeth but it won’t change anything in front of these people. Learn from other Asian communities. Be proud to be an Indian or a Hindu or a Sikh. Start organizing yourself. Start lobbying to protect your interests. Some of you just don’t have the balls to stand up and fight. Some do and I am happy for them.
You can hate the BJP if you want but don’t show your back on this country. Remember that.

sources.news_title: Iran War Plays Major Role in Midterm Blowout
Iran War Weighed Heavily on Midterm Voters as Gas Prices Fueled GOP Backlash, Exit Polls Find
Trump Backs Iran War After JD Vance's Post-Midterms Rebuke
Trump Acknowledges Iran War's Role in Republicans' Midterm Meltdown, But Says He Doesn't Regret It
Iran conflict was 'crucial' factor in Republican rout: Exit polls
sources.text:
Ninety-three percent of voters said that the conflict in Iran impacted their choices.
The lengthy and unpopular conflict in Iran has evidently had an outsized impact on the midterm election.
Exit polling conducted by NBC News and other media outfits showed that when thinking about their vote for Congress, 34% of voters said that the conflict in Iran was "crucial"; 40% said it was a "major factor"; and 19% said it was a "minor factor."
'The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least.'
Twenty-seven percent of those who said the conflict was "crucial" and 42% of those who said it was a "major factor" were Republicans.
Weeks ahead of the election, a Gallup survey indicated that Iran was a top issue among voters, with 47% of respondents stating that the situation in Iran was "extremely important" and 30% saying it was "very important."
After Republicans lost the U.S. House and Senate in a landslide on Tuesday, President Donald Trump acknowledged in a phone interview with Fox News that "part of it was Iran." He also admitted that the conflict drove up gasoline prices and that price increases hurt Republicans at the polls.
The president suggested, however, that historically, the military operation in Iran is "going to be much more important than this evening because you can't let the number-one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon." He also said that he "had no choice," in part because the nuclear deal brokered by former President Barack Obama "was the road to a nuclear weapon."
RELATED: Trump’s 2024 coalition was a loan. The bill just came due.
Trump was long a critic of his predecessors' costly foreign entanglements, stating both that he would end "the era of endless wars" and that it was not the job of American forces to "solve ancient conflicts in faraway lands that many people have not even heard of."
After brokering numerous peaceful resolutions between warring parties, Trump kicked off a conflict with Iran on Feb. 28.
While there were clear indications that such a military operation would be unpopular, a chorus of interventionists inside and outside Congress suggested it was worthwhile. The Washington Post's Marc Thiessen, for instance, penned an op-ed in January titled "There is no U.S. downside to striking the Iranian regime."
Support for the unresolved conflict — the projected cost of which the Pentagon told Congress last month was roughly $47.1 billion — currently sits at 35.9%, according to the Silver Bulletin's polling average. Opposition sits at 56.5%.
Despite the unpopularity of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and the apparent backlash by voters, Trump told the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday that he "did the right thing" and if afforded a do-over, he "would have done it again."
"The Iranian regime is evil. Few people have been as consistently vocal on this issue as I have," BlazeTV host Steve Deace wrote in an aftermath reflection. "But it’s one thing to use American air power to ensure Iran does not develop a nuclear weapon and quite another to drag our military and economy into a months-long quagmire with no end in sight and no clear definition of victory."
BlazeTV host Auron MacIntyre tweeted, "The real retard right were the people who told you the war wouldn't matter."
Conservative commentator Matt Walsh wrote, "The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least. A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles."
