The Latest: Trump defends Iran war after voters give Democrats control of Congress
sources.text:
The Latest: Trump defends Iran war after voters give Democrats control of Congress
The midterm election blowout has set up a new era in Washington, with Democrats eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their congressional majorities evaporate in a revolt against President Donald Trump’s policies. Democrats triumphed in several surprise upsets, marking a decisive rejection of unified GOP control of the House and Senate.
Trump acknowledged the Iran war affected the midterms, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the more than 8-month-old conflict. “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters. He struck a conciliatory tone earlier, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, only to later threaten to use his veto power to strike down their agenda.
The fallout for Republicans is only beginning. Vice President JD Vance, a 2028 presidential contender, blamed the war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout. And Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House speaker, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Democrats, meanwhile, are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.
Here’s the latest:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis says gerrymandered districts prevented further losses in House seats
The Republican told Fox News on Wednesday that while his state was “not immune” to the blue wave, they did not suffer as badly as Texas because of the trust built up with voters over the years.
“That was a potential extinction event over there,” DeSantis said of Texas.
The governor addressed criticism over four Florida congressional districts that were redrawn to favor Republicans. Three of them have been won by Democrats.
DeSantis asserted that they started with 20 Republican seats and the redrawn districts helped them hold on to that many.
If the old map had been in effect, they would have lost two of those seats, DeSantis said. The AP has only called 16 of those races.
He called it the “worst midterm for our party since Watergate and maybe since FDR.”
Pennsylvania Gov. Shapiro says there’s antisemitism among both Democrats and Republicans
Antisemitism is a problem nationally and among members of both political parties, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said on CNN.
He was asked Wednesday what he tells Jewish voters who are concerned that some Democrats elected Tuesday are hostile to Israel.
Though no names were mentioned, Abdul El-Sayed, who won his Michigan Senate race, and Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib, who was reelected, have been sharply critical of U.S. military assistance to Israel and the war in Gaza.
“This is not reserved to the Democratic Party,” Shapiro said. “I think you have seen the vice president of the United States peddle antisemitism. You’ve got people on the extremes” in both political parties.
“To me, there is no place for antisemitism in our country, period, just like I think there’s no place for Islamophobia or racism or hatred or bigotry in any form,” Shapiro said.
Cruz says too many Republicans ‘didn’t understand’ or ‘care’ about voters’ pain ahead of midterms
In a long autopsy of his party’s defeat, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz laid out in a post on X why the GOP saw “Watergate-level repudiation” from Americans on Tuesday night.
High gas prices, increases in homes and cars being repossessed, and a record number of people making plasma donations each week were among some of the signs that Americans were struggling, he writes.
“That is very real pain from real Americans, and too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care,” Cruz added.
Golden State Warriors coach jokes about missing out on Trump’s $5,000 check
Steve Kerr, coach of the Golden State Warriors, joked that he had been expecting to receive the $5,000 check Trump had promised to every American adult if Republicans retained control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
But with a sweeping Democratic victory across both chambers of Congress, the four-time NBA championship-winning coach told reporters Wednesday, tongue-in-cheek, that he would be sorry to not receive the money.
“I’m just disappointed because I was looking forward to that $5,000 check we were all going to get,” Kerr said.
Kerr has been outspoken about issues like gun control laws.
Nevada Democrat declares victory in historically red district. AP has not called race
Teresa Benitez-Thompson has declared victory in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District over Republican David Flippo, whose campaign was marred by disputes over his military service record. The AP hasn’t called the race.
The 48-year-old former state lawmaker campaigned as a moderate Democrat with a long history in northern Nevada. She contrasted herself with Flippo, who moved to the district to run for the open seat when Republican incumbent Rep. Mark Amodei announced his retirement.
Benitez-Thompson told reporters Wednesday that a “perfect storm” of factors happened to allow her candidacy to succeed. Republicans didn’t deliver on their promise to lower costs, she said, adding that she would focus on affordability.
“We have to get in there and make a real difference for working families,” she said.
White House defends Trump’s agenda, pledges to ‘defy the odds’ after midterm losses
In a news release Wednesday, the White House laid out what it believes is the “promises” made and kept to the American people as Trump and his allies scramble to respond to Republicans’ stunning electoral defeat.
Securing the border, launching massive deportation efforts and instituting tax cuts are listed as among the 127 policy actions taken so far in Trump’s second term.
“Every time the Radical Left, the Fake News, and the professional panic class have written President Trump’s obituary, they have been wrong. They will be wrong again,” the release says.
It comes hours after Trump acknowledged the Iran war’s effect on his party’s inability to maintain control of Congress, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the more than 8-month-old conflict.
Sen. Chuck Grassley won’t resign to avoid the possibility of a Democrat naming his successor
The 93-year-old Iowa senator isn’t resigning before a Democrat becomes governor in January, a spokesperson says.
Grassley supported Republican Zach Lahn for governor, but Democrat Rob Sand won Tuesday’s election.
During the campaign, Grassley said he didn’t want Sand to have the opportunity to fill his seat if he were unable to finish his term.
“I don’t plan on dying in office,” Grassley said at an event in September. “But if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor.”
Grassley was trying to motivate his base to vote and intends to serve out his full term, according to spokesperson Clare Slattery.
Grassley will be joined in the Senate by Democrat Josh Turek, who was elected on Tuesday.
Democrat concedes in redrawn Tennessee district. AP hasn’t called the race
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson has conceded in the Memphis-area congressional district that was redrawn to favor Republicans.
Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor declared victory Tuesday night. The AP has not called the race.
The district was one of several Southern districts represented by Black Democrats that were redrawn in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court decision weakening the Voting Rights Act.
Pearson said Wednesday that he came close to victory in the gerrymandered district and noted that “Tennessee politics will never be the same.”
“I accept the results of this election for Congress. But, I will not concede to rigged maps, attacks on democracy in Tennessee, or to billionaire control of our political system,” he said.
Montana Democrat says his generation feels ‘lied to’
Wildland firefighter Sam Forstag has declared victory in a Republican-held House seat in Montana over a Trump-backed conservative radio talk show host who conceded. The AP has not called the race.
Forstag, 32, pitched himself to voters as a candidate of modest means who’s struggled financially like many in his generation while government officials insist the economy is fine.
“What we’ve seen in the last years is a little similar to what we saw the last Democratic administration do, that left a whole lot of folks in my generation feeling alienated and lied to,” Forstag told the AP.
Forstag was born the same year Montana voters last sent a Democrat to the House — 1994. He described his campaign as a “ragtag team of 20- and 30-year-olds” sending a message to the country about working-class people fighting for themselves.
Former Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke is retiring from the House seat.
Haley Stevens doesn’t regret endorsement flip-flop in Michigan Senate race
The congresswoman who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed is defending her decision to switch her to endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers in the leadup to Tuesday’s election.
Stevens posted Wednesday on X that she didn’t regret the change but that she originally endorsed El-Sayed. She pointed to her strong support for U.S. ally Israel.
El-Sayed, who won the Senate seat, has been a vocal critic of Israel. He’s faced criticism for saying that “hurt people hurt people” after a synagogue attack and for appearing with controversial streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail.
Stevens wrote she had hoped to help El-Sayed moderate but says that “instead, he got worse.”
El-Sayed told the AP that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign.” Republicans had sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt.
Pennsylvania Democrats set goals after series of state wins
They began listing their initial pursuits after flipping control of the state Senate and securing control of state government for the first time since 1992.
Gov. Josh Shapiro, in a news conference Wednesday, singled out sending more aid to mass transit agencies, raising the state minimum wage, protecting abortion rights in the state constitution and building more housing.
State House Majority Leader Matt Bradford preached pragmatism, noting that people are hurting and Democrats must not fail or “lose our way.”
State Rep. Jordan Harris, who leads the House Appropriations Committee, said he was excited to once again pass bills that had died in the Republican-controlled Senate.
“Oh, guess what? We’re gonna dust them bad boys off, because we coming for you!” Jordan told reporters on the Capitol steps.
Mitt Romney takes swipe at ‘bad politics’ following GOP losses
The former Republican presidential nominee noted that “bad policy, bad character make bad politics” following his party’s stunning losses in the midterm elections.
Romney was one of Trump’s most outspoken conservative critics before retiring from the Senate last year. In a Wednesday social media post, he offered a list of grievances against the administration, including the “impulsive Iran war, blanket pardons, apparent corruption, weaponized justice, ICE brutality, mountainous deficits, hiding Epstein, abandoning allies and coddling enemies.”
He added that he was “hoping for a course correction, for the country.”
Romney’s two-decade political career included being elected governor of Massachusetts and U.S. senator for Utah. He lost the 2012 presidential election to incumbent Democrat Barack Obama.
Hakeem Jeffries makes pitch to colleagues as he seeks to become next House speaker
The House Democratic leader is telling colleagues that his goal is to empower them to act decisively in the next Congress on affordability, accountability and American values.
The goals were spelled out in a letter he sent Wednesday asking for their votes to serve as the next speaker.
“America is back!” Jeffries opened with, celebrating the party’s decisive victory in gaining the House majority.
Jeffries cited 10 specific areas where he said the Democratic caucus has delivered during his tenure. Those include exposing the harms that he said were included in Trump’s tax and spending cut bill, particularly the cuts to Medicaid. He also cited the efforts to fight for transparency on the Jeffrey Epstein files and opposition to the “reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”
“The next chapter in our country’s 250-year journey begins today,” Jeffries said.
Black caucus members hold on with slim margins after redistricting push
Many Congressional Black Caucus members survived a mid-decade redistricting push meant to dilute their districts. Caucus leaders and legal scholars say that reflects an unusual turnout surge and warn the maps behind the push remain in place.
Following a Supreme Court redistricting ruling this year, caucus Chair Yvette Clarke warned that up to 19 seats were at risk from GOP-led efforts to redraw districts. The exposure runs through the 2028 cycle, meaning not all of those seats were on the Tuesday ballot.
Still, many caucus members held on, including sweeps from Texas’ Christian Menefee and Missouri’s Emanuel Cleaver and squeakers from Alabama’s Shomari Figures and North Carolina’s Don Davis.
Law experts cautioned against interpreting the midterms as a permanent fix to the altered electoral maps.
“This kind of turnout can’t be a once-in-an-election-cycle kind of phenomenon,” said Melissa Murray, an NYU law professor.
Jaime Harrison says Annie Andrews’ Senate win puts South Carolina Democrats ‘on the radar’
Harrison came up short in his own 2020 Senate challenge to Lindsey Graham. But after Andrews’ win over the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, Harrison says Democrats in his home state feel invigorated.
South Carolina had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly 30 years. Andrews’ win, coupled with the state’s leadoff position in Democrats’ 2028 presidential primaries, provides an fresh opportunity, the former Democratic National Committee chairman said.
“We’re going to start recruiting candidates now,” Harrison said, including a 2028 challenger to Republican Sen. Tim Scott. “All of that stuff has to start now. We can’t wait.”
US stocks surge and the Dow soars more than 1,500 points as oil prices tumble
U.S. stocks soared after Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
Stocks of hospital owners and retailers focused on lower-income Americans led the widespread rally. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the AI industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk. Oil prices tumbled, which helped Treasury yields to ease in the bond market.
Kansas City area helped Democrats’ first US Senate victory in 94 years
Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932, defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall largely because of support in the Kansas City area, where he’s the founding pastor of the 25,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation.
Hamilton received more than 60% of the vote in Johnson and Wyandotte counties. In Kansas’ other 103 counties, Marshall prevailed by a comfortable margin.
Republicans concede in tight races for Ohio attorney general, treasurer
Two prominent Ohio Republicans who ran for state attorney general and treasurer have conceded to their Democratic opponents.
State Auditor Keith Faber conceded the attorney general race to John Kulewicz, while former state Rep. Jay Edwards, who was endorsed by his close friend Vice President JD Vance, conceded the treasurer’s race to Seth Walsh. The AP considers both tight contests too early to call.
Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose has claimed victory in the state auditor’s race, which AP also has not yet called.
House GOP leaders describe ‘staggering’ election defeat ‘far worse’ than expected
Rep. Steve Scalise, in a letter seeking his colleagues’ support for minority leader, wrote, “This is no doubt a challenging time.”
He said the election was “far worse than any of us expected” and that Republicans need to be honest about what happened.
Rep. Jim Jordan, in his own letter, called it a “staggering day” and said Republicans “must learn” from the results.
Both are seeking to succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the House GOP leader in a potentially bruising fight.
Democrats flip attorney general seats blue
Some 30 attorneys general offices were on the ballot, and money poured in from technology and tobacco companies, among others that could face legal scrutiny.
Republican-led Texas, Iowa and Georgia chose Democrats. Minnesota and New York remained blue despite Republican targeting. Other attorney general races have yet to be called.
Democratic officials have filed dozens of lawsuits against the administration, winning favorable rulings in most. Republicans have sued over the years as well.
Harris says she’ll keep advocating on economics and civil rights whether or not she runs again
Former Vice President Kamala Harris said she’s elated to see Democrats wins that are so “geographically, ideologically, generationally” broad. And she told the AP in an interview that she wants to play a part in the 2028 campaigns whether or not she runs.
“I believe I have a responsibility to contribute to the direction of a party, in particular around lifting up voices and issues that I have an experience with,” she said. “It’s how I’ve conducted myself throughout my career, and whether I’m in office or not, that’s the role I feel compelled to play.”
Democrats take control of the Texas state House
It follows historic wins for governor and U.S. Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The Texas House has been in Republican control for a quarter-century.
Democrats made sweeping gains in state governments, shifting the balance of power across historically Republican-leaning states. Voters gave them full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in at least five states where Democrats previously shared power.
How Mississippi’s majority-Black counties voted for Senate
Strong support in majority-Black counties for Scott Colom has helped make Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race unexpectedly competitive for Democrats. As of noon Wednesday, with 96% of the estimated vote counted, Colom had received about 73% of the vote in those counties while running neck-and-neck with incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith statewide.
El-Sayed tells AP that Michigan voters rejected GOP’s ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’
In an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said voters did not engage in Republicans’ efforts to demonize him throughout the cycle for being Muslim and Egyptian.
“Michigan proved just how big we are — rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”
El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after defeating Republican Mike Rogers.
Palestinians in Gaza and Israelis in Jerusalem react to the US election results
Abdel Kareem Al-Najjar, a Khan Younis resident, told the AP he’s pleased the Democrats fared well.
“I am very happy for the Democrats’ win and happy for the Republicans’ loss. This is a victory for what is right. And as they say, you reap what you sow. Trump’s acts and his domestic and foreign policies, especially in the Middle East, are what drove him to this point. Trump and his party.”
Jerusalem resident Suzan Yammer expressed fear and pessimism about what it means for Israel.
“I think it’s pretty scary,” Yammer told the AP. “We seem to be losing at this moment a very stalwart, loyal friend, and to lose a friend that is foundational to the way we’ve organized life here in Israel is … our job is to figure out what we can do in the face of it, and that’s what I’m hoping we can do.”
Michigan Democrat William Lawrence flips House seat
Lawrence defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District.
Lawrence, who previously described himself as a democratic socialist, defeated the freshman incumbent in the battleground district that includes Lansing.
Barrett, an Army veteran who voted against Trump’s ability to wage war against Iran without congressional approval, had flipped the seat from Democratic control in 2024 when Elissa Slotkin ran for Senate instead of seeking reelection to the House.
New York Democratic Rep. Thomas Suozzi wins reelection
Suozzi defeated Republican Michael LiPetri in New York’s 3rd Congressional District. Suozzi was aggressively targeted by Republicans but won in a Long Island district that Trump carried by 4 points in 2024.
A lawyer and accountant, Suozzi has served in Congress since 2016, with a two-year break when he ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2022. LiPetri is a lawyer and former state Assemblyman who prominently touted Trump’s endorsement.
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani says ‘it’s a new dawn in America’
Mamdani said the wave of Democratic victories is a “true reflection of what the American people want, which is change they can feel in their wallets.”
“What last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria. And it is time to put those same people first in our politics, and last night shows us that it’s possible to do so all across the country,” he said.
Asked if progressive Democrats should push for wider changes, the democratic socialist mayor said “foot on the gas.”
“This is the moment where we are seeing people across this country vote for a politics that will mean something,” he said. “We want politics to mean the deliverance of dignity into working people’s lives.”
And then there was just one Republican in Congress who supported impeaching Trump
Come January, Sen. Lisa Murkowski will be alone, now that Rep. David Valadao of California lost to Democrat Randy Villegas.
Valadao had been a GOP survivor, defying the odds to win a series of tough races, but couldn’t overcome Trump’s overwhelming repudiation.
Ten House Republicans, including Valadao, voted to impeach Trump following the Capitol insurrection on Jan. 6, 2021. Seven GOP senators voted to convict him, and of the five who remain, all but Murkowski will be leaving Congress in January.
Trump says he has no regrets about final message to voters
Trump defended his Election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Asked Wednesday if he regrets focusing on problematic project in his final pitch as polls showed voters are primarily concerned about pocketbook issues, he instead went into detail about the pool’s plumbing and paint color.
“I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews,” he said while touring the White House ballroom’s construction.
Trump says he’ll stay out of race to lead House Republicans
Two GOP lawmakers, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan and current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, have announced their intentions to run for Republican House minority leader. Trump has wielded significant influence in past House leadership contests, but said “we’ll stay out of it” this time.
Trump said Speaker Johnson was “fantastic” and that he did not ask him to step down. “The people under him were fantastic, all good people,” Trump said.
Trump is not considering replacing Hegseth but talks him up for Tennessee Senate seat
Much of the post-midterms speculation about potential Cabinet shuffles has centered on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of Trump’s unpopular war with Iran who could be a top target of congressional Democrats.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he is not considering replacing Hegseth, saying “I think he’s doing a very good job.”
Hegseth has been talked about as a potential appointed senator in Tennessee, where GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn won the governor’s race and could pick her interim successor.
“I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that,” Trump said.
Hegseth moved to Tennessee with his family in 2022, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel.
Trump, after Vance post blaming Iran war for election defeat, again defends it
The president was asked about the vice president’s comments Wednesday that the Iran war was to blame for deep GOP losses and said, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term.”
Trump, speaking to reporters as he was showing off the construction of the White House ballroom he ordered, defended the conflict.
“The Iran thing, we had to do and we continue to do it,” Trump said.
Embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller concedes Ohio seat, says he ‘fought earnestly’
Miller lost to Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker and councilman, after remaining in a race that both Ohio’s Republican U.S. senators, one his former father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, had urged him to exit. Moreno’s daughter, Emily, is among several women who had accused Miller of physical abuse. Miller denied it.
Trump had stuck by Miller, a top adviser in his first White House, up through Election Day with a final endorsement on X.
California Democrat Randy Villegas wins House election
He’ll represent California’s 22nd Congressional District, defeating Republican incumbent David Valadao.
Villegas is a progressive who was endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders. He overcame concerns among some Democrats that he would be seen as too liberal for the district in California’s Central Valley. In the primary, national Democrats backed a rival with ties to the party establishment.
Navy vice admiral fired by Hegseth declares victory. AP hasn’t called her House race
Nancy Lacore is running as a Democrat to replace Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, who lost a bid for South Carolina governor.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth never gave a public reason why he fired Lacore, a three-star Navy vice admiral, along with about two dozen other high-ranking military leaders in August 2025. But it spurred Lacore to move to Charleston and run for office.
“That was my goal the whole time, right? When I, when I launched this campaign, I said I’m not done serving, and that’s really what I want to do,” Lacore told reporters Wednesday.
She declared victory over Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt in the coastal 1st District. The Associated Press hasn’t called the race.

sources.news_title: Polls Indicate Iran War Above All Drove Voters Democrat
sources.text:
A blue wave has washed over the United States as the Democrats swept the midterm elections and the reason for it, above all else, was the Iran War and its disastrous effects.
Exit polls have shown that the Middle East conflict launched by Donald Trump in February this year was a “crucial or major factor” for almost three quarters of voters (74%), who ultimately turned out in force against the Republican Party.

sources.news_title: Iran War Drags Republicans Down, Gives Democrats Blowout Victories
sources.text:
When Republicans put America First, they won. When they put Israel First, they lost.
That’s it. That’s the plain and simple of last night’s elections.
Tuesday night showed very clearly that the American people do not want forever war.
They do not want our military fighting a war, any war, for another country when there is no serious threat to our own country.
The elections were a huge rejection of President Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran. The biggest losers were Trump, the war criminal Netanyahu, and the Israel Lobby.
The American people were sickened by the killing and starving of so many thousands in Gaza, especially so many little children.
Some who have national TV or radio platforms or who work for parts of the media owned by Israel First billionaires may try to put other spins on it, but deep inside they surely must know that last night was a repudiation of the Iran War and Netanyahu’s control of the White House and the Congress.
Unfortunately, President Trump and almost every Republican in Congress allowed themselves to be led down a Primrose Path by the fanatical Netanyahu.
AI defines a primrose path as “a course of action, lifestyle or behavior that seems easy, tempting and full of pleasure at first but ultimately leads to ruin, destruction, or serious trouble.”
I was in the same boat as Tucker Carlson and Joe Rogan and many millions who supported President Trump because we certainly didn’t want Kamala Harris, the most far Left member of the Senate, as President.
We hoped, too, that President Trump was not going to turn into a neocon and support more war in the Middle East and that he really believed these words that he said in his inaugural address at the start of this term:
“We will measure our success not only by the battles we win, or the wars we end, but perhaps most importantly by the wars we never get into.”

Just a few days before the House voted in 2002 to go to war in Iraq, I was called down to the White House and put in a little secure room with Codoleeza Rice, President Bush’s National Security Adviser, George Tenet, the head of the CIA, and his Deputy Director, John McLaughlin.
They were all there to put pressure on me to vote for the war in Iraq. This came along with pressure from the Republican leadership. This is why I have such great respect for Thomas Massie, who fought so hard against all the powers that be and mega millions from all over the Country.

sources.news_title: Vance blames Iran war for Republicans' midterms defeat. Trump says he would 'do it again'
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the Trump administration’s ongoing war with Iran was to blame for Republicans’ massive losses in Tuesday’s midterm election, during which Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress.
But President Donald Trump, asked about Vance’s comments, remained committed to the ongoing military action despite “largely” agreeing with Vance about the impact of the war on the election.
The vice president wrote in a lengthy social media post that “the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.”
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said of the Trump administration’s ongoing conflict with Iran. “The president himself said so last night.”
Vance said he spoke with pollsters who told him that many people who voted for Trump in 2024 switched to the Democrats in this election because they were “angry.”
The ABC News Voter Poll found about 4 in 10 House voters nationally said they were angry about the way things were going in the country today and a similar share were dissatisfied.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance wrote.
The vice president in the past has publicly been supportive of the war and slammed the president’s critics over the issue.
Trump often suggested on the campaign trail that the war, and inflated gas prices, were “a small price to pay” to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon.
Asked about Vance’s comments during an event at the White House on Wednesday, Trump called them “largely true,” however he defended his decision to attack Iran, which he has done in the past.
“If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer,” Trump told reporters. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump said he knew Vance’s view of the war from the beginning.
“I know how he feels about it. I think it was — I think it was fine. Yeah, I thought it was good,” Trump said of Vance’s social media post. “I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Asked if he felt the war was worth it, Trump said he did.
“I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice,” he said, later adding, “I can tell you that, as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing differently.”
ABC News’ Voter Poll of House voters found that voters nationally were more focused on other factors, including the cost of living, than the Iran war.
Nationally, 34% of U.S. House voters said that the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote, while 49% said the same about the cost of living and 55% said government corruption was crucial to their vote.
Although the Iran war has led to rising gas prices, voters have said that their concerns over the cost of living weren’t just limited to their receipts at the pump.
The Voter Poll found 59% of House voters nationally saying they were “very concerned” about the cost of healthcare.
About 6 in 10 U.S. House voters said that the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare and 55% said the Trump administration’s policies have made their healthcare costs worse. Just 10% said the Trump administration has improved their healthcare costs, according to the Voter Poll.
Trump’s tariffs have also been costing the typical American household almost $1,000 a year.
Vance said in his X post that an unidentified pollster told him that their “economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch.”
Vance argued that Republicans were not failed by turnout among Trump 2024 voters, saying they “showed up,” but that those Americans, according to a pollster, were “pissed and planning to vote for the other guys.”
He also claimed of Republican turnout that “in no state was it catastrophic.”
“The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” the vice president said.
-ABC News’ Elizabeth Schulze contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Trump Brags About Ballroom in First Speech Since GOP Election Wreckage
sources.text:
Trump Brags About Ballroom After Republican Annihilation in Election
Republicans were just obliterated this election. Donald Trump doesn’t care.
President Donald Trump signs the last piece of steel to be used in construction of the White House ballroom during an event on November 4, one day after Republicans lost Congress in the midterm election.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
President Donald Trump signs the last piece of steel to be used in construction of the White House ballroom during an event on November 4, one day after Republicans lost Congress in the midterm election.
President Trump’s first public speech after a disastrous, resounding midterm election defeat was about the White House ballroom, as he offered the American people deranged ramblings about the only thing he actually seems to care about.
“I doubt there’s a ballroom in the country [with] a 50-foot ceiling,” Trump said outside the construction site of his ballroom on Wednesday, just barely more than 12 hours after Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate in a resounding rejection of his administration’s policies and ideology.
You’d think a president would offer words of encouragement to his party or righteous anger in such a desperate moment. Instead, Trump went full lame-duck mode. “There has never been anything built like this, and it’s for the country, and it’s free, we got it free of charge, thank you very much.… When it’s completed it’ll be the best anywhere in the world.”
Trump on ballroom: The kitchen is going t be top of the line. There has never been anything built like this and it is for the country. When I was in China, we went to the great hall of China, and it is incredible. This is actually larger. pic.twitter.com/S4nQ9MDTrt
The president appeared with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
“Why does Trump spend time on the White House? Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me it’s relaxing.… I love construction,” Trump continued. “That’s what I do, I like beautiful things.”
Trump went on to speak about the ballroom’s kitchen, staircase, roof, and marble veining.
It’s incredible that Trump—who seemed particularly calm at the event—can simply act like nothing happened, after his own unpopular decisions in office resulted in a midterm sweep that could cripple the Republican Party for the next decade. His own vice president, JD Vance, admitted that their war on Iran, the cost of living, inflation, and the administration’s close relationship with Israel lost them the election. But rather than address any of that, the president would prefer to talk about buttresses.
JD Vance Throws Trump Under the Bus for Republicans’ Election Wipeout
Vance is doing his best to break from Trump after Republicans’ devastating losses this election.
ANNABELLE GORDON/AFP/Getty Images
Vice President JD Vance is desperate to save himself from the blue wave—even if that means letting President Donald Trump drown.
Just hours after Democrats seized control of Congress and swept state elections across the country, Vance promptly threw the president under the bus.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X Wednesday, blaming the Iran war without mentioning Trump by name.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
In the early days of Trump’s military onslaught, Vance had expressedsome reluctance about the president’s war plans. But that quickly gave way to the spineless sycophantism we’ve come to expect from the vice president.
In his post on Wednesday, Vance claimed that Republicans’ main problem is that many people who supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election had flipped to support Democratic candidates.
Vance claimed that a pollster—”one of the smartest people I know in politics”—found that voters would return to supporting the GOP if they ended the war in the Middle East, focused on the cost of living and inflation, “put America First,” and changed the U.S. relationship with Israel.
Trump’s eight-month-long “six week war” in Iran has proven to be a major political liability. His military campaign has resulted in the deaths of 22 U.S. service members, and hundreds more injured. Trump’s war is responsible for the deaths of thousands of Iranian civilians, including 120 schoolchildren. The president also oversaw the destruction of multiple U.S bases in the Middle East, a series of deadly military morale issues, and the depletion of the U.S. weapons stockpile, leaving the country more vulnerable to foreign threats.
The war effort has already cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion. That’s enough to pay for one year of Medicare coverage for 5.84 million people, based on previous figures from the Center for American Progress. That doesn’t include the skyrocketing price of gas and consumer goods thanks to the war.
In the words of Dwight D. Eisenhower: “Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed.” It seems that Vance is finally catching on to just how damaging this war has been.
Democrats Take Over Total Control in Four States With Trifecta Power
Democrats have secured a trifecta in four states this election—winning both chambers of the state legislature and the governor’s seat.
Jordan McAlister/Getty Images
Democratic candidates flipped control of multiple state legislatures on Tuesday, clinching electoral trifectas in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, and Pennsylvania.
It was a wildly successful night for Democratic candidates in Congress, but Americans also voted to install Democrats in their state governments across the country.
In Wisconsin, Democrats flipped both the state’s Assembly and Senate. In the state’s Senate, Democrats flipped to an 18–15 majority, an exact inverse of the chamber’s current makeup. In the state Assembly, Democrats secured a 53–46 majority. And Democratic candidate David Crowley was elected to the governor’s office, securing the party an electoral trifecta for the first time in 16 years.
In Minnesota, Democrats clinched majorities in both chambers of the state legislature. In the House, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party has won 72 of 134 seats thus far, surpassing the 68-seat majority. In the state’s Senate, the DFL party held onto its 34-seat majority. When coupled with DFL nominee Senator Amy Klobuchar’s victory in Minnesota’s gubernatorial race, Democrats have achieved trifecta control of the state’s government.
In Michigan, Democrats flipped the state’s House of Representatives. In the 110-seat House, Democrats ousted at least five Republican incumbents to secure at least 50 seats. In the 38-member state Senate, Democrats ousted two GOP incumbents, growing their majority from 20 to 23 seats. Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson was elected to the governor’s office, securing the Democrats’ electoral trifecta in the state.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats also achieved a trifecta by flipping the state’s Senate for the first time since 1993. Ahead of the election on Tuesday, Republicans held a 27–23 majority in the 50-seat state Senate. Democrats flipped three seats on election night. Democrats also increased their majority in the state’s House of Representatives from 103 to 111 seats.
In North Carolina, Democrats flipped control of the state’s House of Representatives for the first time since 2010. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats held 66 seats in the 120-seat House. They needed to flip 12 seats to retake a majority, and by the time all the votes are counted, it’s possible they will have flipped 20. Going into the election, Republicans were just one seat short of a supermajority in the chamber.
As if that wasn’t enough, a few other states appeared to still be on their way to turning their state legislatures blue.
In Texas, the House races remained too close to call on Wednesday morning, but the Democrats were closing in on control of the lowest chamber for the first time since 2003. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats needed to flip at least 14 seats but had already flipped six seats, and they were leading in at least a dozen more Republican-held districts. Meanwhile, Republicans maintained control of the state Senate.
In Arizona, Democrats were poised to take control of the state legislatures for the first time in 60 years and potentially achieve yet another electoral trifecta for the Democratic Party.
Every Democratic Socialist Who Won a National Race This Election
The Democratic Socialists of America had a good night this election.
State Representative Donavan McKinney, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Senator Bernie Sanders, United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain, and Representative Rashida Tlaib during the “People v. The Powerful” campaign event in Detroit, on July 18

State Representative Donavan McKinney, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Senator Bernie Sanders, United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain, and Representative Rashida Tlaib during the “People v. The Powerful” campaign event in Detroit, on July 18
The Democratic Socialists of America are here to stay. One of the most contentious—and misunderstood—political groups in the country rode a wave of popular support to groundbreaking victories this election.
First reanimated by the 2016 Bernie Sanders campaign and reaffirmed since then by a lack of imagination and initiative from the Democratic Party’s center, the DSA left wing is now firmly entrenched within the Democratic machine. Eleven DSA House and mayoral candidates won Tuesday after running on platforms emphasizing affordability, ending U.S. aid to Israel, and expanding access to health care. As a whole, with down ballot races included, DSA-endorsed candidates won 149 of the 294 races they ran in, with 37 races still undecided. Eight of them will be in the U.S. Congress next year. Here are the biggest victors:

Maxine Wallace/The Washington Post/Getty Images

Rashida Tlaib — House of Representatives, Michigan

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — House of Representatives, New York
Democrats Won Control of Congress. Here’s What They Can Do Now.
Democrats have a real chance to do something with their victory this election.
Kevin Carter/Getty Images
A blue wave has washed over the nation, as Democrats retake both the House and the Senate and voters across the country offer a resounding rebuke of President Donald Trump and his far-right administration. Democrats have flipped both the House and Senate, and New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries will become the first Black House speaker. Meanwhile, Democratic Senate candidates flipped seven seats previously carried by Trump and the GOP. But now that the Democrats will control Congress in January, what can they do? And will they actually do it?
Impeachment
Let’s start here first, since it’s at the top of everyone’s mind.
Democrats now have the numbers to impeach Trump or any of his Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has headed the disastrous, destructive, and expensive war on Iran, is reportedly the Democratic majority’s top target.
The impeachment process can begin in the House of Representatives with a simple majority, which Democrats now have. The trial then moves to the Senate. To actually convict and remove, they will need a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which means the Democrats will need some Republican votes.
While impeachment of Trump is certainly a possibility, there is a greater likelihood that Democrats will be able to convict and remove someone like Hegseth, who has been losing Republican allies over the course of the Iran war.
Investigations
The Democrats could also open a wide array of investigations into the Trump administration, much like they did last time they controlled the House in 2018.
This is certainly the most corrupt administration in modern history. Some top investigation targets could include:
The Epstein Files
This issue won’t be going anywhere, especially with a Democratic-controlled Congress. The party has called for a renewed push to reopen investigations into the world of infamous sex predator Jeffrey Epstein—and the Trump administration’s botched rollout of the files. Just last week, House Judiciary Democrats released a report on the cover-up, noting that “DOJ and FBI shut down investigations and withheld evidence while claiming no basis to prosecute or even investigate any additional Epstein co-conspirators.”
The UAE chips affair
In May, a firm of Emirati royal Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan gave $2 billion to World Liberty Financial Group, a crypto company controlled by the families of Trump and his Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff. Two weeks later, the Trump administration completed a deal to give the United Arab Emirates hundreds of thousands of the world’s most valuable AI chips—in an extremely questionable display of ethics.
Jared Kushner
Last month, a new book reported that the president’s son-in-law had his phone hacked during the first Trump administration, which revealed Kushner’s control of foreign slush funds filled by the leaders of the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Israel. The report exposed how Kushner appeared to make deals with those governments to violently transform Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, and the greater Middle East region.
Trump selling early access to Truth Social
Trump and his aide Natalie Harp were sued in September over the “Truth API” program, which offers Truth Social users early access to posts from government officials in exchange for $100,000 a month. Watchdog groups alleged that Trump is using the media company that he uses as a personal bulletin board to run a pay-to-play scheme, offering crucial information that affects global markets and policy decisions to whoever can afford it.
Heavily Impede the Trump Agenda While Pushing Their Own
At a bare minimum, any Republican bill or policy is all but guaranteed to die in Congress, as Republicans will need Democratic votes every time to pass anything. The Democrats’ majority allows them to go on the offensive, and it has been reported that they have a “First 100 Hours” agenda focused on ending Trump’s antagonistic and expensive foreign tariffs, reviving expired Affordable Care Act health care premium subsidies, and reversing almost $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts. They could also make efforts to impede the Iran war.
Unfortunately, to make their bill veto-proof, Democrats will need a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate, meaning they will need Republicans to join them. Whether Trump will veto will depend on his own temperament, as he may be likely to reject legislation from a Democratic Congress in his lame-duck era, regardless of how popular or bipartisan it is.

Trump Accepts Democratic Midterm Victory but Threatens Renewed Military Action Against Iran as War’s Economic Toll Reverberates Across America
By: Fern Sidman
President Donald Trump has acknowledged the Republican Party’s sweeping defeat in the 2026 midterm elections while issuing an unmistakable warning to Iran that additional American military operations remain a distinct possibility, underscoring the increasingly consequential intersection of domestic political upheaval and an unresolved Middle Eastern conflict.
In remarks reported on Wednesday by Anadolu Agency, Trump congratulated Democrats on their electoral performance, expressed a willingness to negotiate with the incoming congressional leadership and simultaneously defended his administration’s military campaign against Tehran, notwithstanding its mounting economic and political repercussions.
The president conceded that higher gasoline prices resulting from the confrontation with Iran may have contributed to Republican losses, but maintained that preventing the Iranian government from acquiring nuclear weapons justified the immediate financial consequences. “People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying … more for gasoline,” Trump told Fox News, according to Anadolu Agency. He characterized the economic disruption as “a short-term problem, but for long-term gain.”
The remarks constituted a significant acknowledgment that the prolonged conflict had become an electoral liability, particularly as Democrats successfully emphasized household affordability, energy costs and dissatisfaction with the administration’s foreign-policy priorities.
Reuters similarly reported that Trump recognized the war’s contribution to Republican defeats, although he insisted that his decision to confront Iran militarily had been justified and that he would make the same decision again.
The president nevertheless rejected suggestions that the election constituted a personal repudiation, maintaining that Republicans would have achieved a decisive victory had his name appeared on the ballot.
According to the Anadolu Agency report, Trump praised Democratic candidates for campaigning “hard” and indicated that bipartisan negotiations could produce agreements on several contentious issues, including immigration.
His willingness to recognize the results was accompanied by an equally emphatic declaration that Democratic congressional majorities would not enjoy unrestricted legislative authority.
Speaking about his constitutional veto power, Trump warned that he would reject measures he considered unacceptable, while expressing reluctance to spend the remainder of his presidency blocking legislation. Reuters reported that the president anticipated substantial disagreements with Democratic lawmakers but believed negotiations would eventually become necessary.
The emerging congressional realignment threatens to complicate the administration’s legislative priorities, potentially subjecting military expenditures, executive decisions and foreign-policy initiatives to more aggressive oversight.
Yet Trump’s immediate attention remained directed toward Tehran. Anadolu Agency reported that the president warned American forces could “finish the job” should Iranian authorities fail to cooperate, while simultaneously suggesting that a diplomatic settlement remained possible if it imposed binding restrictions preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
The dual message reflected an administration continuing to employ military pressure alongside negotiations, even as the political costs of confrontation became increasingly apparent.
According to a report at CBS News, American forces conducted limited strikes against Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week after what American officials described as an Iranian attack against a United States aircraft.
Iranian officials subsequently disputed the adequacy of Washington’s response to proposals intended to resolve the confrontation.
Senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei described the American response as “not convincing,” insisting that Tehran’s conditions must be addressed before the strategically vital maritime passage could fully reopen.
CBS News also reported that diplomatic intermediaries, including Qatar and Pakistan, were attempting to bridge disagreements concerning maritime access, economic restrictions and the cessation of regional hostilities.
The continuing confrontation has profound implications for international energy markets because the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world’s most strategically significant petroleum transportation routes.
Meanwhile, the Associated Press reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pressed for additional American military action against Iran, although Trump appeared inclined to allow negotiations further opportunities before deciding upon another extensive offensive.
The divergent pressures confronting Washington have become particularly pronounced following the Democratic electoral victories.
A Congress controlled by the opposition could intensify scrutiny of military objectives, financial expenditures and the administration’s authority to sustain or expand operations against Iran. Nevertheless, congressional control does not automatically eliminate the president’s ability to authorize military action, particularly when administration officials characterize operations as necessary to protect American forces.
The president’s criticism of Fox News for providing extensive airtime to Democratic opponents further illustrated his dissatisfaction with the political environment surrounding the election. For Trump, the immediate challenge involves reconciling his commitment to preventing Iranian nuclear proliferation with mounting domestic demands for economic stability and an end to prolonged military uncertainty.
For Tehran, the administration’s electoral reversals may create additional diplomatic opportunities, although Trump’s latest warnings demonstrate that American military pressure remains an integral component of his strategy.
Ultimately, the president’s response to the midterms revealed two parallel realities: a willingness to recognize an unfavorable democratic verdict and an unwavering determination to retain strategic leverage over Iran.
Whether diplomacy can produce an enforceable nuclear agreement before renewed hostilities further destabilize the region remains among the most consequential questions confronting Washington.

sources.news_title: Trump Concedes Iran Played a Role in GOP Midterm Defeat, But Doesn't Regret it: 'I Did The Right Thing'
sources.text:
Trump Concedes Iran Played a Role in GOP Midterm Defeat, But Doesn’t Regret it: ‘I Did The Right Thing’
"I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," Trump said.
President Donald Trump acknowledged that the Iran war, which contributed to soaring gas prices in the U.S. and around the world, played a role in the Democratic wave in the midterms, but said he doesn't regret his decision.
"Iran was a piece of it," the president told The Wall Street Journal as the results came in. "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he added.
Trump went on to note that rising gas prices, rather than the war itself, turned voters against the Republican party.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed the results, saying voters rejected the war.
"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf wrote on X.
Ghalibaf, who has been involved in negotiations with Washington, also issued a warning to the U.S. government, saying it would face a "Nightmare" if it ignored voters to serve what he called "international paymasters and blackmailers."
The cost of living, partly driven by the war, fueled the Democratic wave. Almost four in five voters said the rising cost of living would be a very important or the most important factor in their vote. 43% said Democrats were better on the issue, compared to 32% of Republicans.
Before the election, an AP-NORC survey found that 64% of registered voters considered the Iran war an important issue. The economy ranked higher at 85%.
Democrats will gain greater oversight of Trump's military decisions when the new Congress takes office on Jan. 3. Their control of congressional committees will allow them to call hearings, demand documents and investigate spending on the conflict.
In fact, Rep. Robert Garcia, set to become the Chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the president to "lawyer up."
In a statement on Tuesday night, Garcia recalled that he has "vowed to take on the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files."
With a majority in the Lower House, Democrats will be able to issue subpoenas as part of oversight investigations.
The party could also seek limits on additional war funding or bring legislation challenging military operations to a vote. Such measures would still face the possibility of a presidential veto, and Democrats would need sufficient support in Congress to overcome one.
Trump has given no indication that the election result will stop him from ordering further strikes. In his Fox News interview, he said additional military action remained an option if Tehran failed to cooperate, although he continued to hold out the possibility of an agreement.

sources.news_title: Trump admits Iran war part blame for Democrat spanking
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has accepted the Iran war played a role in the Republicans' staggering midterm election losses, as the Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and challenge his legislative agenda.
Subscribe now for unlimited access.
or signup to continue reading
In an interview with Fox News, Trump said the Middle East conflict had weighed on Republican candidates, even as voters backed his handling of it.
"I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," the 80-year-old said, as he entered his final two years in office as a lame duck leader.
Democrat candidates flipped Republican-held Senate seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, where the president had personally chosen his party's nominees or tried to rally voters on their behalf with campaign stops.
Trump's hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep scepticism.
Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina after facing questions about her inexperience during her campaign.
Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in Texas, was impeached by his own party in 2023 over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce.
But Trump backed him instead of powerful senator John Cornyn, whom he viewed as not sufficiently supportive.
Trump's loyalty pressures also led incumbent Republican senator Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president.
To try to keep that seat in Republican hands, Trump backed his close ally Michael Whatley, who lost to Democrat Roy Cooper.
Even candidates who sought to distance themselves from Trump were unable to escape voters' wrath.
In Maine, Republican incumbent Susan Collins had her 30-year Senate career end on Tuesday, despite emphasising her willingness to break with the president during the campaign.
Trump was also dealt twin defeats in two midwestern states that had borne the brunt of high diesel prices and his tariff war: Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, while Republican Ashley Hinson lost to Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.
A keenly watched race in Michigan went to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed over Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate - and noted in his victory speech to supporters how his opponents had attacked his difference to them.
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown regained the Senate seat that he lost two years ago, defeating appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted in a state where Trump and Vice-President JD Vance repeatedly campaigned.
With Husted, Trump had an odd fixation on his physique, frequently admiring the former football player's body during campaign rallies in Ohio and elsewhere around the country.
Democrats also retained a key Senate seat in Georgia, where another one of Trump's endorsed candidates faced controversy.
In that race, Democrat Jon Ossoff defeated Republican Mike Collins, a Trump acolyte who struggled to defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.
In another sign of Republican weakness, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Texas Governor Greg Abbott, whom Trump had endorsed and repeatedly praised.
Trump placed himself front and centre in voters' minds, urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot, which was a major gamble.
He told Fox he would accept the election results and congratulated the Democrats for their string of victories.
"The Democrats did a good job. They fought hard," he conceded.
But he maintained the midterms were not a referendum on him, saying: "I don't view it as a hit on me."
The results leave Trump - who watched the results roll in from the White House - with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad.
A Democratic majority will be armed with control of committees, bigger budgets and staff, and subpoena powers that could compel the administration to be responsive to Congress.
The president is also bracing for major legislative fights, saying he had a "strong veto" to use when Democrats sent "insane" bills to his desk.
"And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together."
With AP

Trump links Republican midterm losses to Iran war and higher fuel prices
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to Republican losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
“Iran was a piece of it,” Trump told The Wall Street Journal in a phone interview on Tuesday night. He said he did not regret launching the war earlier this year.
Speaking to Fox News on Wednesday, Trump said he believed voters supported his approach to Iran but had been reluctant to bear the cost at the pump.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran, but they really probably weren't willing to do the short-term consequence of paying ... more for gasoline," Trump said, describing higher fuel prices as "a short-term problem, but for long-term gain."
Trump warned that US forces could "finish the job" if Tehran failed to cooperate, though he said a diplomatic agreement was still possible if it set binding limits on nuclear weapons.
He also defended his decision to cut US aid to Israel, saying the country has "become quite rich" and no longer needs $4 billion a year in assistance.
Trump told the WSJ he had no plans to make personnel changes in his administration and voiced support for Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has led the US war effort.
Working with Democrats
The Democratic victories give the party the votes to block Trump’s legislation in either chamber during the final two years of his term.
“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday as he watched election returns at the White House.
“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out,” he added.
Trump praised Democratic candidates for fighting "hard" and told Fox News he could work with the party "on a lot of things," including immigration.
He also said he expected Democrats to send him legislation he considered "insane" and that he would veto it.
In a separate interview with Politico, Trump said he would prefer to work with lawmakers rather than spend the next two years vetoing bills.

sources.news_title: Could Democrats bring an end to the Iran war?
sources.text:
Midterm elections in the United States typically centre around the bread-and-butter issues that Americans deal with on a daily basis. This year’s contest was an exception in one respect – many of the cost-of-living problems the American electorate is confronting are linked to President Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran that nobody in the Middle East, bar Israel, thought was a good idea. Trump’s approval ratings are hovering in the mid-thirties, in large measure due to the conflict and all of the economic costs associated with it. In terms of popularity, the Iran war makes the 2003 Iraq War look good in comparison; a compilation of polls finds that less than 36 per cent support it.
Given Trump’s character and how he’s turned the Oval Office into Nero’s throne, even a casual observer of this president will find a sudden reversal of his foreign policy difficult to imagine
It’s therefore no surprise that Democrats have had a significant victory in the midterms. The fact that Democrats have retaken both the House of Representatives and the Senate through deep red states like South Carolina and Texas reveals all you need to know about how the country views Trump’s second term. The war’s acrid stench is so strong that many of the Republican candidates who tried to run away from it during the campaign became casualties of it.
The question going forward is whether Trump’s foreign policy will change now that he no longer has control of Congress. This is, to put it mildly, unlikely. Any changes will occur at the margins. His overall strategy of bellicosity will remain intact. Coercion will continue to be Trump’s primary method in dealing with friend and foe alike. There might be a trade deal with Canada by the end of the year and perhaps a slight rapprochement with Brazil now that Lula de Silva is settling in for a fourth non-consecutive term. But US foreign policy in the grand scheme is not going to get appreciably better after the election than it was before.
Democrats, of course, won’t be powerless. Control of the House and Senate means control of committees, the legislative agenda and the ability to investigate anything under the sun. Trump will still retain his veto, so even if Democratic-sponsored bills make it to the White House, they’re liable to die a ceremonious death. Still, launching investigations is nothing to sneeze about. Administration officials, from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth (assuming he doesn’t get impeached or fired by Trump) to Secretary of State Marco Rubio will spend more of their time answering requests for information and, if the White House chooses to be obstructionist, congressional subpoenas. The House Democratic leadership has telegraphed three big foreign policy items that will be the centre of their attention: the Iran war, the US military campaign against alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America and how the Pentagon is doling out contracts.
Will those investigations force Trump to retune or at the very least reevaluate his policies? Anything is possible, and a newly empowered Democratic party could attempt to force the issue. Democratic lawmakers might try to attach a provision defunding the Iran war to the overall defence authorisation or appropriations bills, two pieces of legislation the US defence industrial complex needs to continue operating. Senate Democrats blocked consideration of the defence bill over the summer in protest against the war. There could very well be a political showdown down the line, in which the Democratic majority ties funding the government to Trump terminating a war that he’s repeatedly insisted will be over soon. But are Democrats bold enough to do this, particularly if Trump doesn’t budge and the government shuts down for weeks at a time?
Given Trump’s character and how he’s turned the Oval Office into Nero’s throne, even a casual observer of this president will find a sudden reversal of his foreign policy difficult to imagine. This would be a shame because there is plenty to fix, the war in the Persian Gulf being the prime item on the chopping block. Repeated US bombing waves against Iran’s military infrastructure, the latest occurring on the eve of election day, have failed to produce the Iranian capitulation so many of the war’s cheerleaders predicted at the start. If anything, the off-and-on bombing has reaffirmed a belief within the Iranian political system that escalation may be preferable to a peace deal that Trump won’t abide by anyway. The war has done incredible damage to Washington’s system of military bases in the Middle East, with hundreds of structures and weapons systems damaged and some of the US military’s central nodes in the region, like the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, severely impacted. The region’s leaders are preparing for further destruction ahead as Trump’s military advisers give him a larger target list to work off of. If Trump was smart, he’d cut his losses. But we’re unlikely to see this.
What about the war in Ukraine? Will there be any shifts in the US approach there?
While it’s hard to predict, there’s a decent chance that a more adversarial Congress will hold Trump’s feet to the fire and force him to disburse more military aid to Kyiv. Even some Republicans on the national security committees are a bit skittish about Trump’s diplomatic approach, which essentially revolves around bribing Russian President Vladimir Putin with economic goodies to make peace. Lawmakers were already aghast when Starlink was throttled for Ukrainian troops in the field and when Trump agreed to buy Russian diesel, a decision that will give the Kremlin billions of extra dollars for a war effort the president himself wants to end.
Congressional pressure aside, Trump won’t be giving up on the idea of engagement with Russia. Nor should he; after all, Washington and Moscow were at cross-purposes on a whole slew of issues during the Cold War, yet still kept communication channels open to ensure mixed signals didn’t degenerate into a direct conflict between them. Yet on Ukraine specifically, we should be highly sceptical of pushing Putin into a peace deal. Moscow has demonstrated throughout the conflict that military victory in the Donbas is still more important than any of the economic and political concessions Russia would receive after a peace agreement was clinched.
The election results tonight will complicate Trump’s foreign policy agenda. But they won’t stop it.
