sources.news_title: Exit Poll: Iran War Was 'Crucial Or Major' Factor For 3 In 4 Voters
sources.text:
As Republicans see electoral losses across the country, about 74 percent of voters said the Iran war was a “crucial or major” factor in their vote for Congress, and Democrats won 63 percent of those voters, according to NBC exit polls.
Only 26 percent said the war was a “minor factor or not a factor,” 70 percent of whom voted Republican and 28 percent of whom voted Democrat.
The divide on the war became even greater when voters were asked whether the Trump administration made the “right decision” or “wrong decision” on “military action against Iran. Over all, 37 percent said it was the “right decision,” 91 percent of whom voted Republican and 7 percent of whom voted Democrat, whereas 63 percent said it was the “wrong decision,” 82 percent of whom voted Democrat and 16 percent of whom voted Republican.
The Iran war was proposed to the American people as a short campaign that would last only weeks. When asked earlier this year about the war’s effect on the midterms, House Speaker Mike Johnson said it would be “wrapped up soon” and that it would be a “blip”:
It will be wrapped up soon. And I talk to the president multiple times a day, and he says the same thing privately that he’s saying publicly. This is a very limited scope of mission and objective. We have virtually accomplished the mission entirely incredibly quickly. That was by design. … So the little blip on the screen right now with Iran and oil prices will be very temporary and quick. … And long-term we’re going to be much better off with some stability in Iran instead of an avowed enemy of the United States and Israel trying to develop nuclear weapons to wipe us off the face of the earth. This is going to be a good thing. So this will be a blip.
“People have short memories and when their cost of living goes down, which is what we’re fiercely devoted to … they’re going to be feeling much better about this, and it’s going to be reflected in the outcome of the election,” Johnson said.
The Iran war had turned unpopular among Republican voters, too, particularly young ones, as Vice President J.D. Vance pointed out, as he asked voters not to throw out Republicans solely based on that fact.
The war did not end quickly, and there were multiple occasions when the war had peace deals in the works that all ended up falling apart. However, as The Federalist reported, the war appeared to be set up for a protracted conflict early on.
With a House majority and a Senate majority, Democrats will have subpoena power over Trump administration officials, meaning they can drag cabinet secretaries before committees for the rest of Trump’s term. Many also expect impeachment proceedings against Trump and likely some cabinet secretaries as well.

sources.news_title: Republicans blame Iran war and tariffs for losses
sources.text:
Republican hopefuls blame Iran war and tariffs for Democratic midterm wins, citing cost of living frustration among voters
Republican candidates vying to succeed Donald Trump in 2028 attributed Democratic success in the U.S. midterms to the Iran war and tariffs.
JD Vance, Ron DeSantis, and Ted Cruz cited the impact on living costs due to Republican losses nationwide, including former strongholds.
They criticised Trump’s prolonged Iran conflict, trade policies, U.S.-Israel relations, and Democratic ads that negatively portrayed conservative candidates.
Ted Cruz stated tariffs raised prices and the Iran war needed to end, emphasising its impact on the election outcome.
Republican reactions
Vance suggested voter anger at Trump for redirecting focus from American issues led to losses.
DeSantis described the elections as near “extinction-level” for Republicans, with Democrats using ads linking Republicans to Jeffrey Epstein and stock trading scandals.
Polling indicated voter frustration with Trump’s economic handling, cited as part of Democratic victories.
Democrats campaigned on affordability and overseeing Trump’s agenda, resulting in wins in Congress and gubernatorial races.
Trump acknowledged the Iran war’s effect on gas prices, acknowledging its role in voter alienation.
Cruz criticised Republicans for ignoring economic concerns and voter dissatisfaction over living costs.

sources.news_title: Trump: Vance is right that we lost because of the war with Iran—gas prices went up—but... I would do it again. | Greek News On Demand / ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΑ ΝΕΑ ΤΩΡΑ
sources.text:
Trump: Vance is right that we lost because of the war with Iran—gas prices went up—but… I would do it again.
The U.S. President insists that if he had been on the ballot, the Republicans would have won the midterm elections; he denies considering the removal of Hegseth.
In his first remarks following the Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections, Donald Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to the loss of the House and the Senate. However, he made it clear that he does not regret the military strike against Tehran and that he would make the exact same decision if faced with the same dilemma again.
Speaking to reporters at the construction site of the new White House banquet hall, the U.S. President acknowledged that the conflict carried a political cost for his party, primarily due to the rise in gasoline prices. At the same time, he largely agreed with the assessment of Vice President-elect JD Vance, who had attributed the Republicans’ electoral defeat to a war with Iran; meanwhile, commenting on relevant reports, he noted that he is not considering replacing Pete Hegseth. “I think he’s doing an excellent job,” he remarked.
Trump, asked whether he considers replacing Hegseth:
No, I think he’s doing a very good job. https://t.co/IAWE8AQlnW
— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 4, 2026
“I knew the war would affect the elections”
When asked about Vance’s statements, Trump acknowledged that the military conflict influenced the voting behavior of Americans. “I think that’s true to a large extent [i.e., that the Republicans were defeated because of the war with Iran], because it caused a slight increase in gasoline prices in the short term,” he stated.
He maintained that he had foreseen that the war would have consequences for the domestic political landscape of the United States. “I knew—I knew that the war would have an impact. But regardless of whether it had an impact or not, Iran cannot be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon,” he emphasized.
“If I had to do it again, I would”
Despite his electoral defeat, Trump defended the decision to take military action against Iran, insisting that preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons is a strategic priority.
“At the same time, if I had to do it again, I would do it again, because in the long run, it is the only solution,” he stated. “You cannot allow Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon,” he added.
The American president also claimed that the military operations had dealt devastating blows to the Iranian armed forces.
“As for this war, I wouldn’t have done anything differently. We have completely dismantled their armed forces. Their navy is gone. Their air force is gone,” he declared.
The Day After for the Republicans
Trump also touched upon the uncertainty surrounding future political candidacies, without offering any specific predictions. “Maybe no one will run. Maybe *he* won’t run. I don’t know who will run,” he said, though he did not clarify in that particular instance whom he was referring to.
He also attributed the Republicans’ electoral losses to the fact that he himself was not a candidate, arguing that the massive support seen at his campaign rallies did not translate to his party’s candidates.
“No, look—I mean, if I had been a candidate, we would have won. You saw the crowds. The rallies were packed—thousands upon thousands of people at every single rally. If I had been on the ballot, we would have won. But they just couldn’t transfer that love. There was so much love at those rallies. It was incredible,” he asserted.
“I will get along well with the Democrats, unless they want to destroy everything.”
When asked whether he would be able to work with the Democrats following their electoral victory, the American President indicated a willingness to engage in discussions with them, while noting that he still retains the power of the presidential veto.
“I will probably get along well with the Democrats, unless they decide to be destructive. But I have the veto power. So, if we don’t like what they’re doing… They’ve already called and want to discuss various issues, and that’s fine,” he said. Furthermore, when asked if he was concerned about the possibility of the Democrats attempting to impeach him, Trump categorically dismissed the notion that such a process would affect him.
“Not in the slightest. I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that. I mean, impeachment for no reason? For what? Because we have a successful country? Our country is more successful today than at any other time in its history,” he insisted.

Ο Αμερικανός πρόεδρος υποστήριξε επίσης ότι οι στρατιωτικές επιχειρήσεις έχουν προκαλέσει συντριπτικά πλήγματα στις ιρανικές ένοπλες δυνάμεις.

Απέδωσε, δε, τις εκλογικές απώλειες των Ρεπουμπλικανών και στο γεγονός ότι ο ίδιος δεν ήταν υποψήφιος, υποστηρίζοντας ότι η μεγάλη υποστήριξη που συγκέντρωναν οι προεκλογικές του συγκεντρώσεις δεν μεταφέρθηκε στους υποψηφίους του κόμματός του.
«Όχι, κοιτάξτε. Θέλω να πω, αν ήμουν υποψήφιος, θα είχαμε κερδίσει. Είδατε τον κόσμο. Ήταν κατάμεστες οι συγκεντρώσεις, χιλιάδες και χιλιάδες άνθρωποι σε κάθε προεκλογική συγκέντρωση. Και αν ήμουν στο ψηφοδέλτιο, θα είχαμε νικήσει. Αλλά απλώς δεν κατάφεραν να μεταφέρουν αυτή την αγάπη. Υπήρχε τόση αγάπη σε εκείνες τις συγκεντρώσεις. Ήταν απίστευτο» υποστήριξε.
«Θα τα πάω καλά με τους Δημοκρατικούς, εκτός αν θελήσουν να καταστρέψουν τα πάντα»
Σε ερώτηση για το εάν θα μπορέσει να συνεργαστεί με τους Δημοκρατικούς μετά την εκλογική νίκη τους, ο Αμερικανός πρόεδρος εμφανίστηκε διατεθειμένος να συζητήσει μαζί τους, υπενθυμίζοντας πάντως ότι εξακολουθεί να διαθέτει την εξουσία του προεδρικού βέτο.
«Πιθανότατα θα τα πάω καλά με τους Δημοκρατικούς, εκτός αν θελήσουν να είναι καταστροφικοί. Αλλά έχω την εξουσία του βέτο. Επομένως, αν δεν μας αρέσει αυτό που κάνουν… Έχουν ήδη τηλεφωνήσει και θέλουν να συζητήσουμε διάφορα θέματα, και αυτό είναι εντάξει» είπε, ενώ, ερωτηθείς εάν ανησυχεί για το ενδεχόμενο οι Δημοκρατικοί να επιχειρήσουν την παραπομπή του, ο Τραμπ απέρριψε κατηγορηματικά την πιθανότητα να τον επηρεάσει μια τέτοια διαδικασία.
«Ούτε στο ελάχιστο. Νομίζω ότι θα κατέστρεφε το Δημοκρατικό Κόμμα, αν το έκαναν αυτό. Γιατί παραπομπή χωρίς κανέναν λόγο; Για ποιο πράγμα; Επειδή έχουμε μια επιτυχημένη χώρα; Η χώρα μας είναι σήμερα πιο επιτυχημένη από οποιαδήποτε άλλη στιγμή στην ιστορία της» επέμεινε ακόμη.

sources.news_title: Trump on the Iran war: it “largely” cost the midterms, but he would do it again; he says he is keeping Hegseth
sources.text:
Donald Trump admitted on Wednesday, November 4, that the war with Iran cost Republicans in the midterm elections, but argued that he would take the same decision again. Speaking to reporters in Washington, the US president called Vice President JD Vance’s assessment that the conflict was the reason for the defeat “largely correct”, because, he said, the war “raised gasoline a little for a short time”.
“You can’t let Iran get a nuclear weapon. You have no other choice,” he said. Trump claimed he had expected a much bigger rise in oil prices and proceeded on that assumption, warning that without action “everything you see here might not be here someday”. “We had to do that with Iran, and we keep doing it,” he added.
Vance’s post and Hegseth’s future
A few hours earlier Vance had gone a step further in a post on X: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” The vice president challenged supporters of the war to prove it was worth losing the Senate for six years. On the night of Tuesday, November 3, Trump had attributed only part of the defeat to the war. At the start of the conflict he had said Vance was “maybe less enthusiastic” about the idea.
The president said he was “a little surprised” by the size of the defeat and accepted the result. Asked whether he is considering replacing War Secretary Pete Hegseth, he ruled it out: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.” Earlier the same day CBS News had reported, citing several sources, that Trump was asking associates whether Hegseth should stay, with one source naming Florida Governor Ron DeSantis as a possible replacement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said the president has “full confidence” in the secretary.
On the Democratic majority in Congress, Trump said he would get along with them, “unless they want to act destructively”, reminding them that he holds the veto. He also claimed Republicans would have won by a landslide had he been a candidate himself.
Majorities in both chambers for the Democrats
Democrats took the House of Representatives with at least 228 of 435 seats and gained seven Senate seats from Republicans, in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina, reaching at least 54 of 100. It is the first time in two decades that a Republican president has lost both chambers, the last precedent being George W. Bush in 2006. See our report on the Democratic win in the Senate.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said the war with Iran “must end”, and a similar message came from Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become House Speaker. From January the new majority will gain significant powers of oversight and appropriations. In a message, Mojtaba Khamenei warned that those expecting a change in Washington’s stance are making a “grave mistake”, while the US naval blockade around the Strait of Hormuz continues and negotiations with Tehran have brought no clear progress.

sources.news_title: Iran War Becomes a Political Liability for Trump After Midterm Defeat
sources.text:
International-News
Iran War Becomes a Political Liability for Trump After Midterm Defeat
The president acknowledges the conflict hurt Republicans but refuses to change course. Steve Bannon is demanding an independent investigation, while Tehran warns that a Democratic shift in Congress will not alter U.S. policy
Donald Trump is facing a growing political reckoning over the war with Iran, but the Republican defeat in the midterm elections has done little to change his position on the conflict. The president has conceded that the fighting contributed to his party’s losses, while insisting that the decision to attack Iran was necessary and that he would make it again. Inside his own political movement, however, the demand for answers is becoming harder to ignore. Former Trump adviser Steve Bannon is now calling for an independent presidential commission to investigate how the United States entered the war and disclose its findings to the public.
The dispute reaches beyond the White House. Vice President JD Vance has described the conflict as a catastrophe for the Republican Party, while Bannon has argued that Americans — particularly younger voters who supported Trump on a promise to avoid new wars — have lost confidence in the explanations offered for the military campaign. In Tehran, meanwhile, the election result is being presented as a political blow to Trump, not as evidence that Washington is about to change its approach to Iran.
Bannon made his case on his podcast, Bannon’s WarRoom, calling for a commission made up of American citizens and institutions to examine the events surrounding the war. He said the inquiry should investigate the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and the subsequent decisions that drew the United States into the conflict. If Israel chose not to conduct an investigation for political reasons, he said, that was a decision for Israel to make. But the United States had been pulled into a war with significant consequences for American politics, he argued, and the public deserved an independent account of what happened.
His proposed inquiry would also examine how, years after Oct. 7, the United States became involved in Operation Midnight Hammer and what Bannon described as a second phase: regime change. National defense, security and the administration’s understanding of the conflict should be scrutinized by independent third parties, he said, adding that the process should begin immediately. His remarks, reported by The Washington Post, connect the war directly to the loss of support among voters who had backed Trump in 2024 expecting him to keep the United States out of another major conflict.
Trump has acknowledged the electoral damage, including the effect of higher gasoline prices. Speaking to reporters at the construction site of the White House ballroom, he said Vance’s assessment was largely correct and suggested that the short-term rise in fuel costs had probably contributed to the Republican defeat. But he rejected any suggestion that the military campaign had been a mistake. The United States could not allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon, he said, adding that the war had been worth the cost and that he would not have acted differently.
The conflict has inflicted damage across the region estimated at tens of billions of dollars and has had wider consequences for global energy costs. Analysts warn that further escalation could push energy prices higher, although Brent crude fell below $95 a barrel after the midterm vote. The administration is weighing several possible courses. Haggerty has argued for maintaining the current strategy of defensive strikes and a naval blockade. David Schenker, a former assistant secretary of state, has suggested striking the nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain before moving toward de-escalation and a deal that would restore freedom of navigation and ease sanctions. Schenker has cautioned that Tehran may see Trump as weakened and constrained by Congress, but that assumption could prove wrong.
Regional governments are watching for clues about the next phase. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged further military action, while Middle Eastern officials have reported signals from the Trump administration suggesting that operations could intensify after the elections. The possibility of escalation therefore remains on the table even as the political costs of the war become more visible in Washington.
Iran’s response to the midterm results has been notably cautious beneath its public claims of victory. Al Jazeera’s analysis of Iranian media coverage describes two separate conclusions in Tehran: the war has imposed a political cost on Trump, but the change in congressional power does not guarantee a shift in U.S. policy. Iran’s Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has dismissed the idea that changes in American political parties or concessions to Washington could alter what he describes as the hostility of the United States toward the Iranian people. Anyone who believes otherwise, he said, is under a “complete illusion.” His remarks came as Iran marked the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, with official events and public demonstrations held for the National Day of Fighting Global Arrogance.
Iranian outlets have reflected the same combination of triumphalism and caution. Tasnim, an agency historically linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, framed the Republican setback as a victory for Iran, declaring in a headline that Trump had “lost to Iran” and suffered a major defeat in the Senate. Yet the agency warned against placing hopes in the Democrats, arguing that the two American parties do not differ fundamentally in their approach to Tehran and that Iranian policy should not depend on which party controls Congress or the White House. State broadcaster Irib used the phrase “regime change in America” to describe the shift in congressional power — a reference to the change in the congressional majority, not to a transformation of the U.S. system of government.
The semi-official Fars news agency focused on the erosion of Trump’s support in traditionally Republican strongholds. Its analysis, titled “The Fall of the Red Walls: Why Did Trump Lose Even in His Strongholds?”, argued that dissatisfaction had spread beyond the president’s usual opponents and reached voters who had helped return him to the White House. It pointed to the cost of living, economic anxieties and dissatisfaction with the administration’s handling of Iran, while warning against attributing the defeat to the war alone. The result, Fars argued, reflected the combined effect of domestic and foreign policy on voters.
That distinction captures the dilemma confronting Trump. The war has become a source of friction within his own political camp and a factor in the Republican defeat, but neither the president’s defense of the campaign nor Tehran’s skepticism suggests that the conflict is nearing a political resolution. For now, Trump is refusing to retreat, Bannon is demanding an accounting, and Iran is signaling that a change in congressional power will not be enough to change its calculations.

sources.news_title: Trump hits back after JD Vance blamed Iran war for midterm election defeat
sources.text:
US3 min(s) read
Trump hits back after JD Vance blamed Iran war for midterm election defeat
Donald Trump has spoken out following JD Vance's lengthy statement on why the Republicans suffered a humiliating loss in the midterm elections.
Despite the President's perceived confidence, his party has fallen short, leading to him claiming that results did not go his way because he was not on the ballot.
He claimed that if he was, he'd have won 'in a landslide', having used the same excuse when the Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during his first term.
The historic victory saw the Democrats win the Senate and the House, meaning the current government is what is known as a ‘lame duck’ government.
As the Democrats will soon hold the majority of seats in Congress, it means that the party will have more power to influence laws, stop Trump's plans, and have a bigger say in the US' political direction until at least 2028.
Vance took to X after the defeat, writing: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."
Trump's response to Vance's claims
During a White House Q&A session, the 80-year-old has defended his administration's foreign policy.
While Trump acknowledged the effects of the Iran war on the midterms, he stated: “I knew the war was going to impact it, but whether it impacted it or not, Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon.”
He was then asked about his Vice President's detailed X post, which claimed that the election loss was due to the war.
“Well, I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine. I thought it was good,” Trump responded.
He added: “We stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Speaking about whether he had any regrets in how he handled the midterm election campaign, the President insisted once again that he would have won if his name was on the ballot.
“No, look. I mean, if I were on the ballot, we would have won," he claimed to reporters, adding: "You saw the people that were packed thousands and thousands of people at every rally, and if I was on the ballot, we would have won.”
Trump insisted: “But...you just couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies. It was incredible. We weren't able to transfer the love to candidates.”
JD Vance's statement on X
Once a catastrophic Republican loss became clear, Vance clarified via a lengthy post: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.
"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
He also addressed voters who used their vote to hold the Trump administration accountable for the decisions made over the last two years; he admitted: "To the people who are pi***d off and want to say, 'I told you so': you're right, you did tell us so.
"Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."
Bizarrely, the vice president also argued that he remains 'hopeful about our country.'

sources.text:
TRUMP ACKNOWLEDGES IRAN WAR HELPED COST REPUBLICANS CONGRESS
Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war in Iran contributed to Republican losses in the midterms, as Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. He nevertheless defended the decision to launch the war, saying he would do it again.
Trump pointed particularly to higher gasoline prices. But the consequences stretched across months, adding to the financial pressure on American households and becoming a major campaign issue. Calling that simply a short-term inconvenience overlooks the burden voters were carrying. 
For Ukraine, the distinction matters. Kyiv cannot be made responsible for Washington’s decisions in the Middle East or the political consequences that followed. Ukraine is fighting to survive Russia’s invasion, and its defence should never become a convenient explanation for another administration’s failures.
Zelenskyy has continued making Ukraine’s case under immense pressure from its most powerful partner: expressing gratitude for American assistance while defending his country’s sovereignty and challenging narratives that shift responsibility away from Russia.
That requires resolve. Maintaining a vital relationship with Washington does not mean accepting every accusation or surrendering Ukraine’s right to determine its future.
The election was decided by American voters for many reasons. Trump’s own acknowledgment makes one thing clear: the consequences of his Iran policy cannot simply be laid at Ukraine’s door.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the Iran war has been worth it despite acknowledging its role in losses in US midterm elections in which his Republican party lost control of Congress.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he told reporters.
The Iran war was responsible for a spike in gasoline prices that were seen as a strong factor in why Democrats made big gains in the elections.
Trump said the war has been worth it to stop Tehran from “having a nuclear weapon.”
He said he was okay with Vice President JD Vance’s social media post earlier on Wednesday in which Vance referred to deep electoral losses and said “the reason we lost is the war.”
“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” Trump said.
Trump also again said that if he had been on the ballot, he believed “we would have won.”
“But they just, you couldn’t transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible and we weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said.

sources.news_title: Trump's Electoral Setback: Iran War, AIPAC and America's crumbling pro-war consensus
sources.text:
Editorial
The results of the US midterm elections are interesting, not simply because Republicans have suffered a political setback, but because the defeat has also exposed the declining influence of the old guard within the Democratic Party, particularly those associated with the pro-Israel lobby, AIPAC, and Washington’s traditional militaristic foreign policy.
The outcome represents a much bigger political message than an ordinary electoral reversal: American voters appear increasingly unwilling to finance endless overseas wars, support unconditional Israeli military adventures or accept a foreign policy that puts the interests of other countries ahead of America’s own domestic priorities.
“Results leave a lesson to White House that winning wars is not about destroying countries, and winning elections is not about starting wars”
Perhaps the most consequential outcome is that President Donald Trump has lost much of the political protection he enjoyed before the elections. Having suffered a major electoral defeat, he now faces a difficult choice: either reconsider the disastrous direction of his Iran policy or attempt to demonstrate American military strength through further escalation. The latter possibility is particularly dangerous because a president who has already suffered a significant political defeat may feel less constrained by electoral considerations when making decisions about war and peace.
Those who once hoped to see Trump emerge as a Nobel Peace Prize winner are now watching from the sidelines, perhaps sipping their lattes and smoking cigars, as the president who promised to end America’s overseas wars finds himself associated with one of the most consequential military confrontations of his presidency.
The irony is difficult to ignore. Trump built much of his political appeal on his criticism of America’s endless wars, his promise to put America first and his commitment to stop conflicts rather than initiate new ones. Yet, his decision to attack Iran, reportedly under considerable pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has placed his administration in direct contradiction with the political promises that helped bring him back to the White House.
The central argument of western writers is that the US midterm election results represent more than a setback for the Republican Party: they expose the collapse of the bipartisan pro-Israel, pro-war political establishment.
What makes these election results particularly interesting is the argument advanced by several Western political commentators that the defeat was not confined to Republicans. The traditional Democratic establishment, which had consistently supported unconditional military and financial assistance to Israel, also suffered a serious political setback.
For years, both major American political parties operated within an almost unquestionable bipartisan consensus on Israel. Democratic and Republican administrations alike continued providing military assistance, diplomatic protection and political support to successive Israeli governments, irrespective of their conduct in Palestine and the wider Middle East.
The Biden administration was particularly associated with this approach. Former President Joe Biden and his political establishment maintained unwavering support for Israel during Benjamin Netanyahu’s military campaign in Gaza, while continuing to approve weapons transfers and defend Israeli actions internationally. Kamala Harris, who served as vice president and subsequently became the Democratic presidential candidate, also remained within the established Democratic foreign policy framework.
The political establishment repeatedly presented this approach as a defence of democracy and regional stability. However, for an increasingly dissatisfied section of the American electorate, it represented an expensive foreign policy that prioritised overseas commitments over domestic economic and social concerns.
The same establishment also promoted an expansive vision of American global leadership through military alliances, political interventions and initiatives presented as international democratic cooperation. The Biden administration’s Democracy Summits and the rhetoric surrounding the so-called rules-based international order were part of this broader approach.
However, Washington’s credibility suffered because successive American administrations have themselves been accused of applying international law selectively, defending allies when convenient while invoking legal principles against geopolitical opponents.
As foreign policy adviser Matt Duss argued in a January 2025 assessment of the Biden administration’s foreign policy failures, international law increasingly appeared to be treated as an instrument against adversaries rather than a universally applicable standard.
This contradiction is not exclusive to Biden. Trump has also repeatedly faced accusations of violating international law. Nevertheless, the continuity between successive administrations demonstrates that the problem is considerably deeper than the personalities occupying the White House. It concerns the American foreign policy establishment itself.
One of the most significant political messages emerging from the elections concerns the influence of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
For decades, AIPAC and its political network exercised considerable influence over American electoral politics by supporting candidates favourable to Israel and campaigning against those advocating a more critical approach towards Israeli policies.
However, the growing electoral success of candidates openly questioning unconditional support for Israel suggests that the political environment is changing.
Reports of substantial campaign spending against pro-Palestinian candidates, including the reported expenditure of more than $40 million against Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, illustrate the extent to which the Israel question has become a major electoral battleground. His reported electoral breakthrough, despite the financial resources deployed against him, is particularly significant.
As Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, reportedly observed, the old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over.
This does not necessarily mean that Washington will immediately abandon its strategic relationship with Israel. American political institutions, defence interests, lobbying networks and established foreign policy commitments remain deeply entrenched. However, the emergence of candidates prepared to question unconditional military assistance to Netanyahu represents an important political development.
For the first time in decades, the political cost of supporting every Israeli military decision may be becoming greater than the electoral advantage traditionally associated with doing so.
This changing political environment could eventually create space for a more balanced American approach towards Palestine, the occupied West Bank and the wider Middle East. It could also encourage Washington to reconsider the continued supply of weapons that have contributed to the destruction of civilian communities.
The most immediate international consequence of the election results concerns Iran.
According to reporting by Axios, Vice President JD Vance had reportedly advocated an agreement to end the war and privately expressed strong reservations about Netanyahu’s assessment of Iran. Several senior officials within Trump’s administration were also reportedly uncomfortable with the prospect of renewed large-scale military operations.
The reported disagreement was not simply about the timing of military action. It concerned the strategic wisdom of allowing Israel to determine the direction of American foreign policy.
According to the reported account, Netanyahu was considered wrong in his assessment of several aspects of the Iranian confrontation, while Vance warned that the war could carry serious political consequences for Republicans in the midterm elections.
There were also reports that Trump had considered striking Iran before the elections under pressure from Netanyahu but ultimately decided to wait until the electoral outcome became clearer.
This raises a fundamental question: why should an American president allow the strategic calculations of a foreign leader to determine whether the United States enters another major war?
The United States possesses enormous military capabilities, but military superiority does not automatically translate into political victory. Iran has spent decades preparing for asymmetric warfare, developing missile and drone capabilities, strengthening its regional deterrence and preparing for the possibility of a prolonged confrontation.
The assumption that American airpower and overwhelming conventional military superiority could quickly compel Tehran to surrender its strategic positions was always questionable.
The consequences of the confrontation, including the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, the regional security crisis and the enormous expenditure of military resources, demonstrate the risks of underestimating an adversary that has prepared for precisely such a confrontation.
Even after extensive military operations, the political objectives attributed to the American-Israeli campaign remain far more difficult to achieve than its proponents initially suggested.
Regime change has not necessarily followed military destruction. Iran’s strategic institutions have demonstrated resilience, while the country’s missile and drone capabilities and its capacity to impose costs on adversaries remain central considerations.
The reported preparations by the US military for potentially resuming large-scale combat operations, including the deployment of additional military capabilities to the region, therefore represent a dangerous development.
At the same time, Qatari mediation efforts to secure support from Washington and Tehran for a draft agreement offer a possible diplomatic exit.
The question is whether Trump will choose diplomacy or allow Netanyahu’s calculations and the demands of hawkish advisers to determine America’s next move.
The reported position of JD Vance deserves particular attention. Vance has long been associated with an American foreign policy that places greater emphasis on domestic priorities and avoids unnecessary overseas military commitments. His reported opposition to renewed escalation against Iran reflects a broader political constituency within the Republican Party that is increasingly sceptical of foreign interventions.
If the Axios reporting accurately reflects the internal debate, Vance and other senior officials understood that another major military confrontation could damage Trump’s political standing and undermine the Republican Party’s electoral prospects.
The mediators’ reported question to White House officials before the elections is equally revealing: what would Trump do if he lost?
The inability of his advisers to provide a clear answer reportedly reflected the uncertainty surrounding the administration’s strategic direction.
Now that the elections have delivered a serious setback, the situation has become more complicated.
Tehran’s public celebration of Trump’s political defeat may also influence the calculations in Washington. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, reportedly described the electoral outcome as a political defeat for Trump, alongside what he characterised as an Iranian strategic victory in the field and around Hormuz.
Such statements may irritate the American president and strengthen the arguments of those within his administration advocating a tougher military response.
However, a decision to resume war merely to demonstrate political strength or punish Tehran for celebrating an American electoral defeat would be an extraordinary strategic mistake.
The real test of American leadership is not how many bombs it can drop but whether it can achieve its political objectives without dragging an entire region into prolonged conflict.
Another important political development concerns Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose future has reportedly come under scrutiny following the Republican electoral setback.
Hegseth was among the most vocal advocates of military escalation against Iran and represented the administration’s hardline approach towards the use of American military power.
His rhetoric about overwhelming military force, destruction and the elimination of perceived enemies reflected an assumption that American conventional superiority would be sufficient to achieve the desired results.
Yet, the fundamental weakness of this approach was its failure to distinguish between destroying military infrastructure and achieving sustainable political objectives.
Military campaigns can destroy facilities, eliminate commanders and inflict enormous damage. However, they cannot automatically manufacture a favourable political outcome, dismantle a country’s national identity or compel an adversary to abandon its strategic red lines.
The reported failure to achieve the broader objectives associated with the Iran campaign has consequently raised questions about the advice provided to Trump by his military and political advisers.
There have also been reports that Trump has begun questioning Hegseth’s performance and that the defence secretary could become a political casualty of the electoral defeat.
The irony is particularly striking. Hegseth’s supporters promoted an image of uncompromising military strength, while the administration’s critics argued that his approach was taking America towards a conflict whose strategic and economic costs had not been properly assessed.
If the reports about his possible removal prove accurate, it would demonstrate that the political consequences of a failed military strategy do not necessarily remain confined to the battlefield.
Hegseth may have sought to demonstrate American military supremacy through the Iran confrontation, but the political consequences could eventually reshape the leadership of the Pentagon itself.
For years, Washington has presented itself as the principal defender of the international rules-based order. However, successive administrations have weakened that argument through selective interpretations of international law and the use of military power outside universally accepted legal frameworks.
The Biden administration faced serious criticism over its approach to Gaza, while Trump’s administration has faced criticism over its military actions and threats against several countries.
The problem is that international law cannot remain credible if its application depends on whether a country is an American ally or adversary.
The world does not need another demonstration of American military superiority. It needs a United States willing to respect the same international principles that it demands from others.
This is particularly important for smaller countries, which depend on international law, sovereign equality and multilateral institutions to protect themselves against the coercive policies of major powers.
When Washington treats international law as optional, it weakens the very international system it claims to defend.
For Asia, the American electoral outcome carries mixed but potentially encouraging implications.
The region has little interest in becoming another battlefield for great-power competition. Its economic future depends on trade, investment, connectivity, energy security and regional stability.
For years, successive American administrations have strengthened military partnerships and security arrangements involving Japan, Australia, the Philippines, Taiwan and other regional actors as part of their strategy to contain China’s growing influence.
Washington has repeatedly presented these arrangements as necessary for regional stability. However, from Beijing’s perspective, they represent an expanding network of military pressure around China’s neighbourhood.
The same contradiction applies to American policies towards Hong Kong, Taiwan and other regional questions.
China’s economic rise has fundamentally altered the global balance of power. Rather than accepting this development as an inevitable feature of changing international economic realities, sections of the American establishment have increasingly treated China’s rise as a strategic challenge that must be contained through political, economic and military pressure. The consequences of this approach are not limited to China. They affect the entire Asian region.
Countries across Asia need economic cooperation and freedom from unnecessary military confrontation. They do not want to be forced into choosing sides in an increasingly polarised international environment.
A weakened bipartisan pro-war consensus in Washington could therefore create some diplomatic space for a more balanced American approach towards Asia. However, it would be naïve to expect a fundamental transformation overnight.
The American strategic establishment remains influential, and its geopolitical ambitions are not necessarily dependent on which party controls Congress or occupies the White House.
Nevertheless, the emergence of more diverse, anti-war and pro-Palestinian political voices in American electoral politics provides some reason for cautious optimism.
The midterm elections have delivered an important message to the White House: Americans do not necessarily support a foreign policy based on permanent military confrontation, unconditional support for foreign governments or the expenditure of unlimited taxpayer resources on overseas conflicts.
Trump won political support by promising to put America first and stop unnecessary wars. His decision to engage militarily with Iran has undermined that promise and created an increasingly difficult political situation.
He must now decide whether he wants to be remembered as the president who escalated another disastrous Middle Eastern war or the leader who recognised the limits of military power and pursued a diplomatic settlement.
The electoral defeat has also exposed the vulnerability of the old bipartisan consensus on Israel and the declining ability of powerful lobbying networks to guarantee political outcomes through financial influence alone.
However, the most dangerous possibility is that Trump may interpret his electoral defeat not as a warning against war but as a reason to become more aggressive abroad.
A president who believes he has little left to lose politically could be tempted to take decisions with consequences extending far beyond his remaining time in office. Such a calculation would be disastrous for the United States, Iran, the Middle East and the international community.
The world does not need another war to satisfy the political ambitions of Netanyahu, the ideological preferences of hawkish American officials or the domestic political frustrations of the White House.
If Trump genuinely wants to restore his legacy as a president committed to peace, he must listen to those advisers who favour diplomacy, including the reported position of JD Vance, and give Qatar’s mediation efforts a genuine opportunity.
America’s military might have already been demonstrated. What remains to be demonstrated is its political wisdom. Results leave a lesson to White House that winning wars is not about destroying countries, and winning elections is not about starting wars.

sources.news_title: Trump Under Pressure On Iran War After Republicans' Midterms Defeat
sources.text:
- Democrats seize control of both House, Senate.
- US voters angry over high prices, war on Iran.
- Sources say Trump could still replace Hegseth.
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump concedes that the war he ordered on Iran was partly to blame for his Republican Party’s sweeping midterm losses — but even as he comes under pressure, analysts said Wednesday that he has few good options ahead.
It remains to be seen what path Trump will take after emerging politically weakened as Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday’s vote.
The US leader also remains caught between a desire to diplomatically end the war with Iran — which has sharply driven up gasoline costs for American voters — and his threats to “finish it off” with Tehran.
“Trump is now in a bind: Escalation offers no clear path to victory and risks further wrecking his presidency, while diplomacy offers a potential way out,” said Sina Toossi, senior non-resident fellow at the Centre for International Policy.
“The new Democratic Congress will also have significant oversight and funding powers come January, further constraining his options,” Toossi told AFP.
Trump acknowledged Wednesday that “it’s largely true” that Iran and the high fuel prices provoked by the conflict had led to the massive defeat for Republicans.
Still, he maintained, echoing a similar statement after polls closed Tuesday, that he’d “do it again” despite the election hammering.
Vice President JD Vance, a potential contender to succeed Trump in the 2028 presidential election, was more definitive.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a post on X.
A ‘clear’ message
Many American voters cited high costs of living and the Iran war as reasons behind their vote.
For usually reliable Republican voters, like farmers, steep energy costs are “really just leading to despair,” Charles Hall, executive director of the North Carolina Soybean Producers Association, told AFP.
Hall, a North Carolina voter himself, noted huge shifts towards Democrats in his state: “That tells me that they’re voting against something.”
“If they’re farmers, they’re probably voting against high diesel prices,” Hall said.
Tehran retaliated against US-Israel strikes on Iran since late February by blocking off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global energy transit. This sent oil prices soaring.
But Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow James Lindsay told AFP that “the historic drubbing that Republicans took on election day happened for reasons that go well beyond Iran.”
He called the “blue tsunami” a repudiation of much of Trump’s agenda, with the president being elected in 2024 on a pledge to make life more affordable.
“What we’ve seen over the past two years is that Americans believe that life has become even more unaffordable,” Lindsay told AFP. “The Iran war clearly played into that by driving up the price of gas and diesel.”
Adding fuel to the fire, Trump has “often behaved in ways that suggested he was indifferent to the pain and suffering of Americans,” he said.
Toossi added: “The message from voters is clear: They want relief from the war’s economic costs, not more war.”
‘Difficult position’
Already, top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer said on Wednesday that the Iran war “must end,” with prospective Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries echoing a similar message.
But it remains unclear if Trump will listen to voters and try to end the conflict quickly, or push on with it.
“Putting aside the election, doubling down on Iran was always a dangerous strategy,” Lindsay of CFR said.
A new round of intense attacks — even if designed to be short-term — could backfire with Iranians responding by targeting installations across the Gulf.
“This could spiral out of control,” he added, although acknowledging that Trump’s other options “aren’t terribly good either.”
Meanwhile, maintaining the US naval blockade in the Middle East is a strain on the country’s military, while negotiations have so far failed to yield clear progress.
“The president’s in a difficult position regardless,” Lindsay said.
And if Vance’s comments on the war are widely held by other Republican lawmakers, he added, Trump faces new political risks if he were to double down on Iran.
Hegseth doing ‘a very good job’
Trump backed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, a day after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in midterm elections that reflected voter anger over the Iran war.
Asked whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, whom he has described as a champion of the war, Trump told reporters: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.”
The response contrasted with then-President George Bush, who fired Defence Secretary Donald Rumsfeld the morning after the 2006 midterm elections, when voter discontent over the Iraq war helped Democrats win control of Congress.
But sources said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their losses.
— With additional input from Reuters

sources.news_title: Trump’s Iran War Setback Revives America’s Political Lesson: Presidents Who Fail to Deliver Victory Often Pay at the Ballot Box
Donald Trump defends Iran war after midterms loss, says I would do it again
sources.text:
Intense political debate continues following the defeat of President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the United States midterm elections. The blame for this electoral setback is increasingly being attributed to the ongoing conflict with Iran, prompting a major statement from President Donald Trump himself. Trump has clearly stated that if he had to do it again, he would do the exact same thing. Following the crushing defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm elections, President Donald Trump has faced significant criticism from various quarters, with analysts and party members questioning the repercussions of his administration's foreign policy decisions.
Vice President JD Vance statement and Trump response
United States Vice President JD Vance has also explicitly blamed the war with Iran for the Republican party defeat. Following this statement by JD Vance, President Donald Trump has released an official statement regarding the conflict with Iran. Trump asserted that if he had to do it again, he would repeat the same actions without hesitation. Responding to Vice President JD Vance remarks attributing the midterm losses to the war with Iran, US President Donald Trump stated that he can work together with the Democrats, provided they don't adopt a destructive attitude. He noted that they've veto power, which means he doesn't like what they're doing, but added that they've already called and want to negotiate on certain issues.
Justifying the action and petrol price impact
Elaborating further, Donald Trump stated that he thinks it's largely true that the military action caused petrol prices to rise slightly for some time. However, he emphasized that if he had to do it again, he would do the exact same thing because, in the long run, it's the only viable solution. You simply can't allow Iran to acquire nuclear weapons, and there is no other choice available. He mentioned that he had anticipated oil prices would surge even higher, and he took action based on that assessment, while you've no choice, you've to do it, and you can't let Iran have nuclear weapons. Otherwise, everything you see here today might not even exist one day. Reiterating his stance on bipartisanship, he mentioned again that he can work with Democrats if they avoid destructive behaviors, noting that communications have already been initiated.
When will the war end and thoughts on impeachment
When asked when the war with Iran will finally come to an end, US President Donald Trump responded that it can end whenever he wants, but it must be done the right way. He reiterated that they will never let Iran acquire nuclear weapons and the matter must be handled properly. Trump acknowledged that he knew fuel prices would rise, estimating they could go up by two to three times the current prices, but pointed out that prices are now coming down, noting a ten-point drop the day before yesterday. Also, when asked if he's worried about a potential impeachment, US President Donald Trump firmly stated that he isn't worried at all, asserting that if Democrats pursue impeachment, it will completely ruin the Democratic Party itself, questioning what the impeachment would even be for, asking if it would be for being a successful country.

sources.news_title: Trump admits Iran war hurt Republicans, but says he would do it again
sources.text:
Trump admits Iran war hurt Republicans, but says he would do it again
text_fields
Washington: US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to the Republican Party’s poor showing in Tuesday’s midterm elections, attributing the setbacks largely to a rise in petrol prices. He nevertheless defended the military campaign, saying he would take the same decision again to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday at an event marking construction progress on the White House ballroom, Trump was asked whether the conflict had hurt Republicans at the polls.
“I think it’s largely true,” he said, adding that the war had pushed petrol prices higher in the short term.
Despite the political cost, Trump stood by the operation. “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” he said, arguing that Iran could not be allowed to develop nuclear weapons.
Asked whether the war had been worth its electoral impact, Trump replied, “I do, yeah.” He said he had anticipated a sharper increase in oil prices than ultimately occurred.
Trump framed the campaign as a national security necessity rather than an electoral calculation. He claimed that US operations had badly damaged Iran’s Navy, Air Force and air defences, and said oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz had recovered. He asserted that the waterway was now carrying more oil than before the war, though he offered no supporting figures.
Trump also responded to Vice-President J.D. Vance’s assessment of the election results, after a reporter referred to a lengthy post linking the war to the Republican performance.
“I knew the war was going to impact it,” Trump said. He added that he was aware of Vance’s thinking and approved of the post, calling it “good.”
While Trump did not dispute that the conflict had carried a political price, he rejected any suggestion that the election outcome would change his position on preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Asked when the fighting might end, he said the timing depended on achieving the right outcome: “It’s got to be done right.”
Trump dismissed suggestions that his own campaign appearances had fallen short. When asked whether he regretted holding roughly 30 rallies, he said, “No,” and argued that the results would have been different had his name been on the ballot.
“If I were on the ballot, we would have won,” he said, citing the size of the crowds at his events. He added that enthusiasm for him had not fully transferred to Republican candidates: “We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates.”
On working with Democrats after the vote, Trump said he would probably be able to deal with them unless they adopted what he called a destructive approach. He said Democrats had already made contact to discuss issues, while emphasising his ability to veto legislation he opposed. He also brushed aside concerns about a possible impeachment effort, saying that pursuing one without grounds would damage the Democratic Party.
US midterm elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term, determine all 435 House seats, about one-third of Senate seats, and numerous state and local offices.
(Inputs from IANS)

sources.text:
Trump concedes Iran war angered voters — but said he would do it again
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed Republicans’ stunning midterm losses on his unpopular war with Iran, though Trump said he had no choice but to launch the conflict and would do it again.
“It’s largely true because it drove the gasoline [prices] up a little bit,” the president said Wednesday afternoon on the site of his half-finished White House ballroom, his first public appearance since the election.
“At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump added before directing the attention of his aides and reporters to the helipad he had installed on the White House lawn in September. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Though Trump himself made the decision to go to war with Iran — egged on by powerful outside advisers and some aides, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — Trump continued Wednesday to distance himself from the GOP’s losses, which handed the Democrats significant majorities in the House and Senate.
Late Tuesday, he insisted that “if I was on the ballot, we would have won.” [Continue reading…]
